sources.title: Jacky Chou: Clone indie hacker SaaS, outrank them, and diversify across many launches
sources.originalTitle: Jacky Chou: Clone Indie Hacker Apps, Then Outrank Them on Google
sources.outlet: Edward Sturm and Jacky Chou from Indexsy
sources.summary: Jacky argues SaaS is SEO's biggest opportunity because indie hackers are weak at SEO and expose revenue on TrustMRR. He explains building tools from your own needs, validating with cheap Meta retargeting, and parasite SEO with indexers. He also covers off-site focus, buying subreddits, and backing many ventures.

principles.text: Find indie hacker SaaS on TrustMRR, clone it, then out-market and outrank them since they are poor at SEO.
principles.quote: the entire SOP will just go like go on TrustMr, go find some app, out market them, outrank them, bada bing bada boom, you're done.

principles.text: Build software from your own daily pain; other agency owners likely share the same problem.
principles.quote: all my software that I launch, I launch because I have a personal need. And then hopefully other agency owners have something similar.

principles.text: Replace tools you already pay for with a better, cheaper version; people with the same issue will come.
principles.quote: you just replace tools that you already use with something that is better and people will come if they have the same issue.

principles.text: Validate new launches cheaply: share one Meta pixel across sites and spin up a retargeting campaign per launch.
principles.quote: I like to connect the same meta pixel across all my sites and then anytime I launch a new one, I just create a new retargeting campaign and it'll spend like 30 bucks

principles.text: Judge paid acquisition purely by CAC to LTV ratio; study winners' Meta ad libraries and copy their funnels.
principles.quote: it's literally just a function of like um CAT to LTV ratio. It's it's just that ratio. That's all you have to think about and then it's done.

principles.text: Diversify and keep launching many ventures; you can't know which will take off, and winners cover losers.
principles.quote: the winners cover the losers right and it's just like a almost like a portfolio angle.

sources.title: Jacky Chou on SEO after a $500K/month wipeout: link tactics, AI citations, CRO and launching fast
sources.originalTitle: He Made $500K/Month from SEO - Then Google Destroyed His Sites (Jacky Chou)
sources.summary: Jacky Chou explains how he rebuilt after Google wiped out his 15-site partnership business (about $500K/month). He covers white/gray/black hat link building, CTR signals, getting cited by AI, and how he launches and bundles software. He also gives CRO rules for paid landing pages.

principles.text: Never trust a guru's tactic until you've tested it on multiple sites; anyone whose claims fail repeatedly is written off.
principles.quote: you have to always validate it. You can't just like assume that people what people are telling you is the truth.

principles.text: Launch fast, check for product-market fit with your audience, then go all in; otherwise kill the product or leave it on autopilot.
principles.quote: I validate it, make sure there's a product market fit within my audience. If there's a fit, then I go all in on it.

principles.text: Compete in mature software markets by bundling many features under one subscription rather than being best at any one.
principles.quote: It's like the Adobe approach. We just give everything under one subscription.

principles.text: Keep the core money site clean of mass AI content, because blasting thousands of articles exposes you to a destroyed business.
principles.quote: a huge fan of uh spamming hundreds of blog posts on a money site where I need that to like last forever

principles.text: Paid traffic needs a dedicated, stripped-down landing page with no nav, so the only actions are convert or leave.
principles.quote: if you're running paid ads, you need a dedicated landing page. Do not send it to your home page.

principles.text: Consistency beats talent: sticking with one thing daily for 90 days will get most people to $10K/month.
principles.quote: if they stick to anything for 90 days, they're 100% make 10k per month.

sources.title: Jacky Chou on 9 income streams: agency, dropshipping, FBA, content sites and newsletters
sources.originalTitle: Jacky Chou Reveals 9 Sources of Income that Makes Him $160,000/month  // THE TOM WANG SHOW EP. 30
sources.summary: Jacky walks through every business model he has run, with the real numbers, pros, cons and mistakes. Key lessons: use your own assets as case studies to sell services, avoid correlated risk across content sites, and prefer newsletters for their lack of platform risk.

principles.text: Optimize for income that arrives while you're away, not billable hours, even at high hourly rates.
principles.quote: you should be trying to make money when you're out golfing for example or when I'm at the gym money's still coming in. I'll get stripe notifications.

principles.text: Sell agency services by building your own asset as a case study and talking about it openly; clients then come inbound.
principles.quote: I think you should have a case study, so you should build up an asset via SEO and just talk about it. And then clients will just start flowing in.

principles.text: Agencies give great cash flow but margins compress as you add headcount; keep yours deliberately lean.
principles.quote: Pros, cash flow, it's great. You get paid right away. Cons, margin.

principles.text: If clicks are cheap but sales are low, the problem is conversion, not ads or targeting. Fix the site first.
principles.quote: if you have like low cost per clicks on Facebook, it's not the ad problem. It's not a targeting problem cuz people are clicking, they're just not converting.

principles.text: Rolling up many risky assets only diversifies if they use different tactics; shared tactics mean correlated failure.
principles.quote: when the same person operates these 10 different businesses and utilizes the same tactics, the risk is still there.

principles.text: Newsletters are attractive because you own the audience, with no platform dependency, unlike Amazon, Facebook or Google traffic.
principles.quote: I love the business model because there's no platform risk.

sources.title: How Jacky Chou built 13 income streams ($374k in a month): diversification, B2B SaaS, YouTube and LLM SEO
sources.originalTitle: These 13 income streams made me $374,000 last month
sources.outlet: Florian Darroman and Jacky Chou from Indexsy
sources.summary: Jacky Chou explains how he went from $450/mo to 13 income streams, including a $374k month, by diversifying, taking money off the table, and building B2B SaaS for agency owners. He covers YouTube-driven launches, LLM-citation listicles and high-ticket no-brainer offers.

principles.text: Take money off the table and diversify income instead of riding one SEO channel.
principles.quote: if you don't take money off the table just look at my peers in SEO.

principles.text: Build products from a deep problem you understand; others share that problem.
principles.quote: If you have a really strong like deep understanding of something... other people will have that issue as well.

principles.text: Sell to agency owners: high LTV and big switching costs make B2B SaaS sticky.
principles.quote: LTV of agency owners are skyhigh, massive switching costs...

principles.text: When you spot a real opportunity, go all in and deprioritize everything else.
principles.quote: if you see an opportunity, you should like really really go in hard and nothing else should probably matter in that in during that time frame.

principles.text: YouTube can drive the bulk of a software launch's revenue.
principles.quote: when I launched my software company, Local Rank, we did 20K out the gate, right? 90% of that revenue came from YouTube.

principles.text: Make a high-ticket offer a no-brainer by removing risk, starting performance-based.
principles.quote: high ticket, but no-brainer offer. Um, meaning like zero risk. So, in the beginning, I'd do performance-based

sources.title: Jacky Chou on SEO: rank and rent, blogs, and daily YouTube as a funnel
sources.originalTitle: $4M+ SEO Masterclass in 58 Minutes (Jacky Chou)
sources.summary: Jacky Chou talks through his current business mix (local SEO software, display ads, agency, private community) and what is working in SEO now. He covers rank and rent via verified Google locations, careful blogging after Google's crackdown, and daily YouTube content as a trust engine that feeds a paid community.

principles.text: SEO shifts fast and penalties are near-permanent, so pivot quickly rather than clinging to one play.
principles.quote: That's why I think in the SEO space you gota you got to pivot so fast.

principles.text: Daily YouTube builds trust, and a large share of viewers convert into a paid private community.
principles.quote: it kind of proved out doing daily YouTube videos is worth it despite my low numbers cuz like a huge percentage of those people will convert to um a private community member cuz they feel so close to you and they trust you.

principles.text: For local rank and rent, getting a Google location verified is the step that unlocks inbound calls.
principles.quote: What you typically need to do in rank and rents is get a Google location verified. If people want to get into it, just get it get it verified.

principles.text: Local SEO is far easier to rank outside the US, in markets like Australia, Canada, the UK and Germany.
principles.quote: you go to out go outside of the US like Australia, uh, Canada, UK, so easy.

principles.text: Blogs still work, but publish a couple of optimized posts a day, not hundreds, or your domain gets burned.
principles.quote: Try to do maybe one, two posts a day. That's it. Don't do the hundreds of posts a day you see on X.

principles.text: When starting content, post daily and double down on whatever format performs; opportunity inflow alone can justify it.
principles.quote: just create content every day, cuz then it's it's so easy right now to just pop off cuz if you're not dumb and you see like, oh, this video is doing well, this video flopped, just do more of the ones that are doing well

sources.title: Jacky Chou on dropshipping mistakes, Amazon affiliate moves and buying penalized sites
sources.originalTitle: Jacky Chou on Dropshipping Mistakes & Amazon Affiliate Tips
sources.summary: Jacky Chou walks through his dropshipping exit and its biggest mistake, how he sources cheaper from 1688, and why Amazon affiliates should sell their own FBA products. He also covers buying algo-hit sites and expired domains, and hiring operators by buying their sites or giving equity.

principles.text: Once a dropshipping product wins, immediately source it, ship it to a local warehouse and cut delivery to about a week.
principles.quote: if you find a winner you immediately source it ship it to the us or wherever your winners are and then keep in a warehouse so people actually like get their products within a week you know

principles.text: Source from China's domestic wholesale site 1688 (or hire a Chinese speaker) to cut product costs 20-30%.
principles.quote: there's a chinese version of alibaba called 1688 uh it's literally alibaba's chinese version and it's only for chinese people and the prices are like 20 to 30 percent cheaper

principles.text: Amazon affiliates controlling traffic should launch their own private-label FBA products, since Amazon converts far better than a Shopify store.
principles.quote: 1.5 conversion rate on shopify versus like 30 conversion rate on amazon same exact same product

principles.text: Buy sites hit by Google algo penalties: demoralized sellers sell cheap for cash, and fixing speed, design and links often revives revenue.
principles.quote: i absolutely love sites hit with algo penalties it's um okay your viewers might not like this but it's a bit predatory but it plays on the psychology of the seller

principles.text: Judge expired or auction domains by the number of Ahrefs ranking keywords, not DR or backlink cleanliness.
principles.quote: it's always number of ahrefs keywords i don't care about any other metric

principles.text: Find top operators by buying their site and hiring them, and use equity upside to recruit when commission-only fails.
principles.quote: you just buy buy their site and then offer them a job because you like what they're doing right you know like they have a system in place they know how to rank

sources.title: How Jacky Chou monetizes SEO: partnerships, rank and rent, lean teams, personal branding
sources.originalTitle: Jacky Chou - How To PROPERLY Monetize Your SEO Efforts
sources.summary: Jacky explains why he prefers revenue-share partnerships on big authority sites over client retainers and niche sites. He covers rank-and-rent monetization, running paid ads to drive branded search, delegating with an EA, and keeping a team lean. He also argues links matter more than content.

principles.text: Partner with established sites: carve out a subdirectory on their domain and run an affiliate site inside it for a revenue share.
principles.quote: you approach a company where their core product is not display ads or affiliate Revenue so for example you go up to some local newspaper and say Hey yo uh morning son let me let me carve out a subdirectory on your site

principles.text: Revenue-share partnerships align incentives and scale better than retainers, where the math doesn't work.
principles.quote: I think everyone's aligned right because you make more money if they make more money and with retainers it's not so yeah everyone's interests aren't so aligned and also the math doesn't work out for retainers

principles.text: Rank the same keywords across multiple partners, then charge brands for top slots (rank and rent); it can out-earn affiliate.
principles.quote: we make more in rank and rents so like client uh companies paying us to be top slot for like best protein powder then Affiliates

principles.text: Share what you do publicly; it generates inbound deals so you don't have to pitch.
principles.quote: I think I'm able to make this much money because I share and then if you talk more about it the more you get

principles.text: Personal branding pays through deal flow, and most people under-monetize; put an offer at the end of every post.
principles.quote: everyone should have an offer at the end of the at the end of a tweet you know

principles.text: Links matter more than content. Don't believe 'content is king'; build links if you have no partnership.
principles.quote: people who say links don't matter are also idiots like links are everything everything uh so if you don't have a partnership then you need to start building links

sources.title: How Jacky Chou runs 34 content sites and manages risk across a diversified portfolio
sources.originalTitle: How Jacky Chou Makes Over $60k Per Month From a Portfolio of Starter Sites
sources.summary: Jacky explains how he buys starter sites, scales them with content and varied link building, and measures everything by payback period. The core theme is risk management: diversify link tactics, sites and asset classes, and take chips off the table.

principles.text: Judge site purchases by payback period; if it pays back before a core update kills it, you're in the green.
principles.quote: i personally calculate payback periods as like a main metric that i run our projections on so typically i buy sites with a payback period between two to three years

principles.text: Use a different link building mix per site so one link update can't wipe out the whole portfolio.
principles.quote: you're supposed to implement different link building tactics for each site because if you follow the same uh you if you have an sop for link building then if a core update hits all it's going to hit all of your sites

principles.text: Buy starter sites on ahrefs trends alone and move fast; speed of offer and escrow is a competitive edge with sellers.
principles.quote: i push for a speed that's why people actually sell to me because i i move a lot quicker than someone who's gonna be like oh let me take a look at ga

principles.text: Take profit when you feel on top of the world or when a site is too much of your net worth; selling a partial stake works.
principles.quote: it's when you're when you think you don't need to sell that's when you should sell and when it takes up too much of your net worth you should sell

principles.text: Keep sellers as minority-owner operators and give them your resources so they take the business from one to a hundred.
principles.quote: when i buy a business from someone i would keep them on as an operator as like a minority uh you know let's say uh owner and you know have some skin in the game

principles.text: Allocate content by performance: pause new posts on hit sites to fix existing ones, and double down on winners.
principles.quote: if they're hit by the core update i'm i told them to like pause all the articles where we're fixing up the existing ones before we move on to new articles and for the sites that are doing well i we like double down on them

sources.title: How Jacky Chou built niche sites, e-commerce and an SEO agency into a diversified online portfolio
sources.originalTitle: Building an Online Business Empire w/ Jacky Chou (MI286)
sources.summary: Jacky Chou walks through his path from electrical engineering to SEO, a Drop Shipping win that crashed, and launching Far and Away via Kickstarter. He covers Facebook ads, conversion fixes, why e-commerce stores should add affiliate and display revenue, and how niche sites, agencies and e-commerce balance each other.

principles.text: Launch a physical product on Kickstarter to validate demand with little cash and no factory minimums.
principles.quote: all you have to do is go to the factory shoot some beautiful uh videos and imagery and launch on Kickstarter

principles.text: Facebook ads: test many creatives, nail targeting, and burn budget early to mature the pixel.
principles.quote: the key to Facebook ads is one test a lot of different creatives to uh the proper targeting and three is uh maturing your pixel

principles.text: When ads get clicks but no sales, the website's conversion rate optimization is usually the problem.
principles.quote: nine times out of ten uh the websites of the businesses I've taken to look at are absolute garbage and they don't they they don't have proper uh cro in place

principles.text: Add affiliate and display revenue to e-commerce stores, since thin net margins make core growth hard to fund.
principles.quote: I believe all Ecommerce stores should open up different channels of Revenue or revenue streams and that would include display ads and affiliate Revenue as well

principles.text: Require very high gross margins on e-commerce products so ads and shipping don't erase profit.
principles.quote: it's got to be like 70 80 plus gross margins

principles.text: Pair slow-ramping niche sites with an agency for cash flow, so one business going to zero doesn't sink you.
principles.quote: agencies are great for cash flow uh pretty decently high margin business and extremely low risk

sources.title: How Jacky Chou buys, builds and distributes 50+ online businesses (and why he now builds over buys)
sources.originalTitle: The brutal truth about online business acquisitions (from someone who's done 50+ of them)|Jacky Chou
sources.outlet: SMB Deal Hunter by Helen Guo
sources.summary: Jacky Chou walks through 50+ small online business deals, including wins (towing directory, sponsored brand placements) and losses (Amazon rate card removed, commodity web hosting). He argues software has no product moat anymore, so distribution, public building, diversification and taking chips off the table matter most.

principles.text: Software has no product moat now; distribution is what you need, so he leans toward building over buying.
principles.quote: I think there is no product mode at all. Zero at this point in especially in software um zero. We could probably replicate most B2B SAS companies in like a couple weeks max.

principles.text: Plug acquired or new products into your own audience; distribution engine is YouTube, X and newsletter.
principles.quote: pretty much I just plug in my distribution engine and that's what's been working.

principles.text: Rank for a buyer keyword, then charge brands flat fees plus commission; most affiliates don't sell, so they leave money behind.
principles.quote: you can actually go out and reach out to protein powder companies and demand them pay you a flat just to be there like 10K per month plus a super high affiliate commission. Like you are you have all the leverage.

principles.text: Build in niches you know deeply from daily content; your own pain points reveal gaps outsiders can't copy.
principles.quote: my thesis was if I have their pain point and I'm very deep in the trenches on this topic, most people have that as well.

principles.text: Post a video every day without missing; start with short form, then repurpose it everywhere.
principles.quote: video every day without missing. Cuz if you're doing it every day, even if you're not the brightest, you'll notice, oh, this this video has more views.

principles.text: Take chips off the table periodically and don't put all your net worth in one asset.
principles.quote: take your chips off the table periodically. Please don't keep going all in.

sources.title: How Jacky Chou makes money in SEO: affiliate rev-share partnerships, retail rank and rent, and closing the loop
sources.originalTitle: How to make money in SEO with Jacky Chou
sources.summary: Jacky Chou walks through his SEO income streams for 2024. He favors affiliate revenue and rev-share partnerships with struggling funded sites, sells top placements to brands, and expects informational and display-ad traffic to die. Includes tactics for landing a first client and why he's moving toward owning products.

principles.text: Partner with funded sites that can't monetize: do the affiliate content, take a rev share on those commissions only, and piggyback their authority.
principles.quote: it's just piggybacking off of their existing Authority right because if they raise $100 million in VC funding all that spent into PR they have like a huge team before and now if they're struggling they're they're looking for ways to make money and that's where we comeing

principles.text: Once you rank a keyword, sell the top slot to brands in that category for a flat fee plus commission on top of normal affiliate revenue.
principles.quote: if we rank for best protein powder we'll go reach out to the top protein powder companies we'll be like yo pay us 20K a month we'll put you on number one and 50% commissions on top of that and it's like a no-brainer

principles.text: Start partnerships small and local. Big brands won't talk to a nobody, so use businesses you already know.
principles.quote: you should start small you can't start off with a dr90 software company doing like 10 million a year you're like no offense if you're nobody they're not going to talk to you

principles.text: Bet on commercial, trust-driven affiliate content and expect informational content and display ads to be wiped out by AI search and cookie removal.
principles.quote: I think informational content is dead is going to be dead in the next like two years so if you're relying heavily on display ads

principles.text: Against big-publisher dominance, don't compete with a niche site. Partner with the big company instead.
principles.quote: they don't like Niche sites so what do I do in response to that you partner up with one of the big companies and that's what a partnership is right so you fight fire with fire

principles.text: Land a first client by ranking something guaranteed, then pitch the business you already ranked, moving down the list if they don't pay.
principles.quote: you could do like I I've always done when I was young like rank guaranteed um and it's it's quite easy

sources.title: Parasite SEO vs Partnerships: how Jacky Chou runs 50/50 publisher deals and humanized AI content
sources.originalTitle: How To Make $100k+ A MONTH w/ Parasite SEO Partnerships - Jacky Chou
sources.summary: Jacky Chou explains how he uses public parasite SEO as a tester to attract publisher partnerships, then runs 50/50 deals with content ownership and residuals. He covers humanizing AI content, limiting publishing velocity, and monetizing rankings with 40%+ commissions via Amazon.

principles.text: Less-known parasite sites still work until Google notices them
principles.quote: the quote unquote private or less well-known parasite sites that I've tested which I did a video on recently those still work like a charm so as long as Google doesn't know really know about it just yet it's still easy to abuse

principles.text: Standard publisher deals are 50/50 with no negotiation
principles.quote: contracts it's it's always 50/50 there's no negotiation you could probably get away with less

principles.text: Own the content and keep two-year residuals on termination
principles.quote: we own the content to to the stuff we create and we get two-year residuals if they want to terminate

principles.text: Humanize and re-optimize AI content before publishing
principles.quote: we humanize and then reoptimize first so we make sure it passes all AI detector tests

principles.text: Keep publishing velocity modest on partner sites
principles.quote: we've had certain sites partnership sites where we would blast like thousands of Articles a month and then that would get hit really quickly versus where we did like 50 to 100 a month totally okay

principles.text: Monetize rankings at 40%+ commissions, Amazon over custom affiliates
principles.quote: we try to get paid at least 40% commissions on the articles that we rank for and we only go to Amazon all these like custom affiliate guys

sources.title: How Jacky Chou grows Local Rank: community-led funnel, YouTube-first launch and local SEO levers
sources.originalTitle: Local SEO: How to Dominate  Rankings in Just One Week
sources.summary: Jacky Chou explains how Local Rank sells software by first building a paid education community, gating free checklists on X, and using YouTube to launch. He also covers local SEO ranking levers (reviews, citations, CTR) and how to sell local SEO to high-CPC niches.

principles.text: When the market is tiny, educate people to create new buyers (build the TAM) instead of only selling to existing ones.
principles.quote: the local SEO space is so small. It's it's super small. So what we have to do is we have to start educating people. We have to like build the actual TAM.

principles.text: Software with a learning curve sells better through a community that teaches with the tool than by pushing the product directly.
principles.quote: I realized you can't just raw dog push people into local rank. It's like too hard for people to use. So, we have to have a lot of education.

principles.text: Run the paid community at break-even to fund ads; the software upsell is the profit.
principles.quote: we try to run the community at break even and then the software is like the gravy.

principles.text: Talk about a topic on YouTube for a long time before launching; the built audience makes the launch pop.
principles.quote: if you talk about something for a year and then you launch a product about that topic, it's going to it's it's going to pop no matter what.

principles.text: Give away gated free checklists on X: comment-to-get engagement bait, then email capture, VSL, retargeting and a long email flow.
principles.quote: We don't even give we don't even give the template right away. They have to give us their email for us to give them the template. And guess what happens after the sign up? VSSL right away and then hella retargeting

principles.text: Being your own customer (doing the service you sell) creates a product moat that feature-copiers can't match.
principles.quote: we actually do the thing right so like we actually do local SEO what I found is I I I think that's actually our moat

sources.title: Jacky Chou's 10-year path from €450/mo intern to $500k/mo: SEO, dropshipping, partnerships
sources.originalTitle: $500k/mo from SEO (10 YEAR JOURNEY) - Building in Public Day 74
sources.summary: Jacky walks through his timeline from a €450/mo Berlin internship in 2014 to about $500k/mo in revenue. It covers the Indexsy SEO agency, a dropshipping boom and bust, niche site flips, and the partnerships model that drove 2023 revenue. He also answers practical questions on partnerships and rank-and-rent.

principles.text: Keep a steady cash-flowing business alongside risky bets. The agency kept him afloat when dropshipping collapsed.
principles.quote: luckily indexi kept me afloat during this time um shout outs to indexi keeping the lights on

principles.text: Platform-dependent businesses can be wiped out by policy changes. Dropshipping hit Facebook bans and the iOS update.
principles.quote: we got clapped left and right by first Facebook uh updates being uh they were clapping really hard down hard on Drop Shipping sites

principles.text: Exit niche sites before Google algorithm updates hit them, and sell while they are still valuable.
principles.quote: 2023 happened a lot of my Niche sites got clapped to death by Google luckily I was able to exit a lot of them before um algo updates help happen

principles.text: Partnerships with established sites drove huge revenue. Focus on the agency, then find partnerships.
principles.quote: started focusing more on agency side then stumbled upon Partnerships and that drove huge amounts of Revenue into our business

principles.text: In a partnership, run affiliate accounts through your own tracking tag so you control the monetization.
principles.quote: you should set it up it should run through your account use your tracking tag add them as a website on your website list

principles.text: Value your time and buy cheap commodity work like citations instead of doing it manually.
principles.quote: it's five bucks I don't know if if you really don't have five bucks on for citations uh I don't I don't know what to do um I don't I value my time a bit more than that so I just buy the citations

sources.title: How Jacky Chou's income fell from $500k/mo to $200k/mo: revenue-source breakdown and the sprint-on-winners rule
sources.originalTitle: I went from $500k/mo→$200k/mo in a year...😞 - Building in Public Day 355
sources.summary: Jacky compares his revenue sources from a year ago (about $506k/mo) to the current month (about $200k/mo) after a Google hit. He explains the Partnerships/domain-rental push that built the peak, then gives his rules for repeating success: keep testing, don't trust SEO philosophers, and sprint all-in when something works.

principles.text: Don't trust others' claims about what works in SEO; run your own tests properly.
principles.quote: do not take anyone's word for things like oh this works this doesn't cuz most of these guys are just like SEO philosophers when you do a test you have to you run it properly

principles.text: Always be testing; replicating big revenue comes from continuous experimentation.
principles.quote: you have to be always testing right

principles.text: When a test hits, drop everything and sprint at it with the whole team; the rest of the time you can walk.
principles.quote: once something hits you have to push super hard it's kind of like a Sprint like you're kind of walking the whole time kind of checking out you know smelling the flowers and all that but when when something hits

principles.text: If you find something working, cancel other plans and go all in, even on a weekend.
principles.quote: if I found something that's working on Saturday morning bro I'm canceling all my all my uh plans that weekend we we're doing this all in my whole team is dedicated to this right now

principles.text: Set yourself up to monetize luck: luck exists, but preparation lets you capture it.
principles.quote: there's some luck but like you have to kind of set yourself up to mon ize that luck

principles.text: His peak came from leveraging other people's domains via partnerships and pushing it relentlessly with a large team.
principles.quote: I identified the power of Partnerships leveraging like other people's domains and I kept pushing it you guys don't you you wouldn't believe how hard I pushed it

sources.title: How I lost $1M+ in niche site value to Google updates, and what I'd do differently
sources.originalTitle: How I lost $1m+ from seo this year… - Building in Public Day 331
sources.summary: Jacky Chou openly reports his lows: about $1.4M of niche site value went to zero in 2024 after Google updates hit his ecom brand Farway and several sites sharing one Search Console account. His main lesson is to stop talking publicly about a site once it hits meaningful revenue. He also explains why the public posting still paid off through partnership deals.

principles.text: If you report your highs publicly, report your lows too. Honest reporting builds credibility.
principles.quote: I'm a firm believer that if you can report the highs you got to report the lows as well

principles.text: Stop publicly talking about a site once it hits meaningful revenue; attention can attract scrutiny.
principles.quote: I think in hindsight I should have stopped talking about far and away after it hit certain Revenue s like thresholds I should have just stopped mentioning it all

principles.text: Don't keep several sites in the same Google Search Console account; a penalty on one can drag the others down.
principles.quote: it was in the same Google Search Console account in hindsight stupid right

principles.text: Don't ignore small assets just because a bigger one pays more. Small sites carry real value and can be lost too.
principles.quote: I didn't care cuz my Partnerships were making freaking 500k a month why would I care right it was totaling only 20K a month

principles.text: Building in public can snowball. Posting openly about a site brought partnership deals, and being known for partnerships brought inbound brands.
principles.quote: me posting so highly openly about farway got me my first couple partnership deals and with that I was able to run it up to like C couple Mill in profit this year

principles.text: Know when to go quiet while the money is good. Hype and disclosure carry risk.
principles.quote: I think I did most things right I think I just should have just shut up when money was good

sources.title: How Jacky Chou earns affiliate margins via site partnerships (Amazon, Mediavine)
sources.originalTitle: My Affiliate Marketing Revenue EXPOSED (REAL MARGINS) - Building in Public Day 115
sources.summary: Jacky walks through the margins on his partnership model: partners attach sites to his Amazon rate card and Mediavine account, and he takes a cut. He also covers bundling a free indexer into his Revive plan, cold email response benchmarks, and following up relentlessly.

principles.text: Partnerships beat running your own affiliate sites: taking a cut of partner sites adds revenue straight to the bottom line.
principles.quote: I was making like 30k a month on my own sitze before but since I introduced freaking Partnerships that's like Partnerships minus far away sorry 67k extra a month this is straight to the bottom line

principles.text: A partner revenue cut is justified when you deliver measurable uplift; he cites about 40% uplift for partners on his Amazon rate card.
principles.quote: it's worth their cut because we ran the numbers and the uplift is more like 40% in most cases

principles.text: Bundle cheap-to-build features into a top pricing tier by copying the best features of the leading tools.
principles.quote: it's pretty much just a tag on to our product and it was wasn't that hard to develop so we wanted to set it up so we prettyy much just ripped the best features of the top three indexers and just included it into our baller plan

principles.text: Cold email benchmark: 2 to 5% response is decent; under 1% means the copy is bad.
principles.quote: I think anything from 2 to 5% is decent anything like under 1% you're [ __ ] your copy sucks

principles.text: Follow up persistently; don't be ashamed of it, especially when selling to US prospects.
principles.quote: you just got to keep pounding them with follow-ups guys don't be ashamed to follow up there's no nothing wrong with following up

principles.text: Platform fit affects ad RPM: Mediavine performs best on WordPress sites, worse on random CMSs.
principles.quote: Far and Away has the highest RPM because you just use WordPress and media Vine works really well with WordPress

sources.title: Jacky Chou's 2026 online business tier list: agencies and LLM/SEO over affiliate, ecom and gurus
sources.originalTitle: Best Online Businesses to Start in 2026 (TIER LIST)
sources.summary: Jacky Chou ranks online business models in a tier list, from scalable and reliable down to risky and scams. His view: agencies (especially SEO/LLM) are the most dependable, B2B SaaS and consistent YouTube are strong, while affiliate, ecom, blogging, day trading and forex rank low.

principles.text: Any agency is a more dependable business than affiliate marketing in 2026.
principles.quote: Any agency would be better than affiliate marketing at this point.

principles.text: Bundle LLM optimization into SEO pitches; it closes clients because LLM visibility converts so well.
principles.quote: Anytime I have a client in the door, they're like interested in SEO, I'm like, I'll throw in LLM for you cuz it's this basically it's pretty similar. Okay? And we do that and it's game over.

principles.text: Consistency decides whether YouTube works: daily uploads make it the best platform, monthly uploads make it risky.
principles.quote: if you grind, like if you put out YouTube videos every day, I think it's the best platform.

principles.text: B2B SaaS is reliable, but building it without a brand is hard.
principles.quote: B2B SAS. pretty reliable. I'd say that's after I've seen it all. Um, it's hard though without a brand.

principles.text: Influencer income depends on knowing how to monetize the audience, not just having one.
principles.quote: They just need to know how to monetize like eating Vancouver is so easy.

principles.text: Commoditized services like web-design for locals and managed WordPress are hard to sell; the value is in resellable agency work.
principles.quote: So commoditized nowadays. Probably put it below black hat.

sources.title: Rank and Rent: get your first 5 local SEO clients and reach $10K/month
sources.originalTitle: Rank and Rent is the Easiest Money in SEO (Full 2026 Playbook)
sources.summary: A step-by-step playbook for using rank and rent sites as a foot in the door for local SEO agencies: pick a service plus city, build a structured site, run a citation and branded-link sequence, then monetize leads via partners and upsell them into full SEO. Covers pricing math, partner sourcing, and pitching channels.

principles.text: Rank and rent solves the no-proof, no-case-study problem: you own a lead-gen asset that earns while you land SEO clients.
principles.quote: Rank and rents give you a way to get your foot in the door while getting paid because rank and rents, how it works is you basically target a service and a city and you build a site

principles.text: Rank and rent isn't limited to local; national keywords can land five-figure clients, but local is easier to rank.
principles.quote: it doesn't have to be, for example, accountant Vancouver. It could be something as broad as a national keyword such as, I don't know, best protein supplement

principles.text: Build city pages for every service and nearby suburb, even where keyword plus city volume looks low; they capture near-me and long-tail searches.
principles.quote: Don't be so focused on, oh, I don't know. This the the search volume for payroll Roundrock isn't very high, so I'm not going to create that service page. It actually works for generalized keywords as well

principles.text: On new sites, keep link building conservative: only 1-2 branded links a month to the homepage, not exact-match anchors.
principles.quote: one to two links a month only branded to the homepage

principles.text: Operators are the real bottleneck, not leads. Cycle through partners fast and keep the dependable ones.
principles.quote: Issue with rank and rents is not the getting leads part. It's that partners aren't dependable.

principles.text: Use pay-per-lead or monthly rental when starting; save percentage-of-revenue deals for proven closers.
principles.quote: if you're starting out I would not do percentage of sale like I mentioned it really comes down to how good of a business owner they are

sources.title: Local SEO playbook 2026: silo structure and service-area pages for a vet clinic
sources.originalTitle: Why Local SEO is the Easiest Money in 2026 (Full Playbook)
sources.summary: Jacky walks through building a local SEO site for a vet clinic: a silo structure with pillar and sub-service pages, service-area pages for nearby towns, a repeatable location page template, early CRO wins to cut client churn, and Cloudflare hosting.

principles.text: Link every sub-service page back up to its core pillar page so Google sees the silo.
principles.quote: every sub service link back up to this core this core page, right? ... It just kind of communicates to Google like this is your pillar page.

principles.text: Build service-area pages per nearby town and cross-link them to expand your radius beyond what GBP captures.
principles.quote: you're creating around Newark, you should be linking out to another service area page for each location around Newark, right? This helps you expand that radius and capture searches that like your GBP is not going to be able to capture.

principles.text: Unique branded content is the asset nobody can copy.
principles.quote: branded content is your biggest asset when it comes to something that's unique cuz no one can copy that.

principles.text: Front-load the target keyword in the title tag as the first word.
principles.quote: title tag should have um target keyword in the um we like to front-load it. Like it's usually the number like the first word in the title.

principles.text: Do CRO early so leads arrive fast and client churn doesn't hit.
principles.quote: this is how you start getting them leads immediately so churn doesn't hit, you know, 20 to 40% because you're not showing results quick, right?

principles.text: Niche down as an agency instead of being a general marketing consultant.
principles.quote: carve out your niche. Laser focus, I agree. Get it done. Um don't be the general marketing consultant.

sources.title: I spent $10,000 on backlinks across 10 vendors: a link-building case study
sources.originalTitle: I Spent $10,000 on Backlinks…
sources.summary: Jacky Chou tested 10 link vendors (about $1,000 each) on 10 identical 12-month-old domains targeting 800 low-difficulty informational keywords. A PBN provider won, a no-links control beat several vendors, and he explains how he controlled variables and why results are caveated.

principles.text: Control variables in SEO tests: same domain age, same keywords, same content format, and include a zero-link control.
principles.quote: I tried to minimize the variables as much as possible so I use 10 different domains um they're all aged exactly 12 months

principles.text: Test across different vendor types (niche edits, PBNs, guest posts) so you can compare approaches, not just brands.
principles.quote: I made sure to split the budget across different types of Link vendors for example Niche at providers versus pvm providers versus guest box providers

principles.text: Rankings and traffic are what matter, not link metrics like DR; judge vendors by whether they moved the needle.
principles.quote: 22 links uh low Dr but honestly the rankings is what matters went up stayed up 670 per month

principles.text: On low-difficulty keywords, content alone can rank without links; results likely differ for competitive terms.
principles.quote: keep in mind these are low difficulty keywords so I don't think this would be the case if we targeted something more uh with more competition

principles.text: Many vendors show an initial rankings pop that then fades, so judge link results after months, not weeks.
principles.quote: they always pop up initially and then tank and then kind of just stay dead

principles.text: Disclose bias and caveats openly, and challenge critics to run a better test with real money and action.
principles.quote: I'm sure you can poke holes in my case study but here's a challenge for you losers do a better one

sources.title: Link building reality check: when Jacky Chou actually builds links (and when he doesn't)
sources.originalTitle: It’s time to come clean…about link building - Building in Public Day 337
sources.summary: Jacky argues partnership sites on high-DR domains rank with no backlinks, so most link building is wasted effort early on. He only builds links in specific cases: after ranking top 10 (niche edits), for parasite SEO pages, local guest posts, and tiered citations that never point a PBN at your own rank-and-rent site.

principles.text: Partnership sites on high-DR domains rank by publishing content alone, no backlinks needed.
principles.quote: with partnership sites with a highd site all you have to Simply do is get AI to write the content a human to humanize it bada bing bada boom you post it and it ranks that's it

principles.text: Competitive terms are the hard part when your site is new and low authority.
principles.quote: what's hard is to rank for competitive terms like I don't know best CRM software when you're just starting out like let's say dr30 site

principles.text: Buy paid links and niche edits only after you already reach the top 10.
principles.quote: building links paid links like Niche edits guo so on and so forth is only after you hit like top 10

principles.text: Tier your citations with PBNs and never point a PBN directly at your own rank-and-rent site.
principles.quote: tier the citations with pbn do not point the pbn at your own Rank and rents

principles.text: Parasite SEO: point links at a page on a strong host domain and Google can rank it on page one.
principles.quote: when you send links to a parasite Google will value that page on that parasite website so if you have multiple pages on that parasite SEO domain Google will show yours on the front page

principles.text: Local guest posts combined with naked backlinks and map embeds are the best local growth lever.
principles.quote: local links which is just this local guest post it's uh naked back Ling plus maping bed works extremely well it's probably the best way to grow right now

sources.title: How Jacky built and sold a $190K towing directory using Facebook lead ads and a closer
sources.originalTitle: How I Built & Sold a $190K Directory With Facebook Ads - BIP613
sources.summary: Jacky bought a high-traffic towing directory that was under-monetized, added a strong sales closer, and ran one Facebook lead ad campaign (about $25 CAD/day) to fill cold leads. Clients got the exclusive #1 slot per city with call forwarding, a guaranteed call volume, and a free trial. He sold it for $190K.

principles.text: Buy traffic-rich sites the owner can't monetize, then out-monetize them with better sales.
principles.quote: I thought I was like, "Okay, this guy has a ton of traffic. He's not monetizing correctly. I could probably outmonetize him.

principles.text: When inbound leads aren't closing, the fix is a great salesperson, not more traffic.
principles.quote: my strategy was immediately hire a cracked sales guy. All right. And then start generating leads.

principles.text: Sell scarcity: one client per city in the #1 slot, priced high because you own the traffic.
principles.quote: we only take one client per city and that was like insane. I think the most we've ever charged per city was like 2.5k per month and that's cuz we had all the traffic

principles.text: Reduce buyer risk with a concrete guarantee and refund the shortfall if you miss it.
principles.quote: guaranteed 50 calls per month. We are the largest towing directory in America.

principles.text: Use a free trial of forwarded leads to close: they get real leads, and you move on if they don't buy.
principles.quote: we would just start forwarding them leads and if they closed great if they don't close we move on to the next person

principles.text: Keep paid acquisition simple: one Facebook lead ad campaign with a short form and a small daily budget.
principles.quote: it was only $25 spent per day and it was that simple. So, the lead campaign was called Meta Leads.

sources.title: How Jacky Chou made $231.6k in October: revenue stream breakdown and sprint-based income thinking
sources.originalTitle: I made $231.6k in October… here’s how - Building in Public Day 347
sources.summary: Jacky walks through each October revenue source (link building, Amazon affiliate, adult, private community, SEO agency, Levanta and more), what moved the numbers and how durable each is. His core stance: make-money-online niches decay, so earn aggressively in sprints, diversify, and park profits in lower-risk assets.

principles.text: Earn hard in short sprints, then move profits into lower-risk assets, because make-money-online niches don't last.
principles.quote: I don't think the longevity of making money online niches is good hence why you should do it in Sprints so what that means is you trying to make as much money as possible in a short amount of time

principles.text: Selling a differentiated offer nobody else has can turn it into your best seller (local guest posts outsold niche edits).
principles.quote: I think we are still the only ones on the internet doing it

principles.text: Building in public inside a paid community boosts engagement and retention.
principles.quote: why did advice pop off this month it's because I did two things differently one I built the 2K a day uh par parasite SEO site in public in the secret channel

principles.text: Protect revenue with contracts: partners who moved away without paying a share led him to write a partnership contract.
principles.quote: some Partners moved away from us um they refus to pay us a percentage it's okay um yeah hence why I created the partnership contract so we don't get screwed like this anymore

principles.text: Single-platform and traffic-source revenue is fragile; Google crackdowns cut his Amazon affiliate income from ~100k months, so keep multiple streams.
principles.quote: it's not great historically because I think an alltime high I think we've done like 100k months but we've been clapped down heavily

principles.text: Pick affiliate programs by conversion: trusted, high-review Amazon products convert better than sketchy-looking alternatives.
principles.quote: levanta uh converts way better because if you push someone to a 4,000 review uh product on Amazon people would buy that over their like you know fanfi sketchy sites

sources.title: Why Jacky Chou says not to start an affiliate site in 2024 and what to do instead
sources.originalTitle: DO NOT start an affiliate site in 2024 - Building in Public Day 342
sources.summary: Jacky argues affiliate sites are unprofitable after Google's algo changes, which reward high domain authority over authentic content. He lays out a progression: short-term parasite SEO to get a first dollar, then rank and rent, client work, and finally partnerships. He also stresses daily consistency and building content around a hobby.

principles.text: Don't start an affiliate site in 2024; authentic content isn't rewarded because Google favors high domain authority sites.
principles.quote: the answer is hell no absolutely no not reason being it's just not profitable it's not it's not where you SN in your efforts and then you'll get rewarded for it

principles.text: Get your first dollar online via short-term parasite SEO; it shifts your belief about what's possible.
principles.quote: once you make that first dollar online it's just like I think something switches in your brain at least that was what happened for me

principles.text: Follow a progression: parasite SEO, then rank and rent, then client work, then partnerships.
principles.quote: I think you should move into Rank and rent then client work then Partnerships in the long term that should be like your route right now

principles.text: Dominate one local niche: rank for every suburb, take a client per neighborhood, then become the local SEO agency.
principles.quote: I'd become the physio guy in Vancouver I'd be the physio marketing guy in Vancouver I'd take one client from each neighborhood

principles.text: Local rank and rent can reach a few thousand per month and client work in one niche can exceed 10K to 20K.
principles.quote: I am absolutely confident you can get to probably 3 4K a month in rank and rents then with client work you can boost easily boost out up to over 10K I'd say even like 20K from local client work

principles.text: Consistency is the real moat: most people won't do a simple action daily for a year even if it replaces a salary.
principles.quote: if you posted a YouTube video every single day for a year that you could replace your full-time salary would you do it ... the drop off is incredible

sources.title: How Jacky Chou made $261,661 in August 2025 by diversifying revenue and building in public
sources.originalTitle: Revenue Update August 2025
sources.summary: Jacky Chou's August 2025 revenue update ($261.6k across SEO, SaaS, real estate, affiliates). He explains why he diversifies after losing ~95% of $500k/month affiliate and display ad income, and how building in public and doubling down on traction drive growth.

principles.text: Diversify revenue streams to insure against algorithm changes and platform risk.
principles.quote: Diversification is insurance against algorithm changes and platform risk.

principles.quote: Do not rely on a single revenue source because algorithms can change overnight

sources.title: AI content at scale: Jacky Chou's bulk-publish, rewrite-winners SEO process and marketing takes
sources.originalTitle: This Week in Marketing Ep. 1
sources.summary: Jacky Chou explains how he uses AI to publish thousands of People Also Ask posts a day, then has humans rewrite the ones that rank. He also covers topical authority, performance plateaus and branding, creator-led companies, and diversification.

principles.text: Use AI to test keywords at a scale human writers can't afford, then publish in bulk.
principles.quote: creating content, hiring writers gets very pricey at scale. Yeah. So AI enables us to be able to test certain keywords at a crazy scale that we didn't know it was possible.

principles.text: AI content workflow: post in bulk, see what ranks, rewrite those with a human writer, then optimize.
principles.quote: So our current process with AI content is post bulk if rank. Then you rewrite with rewrite it with a human writer and then optimize it.

principles.text: AI content builds topical authority fast, which makes harder commercial keywords easier to rank.
principles.quote: what you can do is build a topical authority very quickly.

principles.text: AI is weak for buyer-intent content; use it for informational queries like People Also Ask.
principles.quote: Buyer intent content? No, it's not great right now.

principles.text: Direct-response ads saturate over time, so large brands need branding campaigns to reach people outside their current channels.
principles.quote: if you run paid ads direct response ads for too long, eventually people will stop converting.

principles.text: Niche site builders rarely diversify income; spread risk beyond a single source.
principles.quote: I think especially in the niche community, diversification is nonexistent.

sources.title: This Week in Marketing Ep. 2: Recency hacks, review interlinking, and the DTC bust
sources.originalTitle: This Week in Marketing Ep. 2
sources.summary: Jacky Chou and James De Lacey trade niche-site and brand tactics: refresh publish dates to jump rankings, interlink a "best X" roundup with individual product reviews, and use YouTube embeds as a ranking flywheel. They also cover the Made.com collapse as a warning on burn rate after the Covid boom, and expected pain for DTC and affiliate revenue.

principles.text: Refresh blog post publish dates every 1-2 months to get a recency ranking jump, then optimize content after the jump.
principles.quote: I typically do it once a month or once every two months. And I change the publish date to most recent date for my blog posts.

principles.text: On a newly bought site, restyle it and set all posts to the most recent date to trigger an initial ranking jump.
principles.quote: I immediately change it to generate press theme, slap on a nice theme, design it nicely, and change all blog posts to most recent date. And that typically gives it a jump.

principles.text: Recency matters most in tech niches; even changing only the date, without content edits, can work.
principles.quote: I don't even change any content. You just changed the date. Yeah. And that pops up immediately. It's, it works extremely well for tech niches because tech's all about recency.

principles.text: Embed long-form YouTube videos in ranking pages: views feed rankings both ways, creating a self-fulfilling flywheel.
principles.quote: you get organic views and if you embed. In your website that already ranks Yeah. Pushes more views and the more views it gets, it ranks higher on YouTube

principles.text: Over-expanding on a pandemic demand spike without cutting burn when it fades is fatal (Made.com sold for $3M after raising ~$135M).
principles.quote: their burn rate was way too high. And now they've gone bankrupt.

principles.text: Expect a consumer slowdown to trickle down to niche sites via ad and affiliate budgets; consider selling some sites and holding the best.
principles.quote: I think I'll try to offload some niche sites in January just for whatever multiples I can. And hold the big ones for a long time.

sources.title: How to sell an Amazon FBA business: valuation, buyers, and what raises the price
sources.originalTitle: How To Sell An Amazon FBA Business
sources.summary: A buyer-first guide to selling an Amazon FBA business. It covers which business types sell (proprietary > private label > reseller), how to value it with SDE and EBITDA, the factors that raise the multiple, who buys at each price tier, and typical sale timelines.

principles.text: Sell from the buyer's perspective; ignoring it leaves your listing sitting for months.
principles.quote: You must always consider the perspective of the buyer. Without putting yourself in their shoes, your Amazon business for sale could sit on the listings for months.

principles.text: Proprietary and private-label products sell far better than reseller businesses, which buyers see as risky.
principles.quote: In this case, only your company sells the product, and therefore, buyers will pay a premium to get it.

principles.text: Keep immaculate, current books; clean P&L records remove a reason for buyers to walk away.
principles.quote: Buyers are often looking for that one reason not to buy your Amazon business. Therefore, having your books in order eliminates at least one reason for the buyer to turn away.

principles.text: Rule-of-thumb valuation: roughly 2x annual net profit (SDE), with inventory bought at cost on top.
principles.quote: The rule of thumb is to take your annual net profit and multiply it by two.

principles.text: Diversify to cut risk: multiple products and niches, traffic outside Amazon, and no single product above 70% of income.
principles.quote: Avoid having one product or niche bringing in more than 70% of your Amazon business' income.

principles.text: Defensibility raises value: proprietary products, brand loyalty, and higher quality than copycats make market share hard to steal.
principles.quote: If you have a patent for your product, your business's value will increase.

sources.title: Link building services: how to vet vendors and which link tactics work vs. get penalized
sources.originalTitle: Link Building
sources.summary: Jacky Chou's SEO essay ranks link-building vendors (Indexsy first, a self-admitted plug) and explains how to vet them. It covers effective link types (niche edits, outreach, broken-link, citations, PR) versus tactics to avoid (PBNs, article directories, volume-based packages).

principles.text: Links from aged, already-authoritative pages beat fresh posts; niche edits on existing content capture that authority.
principles.quote: Since the content exists and has been in existence for months or years, this ensures that you get a link from a page or a post that has aged well and become authoritative in its own right.

principles.text: Treat unusually cheap link pricing as a red flag for low-quality links.
principles.quote: if the price is too good to be true compared to other link-building services, this could be a red flag that they might not be quality links.

principles.text: Vet any link vendor by demanding link samples and case studies before buying.
principles.quote: Always ask for some link samples and some link-building case studies.

principles.text: Big link-building agencies tend to trade quality for scale as the team grows.
principles.quote: Often, the large link-building companies decrease the quality as the team of the size increases.

principles.text: Outreach differs from spam through personalization: target specific blogs and journalists with tailored reasons to link.
principles.quote: The main difference between blogger outreach and spam is personalization, where a good blogger outreach campaign targets specific blogs and journalists.

principles.text: Skip volume-focused backlink packages and PBNs; they are manipulative and do not stand the test of time.
principles.quote: It is an obvious attempt to manipulate the search engine rankings. But unfortunately, most PBN providers will only rent links on such sites, and they will not stand the test of time.

sources.title: Local SEO strategy: the ranking factors and five tactics for winning the local pack
sources.originalTitle: Local SEO Strategy
sources.summary: A practical guide to local SEO built around Google's three local signals (relevance, prominence, distance). It covers key ranking factors (NAP consistency, localized content, local backlinks, schema) and five tactics: Google Business Profile, citations, website optimization, content, and customer reviews.

principles.text: Local rankings come down to three signals: relevance, prominence, and distance. You can't change distance, so win on the other two.
principles.quote: Although it’s impossible to change your physical distance from the searcher, a great local SEO strategy can assist your company in matching Google’s other ranking criteria

principles.text: Keep NAP (name, address, phone) identical everywhere; inconsistency makes search engines doubt you're legitimate.
principles.quote: All local businesses should observe this since an inconsistent NAP can confuse search engines, which could lead them to think you are not legitimate or have multiple businesses.

principles.text: Claim and fully fill out your Google Business Profile first; it's the cheapest, highest-leverage local move.
principles.quote: A Google My Business (GMB) page should be at the top of every business’s local SEO to-do list because it is the simplest approach to promoting brand awareness.

principles.text: Audit your citations by searching your NAP, misspellings and wrong addresses to find inconsistent or duplicate listings, then fix them.
principles.quote: You can also use methods like misspelling your brand name, typing a slightly different address than the real location, or finding duplicate listings to help figure out your inconsistent citations online.

principles.text: Reviews are a top-three local pack factor; ask for them through many channels and respond to every one.
principles.quote: To get into the local pack, you’ll need customer reviews, which are one of the top three ranking variables.

principles.text: Write content about your whole industry and area, not just sales pitches, to position yourself as the local authority.
principles.quote: Instead of looking for ways to sell your products and services, when writing content, choose a topic that represents your business as a whole.

sources.title: SEO for private equity: an on-site, off-site and technical playbook
sources.originalTitle: SEO for Private Equity
sources.summary: A generic SEO checklist for private equity firms. It leans on one stat (SEO leads close at 14.6% vs 1.7% for outbound) and then covers keyword research, on-page basics, backlinks, local and reputation, and technical hygiene. Mostly standard beginner SEO with little original insight.

principles.text: SEO leads close far better than outbound leads because inbound searchers already have intent.
principles.quote: SEO leads have a 14.6% close rate, compared to outbound leads, with a 1.7% close rate

principles.text: Target long-tail keywords: less competitive and more likely to convert into leads.
principles.quote: Long-tail keywords are the more specific phrases that are less competitive and more likely to convert into leads.

principles.text: Optimize content with target keywords but never stuff them; structure it so it is easy to scan.
principles.quote: Include your target keywords and phrases in your content, but avoid keyword stuffing.

principles.text: For backlinks, prioritize quality over quantity: a few reputable links beat many low-quality ones.
principles.quote: It is better to have a few high-quality backlinks from reputable websites than a large number of low-quality backlinks.

principles.text: Prospects research a firm online before committing, so monitor and manage your reputation and reviews.
principles.quote: potential investors will often research a private equity firm online before investing.

principles.text: SEO is ongoing: monitor and adjust the strategy regularly rather than set and forget.
principles.quote: SEO is an ongoing process, and it’s important to monitor and adjust your strategy regularly to stay ahead of the competition.

sources.title: Negative SEO: attack types, why they rarely work now, and how to defend your site
sources.originalTitle: Negative SEO
sources.summary: Jacky Chou explains what negative SEO is, the main attack types (link farms, fake link-removal requests, hacking, heavy crawling, duplicate content, fake reviews), and why Google's Penguin 4.0 makes link-spam attacks far less effective. He gives a monitoring and defense checklist: traffic and Search Console alerts, backlink audits, disavowing, securing admin logins, and site speed.

principles.text: Negative SEO works far less than it used to, but it isn't zero risk; monitor rather than assume Google handles it.
principles.quote: While negative SEO can still work, it is far less of an issue than it was some years back.

principles.text: Google now devalues link spam instead of penalizing whole sites, so link-farm attacks mostly fail.
principles.quote: Rather than devaluing whole websites, Google now devalues link spam.

principles.text: Defending against negative SEO means watching your whole online presence, not just backlinks.
principles.quote: It is now necessary to monitor your complete online presence and implement good security measures to keep negative SEO attacks at bay.

principles.text: Detect attacks early by tracking organic traffic and Google's notifications; faster detection means less damage.
principles.quote: The sooner you learn about the negative SEO, the sooner you can respond and mitigate the harm.

principles.text: Audit your backlink profile regularly and keep your disavow file updated for toxic links you can't remove.
principles.quote: If you receive fresh harmful backlinks that you cannot delete, update your disavow file regularly.

principles.text: Harden admin access and run regular site audits so hackers can't inject spam, alter redirects or robots.txt.
principles.quote: Hackers usually need administrator access to interfere with your site, and by adding extra layers of protection, you can substantially minimize the chances that they'll be able to break in.

sources.title: Buying backlinks in 2026: why brands do it, how to vet vendors, and what drives price
sources.originalTitle: Buy Backlinks Online
sources.summary: A practical SEO essay on paid link building: brands buy links to save time and keep pace with competitors, safety depends on vendor quality, and price is driven by link quality, niche, and brand strength. Fairly generic, with some self-promotion of Indexsy's niche edits.

principles.text: Brands buy links mainly to get faster results and to save time on outreach.
principles.quote: There are two major reasons that a brand will seek link building services – to get faster results and to save time.

principles.text: Competitor link buying can force you to match it just to keep a level playing field.
principles.quote: If your competitors are buying high-quality backlinks to rank high on Google and other search engines, you may be forced to include that SEO service to have a leveled playing field.

principles.text: Avoid cheap, irrelevant, non-niche links such as PBNs; Google can detect them and they hurt your profile.
principles.quote: When buying links avoid the low quality, cheap, irrelevant, and non-niche specific backlinks.

principles.text: Only work with link vendors who have a proven track record and protect your site.
principles.quote: Only trust brands that have proved track records, show integrity, and are committed to helping you gain a competitive edge without compromising your website.

principles.text: Link prices rise with how lucrative the niche is (e.g. finance costs more than gardening).
principles.quote: Any niche that attracts a fast flow of money translates to more expensive links and vice-versa.

principles.text: Backlinks work as votes of confidence signaling authority, so quality matters more than whether paid or natural.
principles.quote: Since backlinks are a vote of confidence on your website, it sends positive indications on Google bots that you have some sort of authority in your industry.

sources.title: Guest Posting SEO: goals, qualifying sites, pitching, and avoiding penalties
sources.originalTitle: Guest Posting SEO
sources.summary: Jacky Chou's beginner guide to guest posting as an SEO and growth tactic. It covers setting goals, finding and qualifying sites, pitching, writing, tracking results, and spammy practices that risk Google penalties.

principles.text: Set a clear goal for each guest post (leads, sales, backlinks, traffic, awareness). Not every post has to be only about links.
principles.quote: not every guest blog post must solely focus on obtaining backlinks.

principles.text: Qualify guest post sites: real traffic, good authority, quality content, and not built just to sell links.
principles.quote: The site should be created for more than just accepting guest posts. If every published post has outbound links to random websites, it was most likely designed to sell links.

principles.text: Find opportunities by copying competitors' backlinks, contacting influencers, and using search operators.
principles.quote: Checking the competitors’ backlinks and trying to secure guest posts on the same sites

principles.text: Customize each pitch to the site and say how the owner and readers benefit and how you'll promote the post.
principles.quote: Your guest post is more likely to be accepted if your pitch is well-crafted and customized to the site.

principles.text: Keep links few and relevant: one author-bio link, a few contextual links, natural anchor text, no keyword stuffing.
principles.quote: Including a half-dozen backlinks in the main body of the guest blog post is another sign that you are attempting to manipulate it.

principles.text: Track traffic, leads, authority and rankings from each guest post, then use the data to improve the next one.
principles.quote: By monitoring these metrics, you can assess your guest blogging campaign’s effectiveness and make adjustments.

sources.title: How to get SEO agency clients: 12 lead-gen tactics from Jacky Chou
sources.originalTitle: How to Get SEO Clients
sources.summary: A practical checklist of twelve channels and tactics an SEO agency can use to generate leads and win clients: directories, free audits, niching, forums and Q&A, social, speaking, pillar content, LinkedIn, partnerships, packaged pricing, testimonials, and email outreach. The theme is to show expertise, reduce risk for the buyer, and build trust before asking for money.

principles.text: Offer a free audit to break the ice and show prospects how badly they need SEO help.
principles.quote: An average SEO client may understand they need help but do not know how badly or urgently they need the services. A free audit can clue them in and provide an excellent opportunity for you to explain how your company will help them fix things.

principles.text: Target neglected local businesses with free audits; results lead to repeat work and referrals.
principles.quote: Most companies, especially local businesses, overlook SEO and do not bother to update their websites often.

principles.text: Niche down to stand out in a crowded SEO market, based on your expertise or profitable opportunities.
principles.quote: One of the good ways of doing this is narrowing down your niche. For example, you can opt to deal with a specific SEO industry based on your expertise or where you see potential profitability opportunities.

principles.text: Show up where prospects ask for help and answer questions to build trust, even if they won't pay at first.
principles.quote: Basically, you will help people with SEO issues they address on these platforms. This way, you will show your expertise, eventually building trust with a potential client.

principles.text: Publish pillar content consistently; it compounds into keywords, backlinks and engagement that bring leads.
principles.quote: The best part is that if you keep posting content regularly, you practically provide your audiences with new content, keywords, backlinking, social media engagement, and so on.

principles.text: Publish transparent monthly packages and gather testimonials; pricing clarity and social proof win prospects over competitors.
principles.quote: Price packages will improve the chances of potential clients choosing you over competitors without transparent pricing packages.

sources.title: AI SEO: where AI helps with content and optimization, and the human review it still needs
sources.originalTitle: AI SEO
sources.summary: Jacky Chou's guide to using AI for SEO: keyword research, link building, content generation, voice search and analytics prioritization. AI saves time and cuts manual errors, but output still needs human review and personalization. Google penalizes low-value content built to manipulate rankings, not AI origin itself.

principles.text: Google judges AI content on value to the reader, not on whether AI wrote it.
principles.quote: the origin of the content is not an issue; the problem is if the generated content lacks quality and has been created to manipulate the search algorithm.

principles.text: Never publish AI content without a human checking spelling, style, tone, structure and context.
principles.quote: AI content published without a human checker

principles.text: Add your own expertise, experience and brand voice; that real-world perspective is what makes content credible.
principles.quote: Your perspective and real-world experience are what give your content value.

principles.text: AI speeds up keyword research: trends, new ideas, competition analysis and long-tail terms.
principles.quote: AI-powered tools can help creators to identify specific and relevant long-tail keywords which are effective in driving targeted traffic to your website.

principles.text: Use AI to prioritize SEO work: a few high-impact recommendations beat hundreds of low-value tasks.
principles.quote: It is more compelling to offer three recommendations that will greatly boost the website’s statistics.

principles.text: Optimize for voice search by answering the questions people ask; assistants return only one top answer.
principles.quote: voice assistants give one answer only, which is the one at the top of the SERPs.

sources.title: How to become an SEO specialist: Jacky Chou's 7-step path (learn, build a site, specialize)
sources.originalTitle: How to Become an SEO
sources.summary: A beginner's roadmap to becoming an SEO specialist. It covers how search engines work, the three ranking factors (relevance, authority, value), the four SEO categories, then learning by building a real site, specializing as a T-shaped SEO, and showing results in a portfolio.

principles.text: Learn SEO by building a real site and doing the work, not by reading theory alone.
principles.quote: nothing beats getting your hands dirty and working to improve a site’s ranking.

principles.text: Don't over-optimize minor factors before you control the big ones: relevance, authority and value.
principles.quote: Ensure you control significant elements before worrying about page speed and title tags.

principles.text: Match search intent: the page must deliver what the searcher actually expects, not just the keyword.
principles.quote: Optimization for search intent means responding to the “why” behind a user’s search.

principles.text: Authority mostly comes from building more quality, relevant backlinks, which Google treats as votes of confidence.
principles.quote: Google values links as votes of confidence.

principles.text: Pick keywords with traffic potential and business value that aren't overly competitive.
principles.quote: A good rule of thumb is to go after keywords that can drive traffic to your site if you rank well for them (this is known as “traffic potential”), carry “business value,” or have the potential to bring in new clients, and are not overly competitive.

principles.text: Become T-shaped: go deep in one SEO area while understanding the whole field, and choose a niche that breaks even and holds your interest.
principles.quote: A T-shaped SEO expert is strong in one area yet has a comprehensive knowledge of all things SEO.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Jacky argues SaaS is SEO's biggest opportunity because indie hackers are weak at SEO and expose revenue on TrustMRR. He explains building tools from your own needs, validating with cheap Meta retargeting, and parasite SEO with indexers. He also covers off-site focus, buying subreddits, and backing many ventures.

chunks.heading: Cloning indie hacker SaaS apps and outranking them
chunks.text:
- Jacky says the biggest SEO opportunity right now is SaaS, a "beautiful industry" with very high margins, because "indie hackers are terrible SEOs." They follow LLM advice and are some of the worst SEOs.
- The SOP: go on TrustMRR, find an app that shows its revenue, out-market it and outrank it.
