- Indie hackers publish their MRR on TrustMRR, so they make themselves targets. Jacky notes they usually rank for nothing, especially for what they do.
- Example: for an AI interior design app (a wrapper), he would one-shot the build overnight, then rank for "best AI interior design app" with guest posts, parasites or other tactics.
- Do it times 10. To be "extra spicy," launch multiple versions of the same app. Disclose per FTC rules; he says it is legal and still converts.
- Indie hackers all launch the same thing (social media schedulers, meta description checkers, robots.txt/noindex checkers) by ripping whatever Peter Levels, Marc Lou or Jack Friks launched. They blast a site with 1,000 articles, get hit, then say "SEO didn't work for me."
- Anyone who actually does AI SEO and builds a tool will make something "infinitely better" than what indie hackers ship.
- He credits indie hackers with great paid-ad funnels: $300-400K per month does not come organically. To launch an SEO software company, study their Meta ad library and roll it out on YouTube and Meta.
- He finds TikTok buyers weak and the targeting worse than Meta.

chunks.heading: How Jacky picks and validates software ideas
chunks.text:
- He builds software from his own tool stack and personal need: "all my software that I launch, I launch because I have a personal need," assuming other agency owners have the same problem.
- Example: he paid keyword.com $600 a month for rank tracking, then vibe coded his own tracker. He launched it as a bring-your-own-key lifetime deal and sold about 100 licenses.
- To validate, he reuses one Meta pixel across all his sites. For each new launch he creates a retargeting campaign that spends about $30. If there is demand, it converts.
- For the lifetime deal, Meta ads pulled in about 15 sales for a little over $100 spent.
- His audience overlap is high because most of his software is in SEO and sold to SEO agencies.
- If a competitor survives on a $600 a month subscription, the market must have a wide base (a fat margin). The rest is a CAC-to-LTV ratio.
- Ideas for SEO agency owners: all-in-one client reporting; proposal software (he saw one on TrustMRR doing about $10K a month).
- He launches roughly once a week and runs about four AI coding threads in parallel. He argues anyone can build now, and marketers have the edge because engineers have "zero creativity."
- His goal is to plug AI into each app so it generates ads, runs prospecting ads and iterates once traction shows. He says he is nearly there.
- If he started over awkward and without sales skills: consumer software, driven by ASO and SEO. He took an iOS app from 0 to $1K per month in one month with only SEO, solo. He prefers iOS over Android because Apple users convert better.

chunks.heading: Diversifying income streams
chunks.text:
- Jacky says his income from 2-3 years ago is gone. Display ads went away, and Amazon affiliate fell from roughly $300K to about $30K, "a 90% haircut."
- If he had gone all in on one venture then, he says he'd be at about $10K per month today. Hence he keeps launching and diversifying.
- He calls himself the "Thanos of moderate success" (his podcast co-hosts' joke). He launches non-stop and focuses on whatever hits.
- Winners cover losers, like a portfolio. His Reddit marketing tool started at $20-30K per month and is now under $4K. Local Rank went to $50-60K per month and is now about $30K. Index Checks grew 70% month over month last month (absolute revenue not shared).
- His advice: don't buy one domain and give it one shot. Expect to fail multiple times.
- On launching: don't over-engineer. Find out whether others share the problem and whether you can market to them.
- Marketing is now "a skill issue" and mostly about creatives. He says AI closing the marketing feedback loop (generate ads, analyze, iterate) could be "game over" for marketers. He estimates one to two months of leeway, and says now is the time to sprint.

chunks.heading: Affiliate, display ads and mom-and-pop sites
chunks.text:
- Display ads are not dead, but only large publishers and influencers remain. A friend at a Raptive meetup says only big influencers there still make $50-100K per month in display ads, driven by their own social traffic.
- Informational keywords are gone to AI Overviews. His example: "my dog ate chocolate" is answered in the overview, so nobody clicks the blog.
- Affiliate is still alive and a good portion of his income. "Best XYZ" money is there even in industries with AI Overviews and Google Ads, because people still click organic results.
- Display ads and affiliate are not mutually exclusive. Keywords like "berberine supplement side effects" can still carry ads.
- Small blogs at DR 20-30 can't rank for listicle keywords, where most affiliate money sits.
- He checks only daily revenue. If he sees a down day he goes to rank trackers, then Search Console, and GA last.

chunks.heading: Parasite SEO, indexers and ranking tactics
chunks.text:
- He is very bullish on parasites right now. They rank almost instantly, especially with instant indexers that get a URL indexed within about 5 minutes. Then you validate with likes and CTR signals.
- Parasite pages sit deep in a host site with weak internal linking, so without an indexer they never get indexed.
- To keep them ranking, send user signals (CTR, Chrome signals) continuously.
- A trick: 301 dead, penalized domains to the root username URL on a social platform (e.g. linkedin.com/jackie), letting it flow down into the post, which keeps the post stuck longer than pointing at the post directly.
- He does not use social media parasites himself (too weak for his competitive B2B niches). He has private, exclusive deals with high-DR publishers, 50/50 performance splits with nothing paid upfront, and says publishers still contact him.
- Economics: the best parasite placements cost $500 to $5K per month, paid upfront with no ranking guarantee. His targets are KD 80+ keywords, not zero-KD ones. Some placements fail, and winners cover losers.
- Listicles remain the core tactic, for Google and for ChatGPT. Find domains already ranking or cited, and pay them. "Everyone is open to it." Many are glorified content farms making little money.
- For ChatGPT: vary titles, don't repeat "best X 2026" 100 times, and don't always rank yourself #1. Place yourself in the top 1-3 of a top-10 list.
- LLMs no longer rely on Google's index as much (Anthropic always had its own, ChatGPT and Google have diverged). He says what ChatGPT cites is "pure trash" and easy to abuse because its spam filters are new.
- He is also bullish on buyer's guides over listicles, as a one-to-one relationship that adds fewer competing entities.
- His mistakes list: do not publish 1,000+ pages in a day, or a million programmatic URLs. Google hates it.

chunks.heading: Starting SEO: Jacky's framework
chunks.text:
- "Learn by doing." Stop reading, iterate, and feel how the algorithm responds. He dislikes "SEO philosophers" who parrot Google's recommendations and don't practice. LLM-fed SEO advice comes from white hat in-house people at DR90 sites.
- If a site is penalized, don't dwell. It is hard to recover from an algo penalty, so move to a new domain. He jokes about 301ing the old one to a competitor.
- He prefers partial-match domains over exact match. His example: "Local Rank" tracker for "local rank tracker," since the two names differ by one word and confuse Google's entity matching.
- He would not focus on the main site for the first three months. Go offsite instead: paid (Meta), parasites, and guest posts on sites ranking for keywords tangential to your industry. Example: pitch a "best local rank tracker" article on a site that ranks for best SEO software.
- He is "so against" on-site SEO in 2026 because offsite gives more swings, and he wouldn't run aggressive tactics on his own site since Google is "waiting for an excuse."
- Google's response to AI slop: it can only favor high-authority sites (Forbes, etc.), which are harder to abuse but still buyable (a Forbes article for about $2K). So the winner is whoever has the largest wallet. He says Forbes is still safe from penalties partly because of its Google Ads spend.
- Sites hit by site reputation abuse (e.g. Outlook India) moved to a subdomain and left their guest posts behind.
- He regrets going so public about spamming Reddit, which may have cost him revenue.

chunks.heading: Reddit strategy and buying subreddits
chunks.text:
- Reddit marketing is much harder now. Accounts need dedicated mobile IPs, and bans are quick.
- His preferred play: buy aged, active subreddits instead of farming accounts. Rank irrelevant subreddits for any keyword as long as they have members and activity (e.g. buy a fashion subreddit and rank it for "best SEO company").
- A black market exists. Prices he has seen run from about $5K for a small subreddit up to $50K. He would pay up to $50K for high-risk software niches and $50-100K for supplements. Gaming subs are far pricier ($500K-$1M).
- Pricing is "whatever you're willing to pay." Assess the mod team: New York mods won't sell for $20K, but mods in South Africa or in financial trouble might.
- He is not much into Reddit now and focuses on Google and LLMs.

chunks.heading: Choosing a niche and consumer vs. SEO products
chunks.text:
- He says SEO in consumer niches is "way easier," "a walk in the park," compared to ranking digital marketing keywords.
- He has two consumer brands outside marketing.
- Rank and rent is tough for introverts because ranking is easy and selling is the hard part. He is "terrible" on sales calls.
- Fit the business to your strengths: charismatic people can do agency; awkward or engineering-minded people should do SaaS.
- Within SEO, pick narrow tool niches like indexing and rank tracking rather than competing with Semrush or Ahrefs. Many "SEO influencer" indexers are just API calls to other providers.
- Index Checks sees heavy fraud: stolen cards used to buy credits and burn through them, one person tried about 40 cards a day.
- He suggests the "Nord tactic," named after NordVPN owning many VPNs that top every listicle. Publish a listicle and build every tool on it, each with its own brand and backend, with FTC disclosures. People still buy.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Jacky Chou explains how he rebuilt after Google wiped out his 15-site partnership business (about $500K/month). He covers white/gray/black hat link building, CTR signals, getting cited by AI, and how he launches and bundles software. He also gives CRO rules for paid landing pages.

chunks.heading: Software launch and validation approach
chunks.text:
- Jacky pivoted toward software after seeing "the writing on the wall" for SEO and niche sites. He now focuses on local SEO, Reddit marketing and link building.
- He launches fast. Local Rank launched in about 2 weeks and Tracking's in about a week.
- Validation is revenue-based: he checks conversion rates and whether there is audience alignment with the product.
- Benchmarks: Tracking's did about 20K in its first week. Local Rank did 10K in its first month.
- If there is product-market fit, he goes all in. If not, he either kills it or puts it on autopilot.
- Examples of duds still making money on autopilot: a WordPress hosting service and a couple of WordPress plugins at about a grand a month each. They take zero bandwidth.
- He does not look at TAM. He launches in mature spaces and checks whether competitors exist.
- His tactic is bundling, "the Adobe approach": everything under one subscription at the same price.
  - Local Rank bundles GBP posts, review boosting, citation building, a lead source and an audit.
  - The rank tracker is slower than competitors (about double the time) and is given away free as a bonus.
  - "We're not like the best product in any category, but we're just like the only one that's like good enough."
- He works with a co-founder who ships software quickly, and he now always partners with someone who executes.
- On his software money sites (e.g. Local Rank) he does no link building and no AI content spam. Local Rank has about three blog posts.
- He says people blasting thousands of articles a month "have not seen pain before."

chunks.heading: Risks of black hat SEO and public income reporting
chunks.text:
- Jacky reports his numbers publicly every month and has not missed one in about 3 years.
- He deliberately stopped reporting his organic SEO income after a public hit. He had 15+ partnership sites with legacy newspapers (affiliate subdirectories, like forbes.com/advisor but for smaller papers), making upwards of 500K/month.
- Google found them and destroyed the subdirectories overnight, dropping revenue from about 500K to about 80K per month in roughly 2 weeks. He had blasted thousands of articles a day for months.
- The Search Console properties of all 15 were hit. Client sites where he did not own Search Console were not hit.
- He pulled the plug rather than risk the newspapers' core businesses.
- His lesson: when something big works, "sit on my hands" and make as much money as possible instead of announcing it. Announcing brought partnership flywheel inbound, but wins can disappear within a week.
- On haters: they usually never stuck with one thing and were burned by gurus. He says that if anyone sticks with something for 90 days they make 10k/month, and that 30 minutes a day of cold calling for 90 days would replace a full-time job. He also claims posting every day for 100 days changes your life.

chunks.heading: Link building tactics by risk level
chunks.text:
- **White hat (digital PR):**
  - Take public government data and make it visual in Canva.
  - Post it to r/dataisbeautiful with your URL as the citation, and buy upvotes.
  - Pick a controversial angle, e.g. Canadian housing: median wage vs housing prices, "30 years to get your first down payment." Post it to a Canadian subreddit with about 500 upvotes and reporters pick it up the next day.
  - He admits it is arguably gray hat.
- **White hat (citations):** hand-register citations (Crunchbase, Yelp, Foursquare) for any new site, even non-local ones.
  - His service uses VAs with AI, because sites like Yelp have hurdles. Some sites are 100% AI, some need minimal intervention.
  - He hand-wrote a 65-point local checklist before ChatGPT.
- **Black hat:**
  - PBNs still work. Tiered links are great.
  - Anyone saying "PBNs don't work" or "citations don't do anything" gets written off entirely.
  - Canonical or hreflang buffer: build backlinks to alternate-language sites (e.g. Spanish and German) that point to your main English site, and don't link to the English one. Canonicals and hreflangs don't pass on penalties right now, as he sees it. Used in his private community SEO contest (made-up keyword, prize about a couple thousand dollars).
  - Unclappable high-DR domains: Amazon, Facebook, Reddit. He says Google doesn't penalize DR90+ sites.
    - Build your own subreddit: about 5 posts a day with about 10 comments per post, bought, to look active.
    - Facebook groups are starting to rank like Reddit.
    - Redirect penalized or deindexed domains to a subreddit and republish the old articles there. He says penalties are domain-side, and content that once ranked still ranks.
  - Amazon listings are the easiest thing to rank on Google. Send traffic and build backlinks.
- **Parameter indexing:** when a site has no noindex on search pages, you can force-index a search-result URL with an anchor-text-laden link and make it ranking (the Disney Plus example). This is common for selling OnlyFans or phone numbers.
- **Negative SEO:** he won't do it, and says disavow only if you know a penalty exists. If he had to, he'd churn and burn by pointing about 100 PBN links with exact-match anchors at the target page, which rises then drops.
- He thinks Google engineers are focused on AI products, so organic algorithm changes are few right now.

chunks.heading: CTR manipulation and Browser Blast
chunks.text:
- Jacky still does CTR manipulation. He says Google gets its data from Chrome (already confirmed), so Chrome signals still move rankings.
- Traditional proxy-based CTR software no longer works.
- What works now is cheap real human traffic, e.g. from adult sites, sent directly to the URL. He calls his service Browser Blast.
  - It imitates virality: about 10k sessions from 10k users worldwide.
  - It is direct referral traffic, not branded searches.
  - He has tested it across many niches, including casino.
- DIY test: run Meta ads to the specific URL, targeting Chrome users, for 10k sessions. If the page is in the top 3 pages, he says rankings go up. He claims Browser Blast is cheaper than Meta ads.
- AI mode and citations: Google AI mode pulls citations from top-ranking Google articles, so ranking still matters even if clicks fall.

chunks.heading: Rank and rent, retail rank and rent, and where SEO still works
chunks.text:
- **Rank and rent:** rank a site (e.g. a Vancouver tree services site) and sell leads at about 100 per lead, or rent it for about 1,000 a month.
  - SERPs now show 4 ads, an AI overview, the map pack, then organic. Little traffic remains except in rural areas without AI mode or ads.
  - He only recommends it if you can get a Google My Business profile. Ranking GBP is "infinitely easier" than organic, and you can rank local within a week.
- **Retail rank and rent:** rank "best protein powder" (e.g. 100k searches a month) and sell the #1 sponsored slot to supplement brands, who reach out inbound.
  - At peak it got up to 30-40K a month for one page. Now the most is about 2K a month per page because traffic dropped.
  - Leave the buyer margin to run the page profitably: with about 50k traffic a month, run conversion-rate math. He prefers 2K a month for 2 years over 10K for a single month.
- **Where SEO still makes sense:**
  - Restricted niches (casino, cannabis, adult, health, gambling) where AI mode doesn't trigger and SERPs are still 10 blue links with zero ads.
  - E-commerce: paid ads first, SEO as a supplementary budget.
  - SaaS: he wouldn't invest in SEO. Ads are the unlock. At most he does Reddit parasite and "best X" listicles targeting head keywords.
  - Niche affiliate publishers: he saw HouseFresh go from about 50k visits a month (2023) to about 1,000 after the HCU to about 200,000 now, 4x its pre-HCU high. He thinks it is part Google "putting their thumb on the scale" and part great marketing. He notes friends' sites, with real experts and millions of YouTube subs, are still in the gutter.

chunks.heading: Getting cited in AI answers (ChatGPT, Gemini, Claude, Perplexity)
chunks.text:
- Jacky's method: check what each model currently cites, then replicate those citations.
- Top cited per his tracking tool: Wikipedia for ChatGPT, YouTube for Gemini and Perplexity, Yelp for Claude. ChatGPT no longer openly cites Reddit.
- Wikipedia play: get a page with citations that list your product as #1 (e.g. Local Rank as the top local SEO software). Wikipedia links are nofollow but still valuable because ChatGPT reads the page context. He believes Wikipedia and ChatGPT have a direct data stream.
  - You can pay someone to get a page in, or get enough unpaid, controversial press to be prominent. He tried to make one for himself 10 years ago and was not prominent enough. After the Search Console wipeout press, he was.
- Listicles across PR sites that consistently list you #1 help, because the model reads the consensus.
- He says to only quote him as "at this very moment, this thing works right now."
- To filter guru advice, test the tactic across about 10 sites. If it fails, write off that person's future claims.

chunks.heading: Landing page conversion rules
chunks.text:
- Call to action above the fold, always. No carousel above the fold.
- Put a VSL on every page that gets significant traffic, including SaaS and local pages. Few people watch it (e.g. 100 of 10,000 visitors), but those who do convert about 10x higher.
- Paid ads need a dedicated landing page, never the homepage.
  - His Local Rank ad pages are noindexed replicas with no menu and no footer nav. The only footer links are legal ones (privacy and terms). Visitors can only convert or leave.
  - He believes removing the nav and footer can 2-3x conversion (e.g. 1% to 2%).
- The best paid landing pages are long. He cites info-product pages of about 20,000 words, 40 testimonials and a VSL above the fold. They have spent millions perfecting the format, so copy it.
- Design is not conversion. A designer-made redesign tanked his conversion rates, and he says a design agency can convert worse than a ClickFunnels page.
- Use simple language, not sophisticated wording. Sell the result and the transformation in a headline of about six words, not the features.

chunks.heading: AI tooling and Black Friday
chunks.text:
- **Atlas / ChatGPT:** he uses ChatGPT Atlas daily as an A/B test suggester for landing pages: headlines, button design and UX. He and his co-founder have never hired a designer.
- **Writing tools:**
  - Koala for listicle and affiliate blog posts.
  - An in-house tool, Garen.ai, for X posts. Paste a YouTube video link and a past viral post, and it generates a new post in the same format with a "comment Local Rank to get the free ebook" CTA.
  - ChatGPT Projects, one per business, for newsletters and planning, so it holds all the context.
- **Automations:** single-line "if this then that" workflows. He uses Pabbly instead of a Zapier subscription, with Cursor to build and a webhook on Pabbly.
- **Black Friday:** it is among the three biggest days of his year, and he says B2B doesn't push it hard enough.
  - His plan: don't discount in a way that alienates loyal customers (most are on lower pricing). Give existing users bonuses instead, e.g. if the offer is 15% off, give existing users 30% more credits, plus extras like backlinks.
- He advises anyone 18 and starting out to get locked in on Cursor or Claude Code and build something.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Jacky walks through every business model he has run, with the real numbers, pros, cons and mistakes. Key lessons: use your own assets as case studies to sell services, avoid correlated risk across content sites, and prefer newsletters for their lack of platform risk.

chunks.heading: SEO agency: economics, team and how to win clients
chunks.text:
- Jacky ran an SEO agency (Index C) and scaled it to about $250k/month at its peak. When his content sites started "popping off" (around $100k/month), he fired most clients and kept a select few.
- Google algorithm updates then hit the content sites, taking them from about $100k to $20k/month overnight. He now runs a blend of agency and own businesses, and the agency funds the swings he takes on his own ventures.
- At the time of this interview (Nov 2023) the agency did about $70k/month in revenue, with about $30k take-home (his ballpark, books not done).
- Retainers: $5k minimum, up to about $20k, so roughly 5-6 clients. Team is 17 full-timers, mostly offshore, and about 30+ including contractors. He acts as account manager.
- Biggest expense is backlinks (a list of blog owners the agency works with), not payroll.
- Pros: cash flow (paid right away) and variety of projects. Cons: margin. Agencies tend to drift to 10-20% margin at scale because of payroll; he keeps his much higher. Also, "you're someone's [ __ ]."
- Client acquisition: build a case study by ranking your own asset, then talk about it publicly. He reveals every dollar he makes, and clients flow in. His own businesses make about 50% more revenue than the agency, so the case studies are a byproduct.
- He argues many SEO agencies have never run or ranked their own business. His test when pitched: ask where the pitcher's own site ranks.
- Advice for starting any agency: pick a service people want now (e.g. cutting TikTok/podcast clips), offer it free if you're young, and get a foot in the door. Good taste in design matters.

chunks.heading: Trading time for money vs. owning assets
chunks.text:
- Jacky is "super against" trading time for money, even at $1-2k/hour coaching or consulting rates. He calls hourly billing "the wrong unit of measurement."
- His goal is income while he golfs or is at the gym ("Stripe notifications"). He would rather earn less and not be on calls all day.
- He applies the same logic to stock trading: if you must be actively trading, you are still trading time.
- He says doing work you would do for free is the only way to last in entrepreneurship, and money is "a byproduct." He is up around 7:00 a.m. because he is excited about projects.

chunks.heading: Dropshipping: the $1.7M run and what killed it
chunks.text:
- His first dropshipping was before Shopify and Oberlo (learned from Black Hat World): men's bracelets and watches, sold via Facebook ads and fulfilled manually between university classes. One month in 2015 or 2016 made about $30k.
- Home-ware store with partner Albert: each put in $5k, burned about $8.5-9k on Facebook ads before finding a winning product. Scaled from zero to about $1.7M in 7 months, with $2k days becoming $10k days.
- Biggest mistake: not private labeling when Albert suggested it. Facebook began sending feedback forms to buyers who never received (slow-shipped) products, the ad account got banned, and the iOS changes hit too. Revenue fell from $250k/month to $80k/month.
- They sold to a private equity firm for low six figures on an earn-out and were never fully paid (the firm claimed bankruptcy).
- Pros: high margins, strong cash flow, no inventory, fast scaling. Cons: not proud of the products, no moat, and multiples around 1x EBITDA, so it is barely sellable.
- Advice: keep fulfillment times short and keep testing ad creatives. When people say ads aren't working, he looks at click-through rates. If CPCs are normal, it is a conversion problem. Hire a designer for the site. Customers are now more sophisticated and have been burned, so "build a real business" with a great offer, product and site.

chunks.heading: Amazon FBA and D2C: wins, losses and lessons
chunks.text:
- Supplements (ginseng, lion's mane, cannabis oil) on Amazon: up to about $100k/month on the cannabis oil, ginseng about $30k/month, lion's mane about $8k/month, about 30% margins. Late profit was about $10k/month. He closed it because Amazon hassles (account dings) weren't worth it alongside better businesses, and says he would like to do it again.
- Vanilla candles (launched Q4 2019): about 2,000 units bought at about $1 each, sold hundreds a day and sold out. They then ordered $20-30k of inventory (about 20k units). COVID delayed delivery about 9 months, Amazon warehouse restrictions capped inbound at 300 units, and storage fees ran about $1k/month. The relaunch did about $10k/month. They liquidated at cost, losing about $20-something k.
- Lesson on Amazon (stated in the conversation): don't raise prices before running out of stock, because sales velocity and history drive re-ranking.
- Far and Away (dinnerware, with Albert): sourced from family-owned Portuguese factories after touring about 10 of them for 2 weeks. Kickstarter raised about $100k US, which funded the launch. COVID and a 12-month factory lead time hurt, and they switched some factories. It now does mid five figures a month, below expectations after the $250k/month dropshipping store. Germany is the biggest market.
- Positioning: he describes the brand as luxury (branding, storytelling, perceived value) rather than premium (extra features). He tells the factory owners' stories to customers. Plates cost about 10x what they would from China.
- D2C economics: shipping heavy, breakable goods is expensive. Albert (finance) insists on calculating every line item, because margin leaks of about 2% each add up, and you should always know your exact margin.

chunks.heading: Content sites
chunks.text:
- Content sites are blogs that rank on Google and monetize through affiliate commissions (Amazon about 4%) or programmatic display ads (about $20 per 1,000 users).
- Last month: about $75k from display ads and about $50k from Amazon affiliate. Niches: architecture, furniture and home. He wants to eventually refer traffic to his own home products.
- They trade at about 3-4x EBITDA. He reads low multiples as high risk (a 30%+ yield). His model is rolling up many risky assets to diversify.
- Lesson: running 10 sites with the same tactics is not real diversification. A single algorithm change hit them all.
- A million-dollar content business can be run by one person plus a few writers, which he says is far easier than FBA.

chunks.heading: Newsletter (marketingletter.com)
chunks.text:
- Started in January 2023 at about 3k subscribers and is now about 23-24k, with about 45% open rates. He has made "100 something K" year to date.
- It covers marketing and AI news, and he says many readers are there for his revenue and net worth updates (built in public).
- Monetization: sponsorships, plus pushing readers to his own SEO services and private community. Readers include people from LinkedIn, Microsoft and Walmart.
- He likes the model because there is no platform risk. The list is yours, and spam-folder problems are fixable by pausing sends for days or weeks. There is a moat, since lists take time or money to build.
- Growth: paid ads on Facebook and Twitter plus organic. He rolls flight profits into growing the list.

chunks.heading: Personal brand, podcast and building in public
chunks.text:
- He started a podcast because "people don't want to talk to you, but for some reason they'll talk to you on a podcast." He invites everyone he wants to talk to, including guests like Brian Dean.
- A YouTube deep-dive episode got only about 170-180 views because his audience is mostly SEOs, while SEO guests get thousands. He still argues for making content you enjoy, since that is what is sustainable.
- If forced to keep one business for 5 years, he would pick the personal brand side (YouTube, Twitter, interviews). He has published a podcast weekly all year and meets people by tweeting from cities he travels to.
- First online dollars: selling LinkedIn recommendations on Fiverr for $5 each, a couple hundred dollars total.
- He publicly documents revenue and net worth monthly, which doubles as his marketing for the agency and newsletter.

chunks.heading: Money management and investments
chunks.text:
- Mostly equities and ETFs via dollar cost averaging. He knows lump sum wins historically, but DCA helps his emotions. He has about $500k US in cash being averaged in at about CAD 26k/month, paid weekly.
- He treats his businesses as his high-risk bucket and his investments as low risk, focused on keeping the money already made.
- Portugal building (bought for the golden visa, with a 30-year fixed rate at 2.4%): about 15k euros of bookings in a month, about 10-12k profit, and about 70k euros take-home trailing 12 months. A management company runs it, and he holds a short-term rental license, which is a moat.
- Lessons from past losses: he picked individual stocks (including buying companies he used, e.g. Starbucks, Coca-Cola, Spotify, Square, Tesla) and ended down about 80% on most. He lost about 20k on Square. He made about $60k US in an hour on GameStop options, and took profits periodically, rolling some into Tesla.
- He treats retail mania as a top signal: he bought $10k of Bitcoin in 2017 in a brokerage full of older retail buyers, and prices crashed soon after.
- He concluded stock picking is not for him because he checks too often and has to get both the buy and the sell right.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Jacky Chou explains how he went from $450/mo to 13 income streams, including a $374k month, by diversifying, taking money off the table, and building B2B SaaS for agency owners. He covers YouTube-driven launches, LLM-citation listicles and high-ticket no-brainer offers.

chunks.heading: Jacky's 90-day plan to reach $10k/month from zero
chunks.text:
- Jacky says his best starting business for someone with no skills, network or audience is an agency. Knowing what he knows, he says he could get to $10k/month quickly with a couple of high-ticket sales. His own example is an LLM agency.
- He claims that anyone who sticks to the plan for 90 days will get there. His daily "massive lock in":
  - Cold email every day.
  - Cold call every day.
  - Two TikToks, two Instagram Reels, one long-form video.
  - One post on X.
- Offer: it must be high ticket and a "no-brainer", meaning zero risk. At the start he would use performance-based terms ("if you don't hit these parameters, you don't pay").
- He suggests working a McDonald's shift to pay for tools while starting out. He says one shift a week would cover them.
- His outlook for an average-IQ person doing this by brute force: mid four figures in 90 days, and it could replace a full-time salary. A smarter person who knows what they're doing can reach $10k/month.
- His caveat: cold calling US buyers from a country where an accent makes it harder is rough. He says Canada works.
- He says "no one's going to do this", so it takes someone very hungry.

chunks.heading: From agency to SaaS: the playbook he repeats
chunks.text:
- His SaaS pivot came from his daily YouTube videos. He made local SEO videos for about a year and spotted holes in the local SEO software market.
- Cursor's arrival made building easy. With business partner Peter Wang he launched Local Rank, and they now launch SaaS companies repeatedly with the same playbook.
- The playbook:
  - Build deep knowledge of an industry (local SEO, Reddit marketing, getting mentioned in LLMs).
  - Notice the problems you hit yourself. He says about 90% of the time other people have them too.
  - Solve them with software.
  - Talk about those problems publicly and market to your viewers.
- Stay in B2B, and sell software for something you could sell as a service.
- He speaks the language of agency owners because he is one. Agency owners have high LTV and heavy switching costs. His Indexsy customer LTV is about $1,000.
- Agency vs SaaS:
  - An agency is painful to manage but one of the easiest businesses to start. You tell the team to do something and it gets done.
  - SaaS has a never-ending feature list, but margins are far better than an agency's.
- In his November 2025 revenue, much of the software revenue did not exist a year earlier. It all arrived within 12 months of his pivot away from affiliate.

chunks.heading: Ranking in ChatGPT and AI search
chunks.text:
- Jacky says he was cited in ChatGPT within 24 hours and ranked number one in 10 days.
- His SaaS tactic for ChatGPT: get about 20 founder friends to each write a "best [category] 2026" listicle on their blogs and put you at number one. Consistently showing up first is a strong positive signal to LLMs. His line: "2026 is the year of the listicle."
- AI Mode on Google probably needs real Google rankings, since it uses Google's ranking. ChatGPT is the opposite. He cites a study of about 35k cited URLs in which roughly 50% of cited domains had zero traffic.
- He calls these the "golden years" of LLM citations because they are easy to game.
- ChatGPT cites Reddit heavily, so getting onto Reddit also helps with LLM visibility.
- He believes a YouTube "best X" video would likely work for Gemini and AI Mode. He is unsure about ChatGPT.
- Where SEO still pays: industries where ChatGPT and AI Mode won't give answers, such as casino, CBD, drugs and adult. He says the money there is still about 90% of what it was.
- Consumer queries like "best protein powder" are already hit hard by AI answers. He says SEO is now shifting toward LLMs.

chunks.heading: Reddit playbook for promoting a SaaS
chunks.text:
- Jacky calls Reddit the easiest channel to game right now, for both Google rankings and LLM visibility.
- Step by step:
  1. Search your target keyword on Google (for example "best local rank tracker"). He says Reddit shows up about 90% of the time.
  2. Comment your brand in that Reddit thread.
  3. Wait two weeks, then buy upvotes. Traffic starts almost immediately.
  4. If the thread is locked, post the same question in the same subreddit ("what's the best local rank tracker in 2026?") with your parameters, without shilling yet.
  5. Buy around 500 upvotes to make it viral and push it to the front page. It can replace the old ranking thread.
  6. Edit the post to say you found your own tool as the best option.
- Upvotes change the narrative. A post with early hate can turn positive once it has upvotes, because Reddit users follow the crowd.
- Prices: about 10 upvotes for 10 cents, sold at 1 cent each. His own company sells them through a business called Trackings, and other providers exist.
- He suggests using one account to promote your own services.

chunks.heading: Google ranking and local SEO signals
chunks.text:
- Google uses Chrome data. If a page ranks between positions 5 and 20, sending a large amount of real human traffic can lift it. His example: about 50k visits from Facebook.
- If you stop paying for traffic, the page stays up only if people still click it naturally. If users bounce back to search results ("pogo stick"), the ranking falls.
- Google Maps ranking is mostly user signals now. In his order of importance:
  1. User signals such as Google reviews and driving directions (also click-through rate).
  2. Citations, meaning directory listings, which are like link building.
  3. Everything else.
- With two otherwise identical listings and the same review count, he says the one with 150 daily visitors outranks the one with 50.
- Competitors get real people to visit locations by partnering with big mobile games and apps. The user walks to the business and gets in-game currency. He says he lacks the technical skill to build this but thinks it's an eight-figure business if someone cracks it.

chunks.heading: Diversification, exits and surviving volatility
chunks.text:
- Jacky worked in high-risk, high-volatility industries (SEO, affiliate), so he is a strong believer in taking money off the table.
- His revenue went from about $500k/month to roughly $150-200k in about three months, a hit of about 60%. He says it forced team reorganizing, projections and painful cost cutting, down to going through credit card statements.
- Dropshipping story: it reached $240k/month at 40% margins. Because they stayed on dropshipping instead of moving to private label, Facebook changes plus iOS cut it to about $100k/month at 5-10% margins. He sold to private equity for about $150k, received about $100k, and the buyer went bankrupt.
- He has had three or four low-six-figure exits. The biggest was about $300-350k, a content site sold to Thrasio after buying it for about $150k and holding it for two months.
- He says 99% of content-site peers from the COVID era are "completely destroyed" and down about 90% in enterprise value. He says they didn't sell, and he had personally urged several to do so.
- His residual income lines:
  - Binance affiliate: in 2017 he outranked Binance for its own name for about three months, because its homepage lacked title tags.
  - OnlyFans: traffic sent to a network that works with agencies.
  - Mediavine: residual from partnership SEO, where he partnered with legacy media brands, wrote affiliate articles on their blogs and split revenue 50/50.
  - FanFuel: an affiliate network.
- Partnership SEO took him from about $70-80k/month to $500k in about three months. His lesson: "If you see an opportunity, you should like really really go in hard." He rejects "passive income" as a myth.

chunks.heading: YouTube as a growth channel
chunks.text:
- Jacky started daily videos in 2023 with about 20K followers on X. The first video got roughly 100 views.
- Differentiation: other creators in the space did highly edited quick cuts, so he made slow, unedited, long videos. He credits consistency over execution.
- Average views are about 1,000, mostly US-based viewers, many of them agency owners with buying power. He says the same thousand people returning daily is worth more than going viral.
- Prep time dropped from about 2 hours for the first episode to about 20 minutes.
- For the Local Rank launch he did $20k right out of the gate. About 90% of that revenue came from YouTube, tracked via coupon codes. The launch video had about 1K views, and the launch tweet on X had about 50k views but drove only about 10% of revenue.
- His advice to anyone struggling: start posting videos, whatever kind. He calls video "by far the biggest lever".

chunks.heading: Conversion, team and operations
chunks.text:
- VSLs: Jacky says he thought they were "scammy" but A/B tested with and without, and having one helps. He thinks they work especially well for North American buyers.
  - His is about 2 minutes of him selling and showing the product.
  - He doesn't center it on the page. He puts a headline with the top of the VSL visible.
  - He says viewers who watch about 90% convert at around 60%, though he'd need to pull the exact numbers.
  - He writes the script with ChatGPT.
- SaaS landing pages: copy someone doing a lot of revenue, since most converge on what works. He wouldn't copy Peter Levels' page, which he says isn't optimized and sells on personal brand.
- Team and delegation:
  - He has about 13 people on his team, up one or two from the year before.
  - He delegates anything he has to do more than once.
  - Delegated work will never meet your standards, so be OK with "good enough".
- Community is the business he'd keep: Jacky is bullish on his Slack-style community (he mentions "advice"). He says it's the easiest, and he talks daily with like-minded marketers.
- Reality check: November 2025 revenue of $374k is gross. He says net is about 40%, and take-home after taxes is less. Net worth is about $10 million after about 10 years, and he lives humbly.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Jacky Chou talks through his current business mix (local SEO software, display ads, agency, private community) and what is working in SEO now. He covers rank and rent via verified Google locations, careful blogging after Google's crackdown, and daily YouTube content as a trust engine that feeds a paid community.

chunks.heading: Business snapshot and revenue mix (Nov 2025)
chunks.text:
- Jacky Chou (X handle "Indexy") started in ecom (private labeling, which he calls disgusting and won't do again), then moved to SEO. He describes himself as a victim of shiny object syndrome.
- Last month's highest revenue was his local SEO software (Local Rank), at $34K. It launched about a month and a half earlier, and the revenue surprised him.
- Other streams:
  - About $30K a month from display ads (a network) on content sites.
  - An agency.
  - A private community of local SEOs, which he calls his first taste of success from the YouTube channel.
  - Amazon affiliate.
- The SEO community peaked at about $100K a month and sits at "30 something" thousand now. It is "literally just a Slack channel and then a course", a "cool kids club" where people share openly.
- He says he is down about 50% year on year, because SEO is rough and "you got to pivot so fast".
- About a year earlier, Google went after assets connected to him personally and wiped the sites on those accounts. His take: "I game the algo for a living, so it's bound to happen."
- He tracks and shares numbers publicly: monthly revenue updates on X and a monthly net worth update in his newsletter, which is the most popular newsletter he sends. He says SEO people are usually not transparent and only post top-line screenshots.

chunks.heading: Legacy media partnerships and rank-and-rent affiliate
chunks.text:
- He partnered with dying legacy media outlets that have strong domain authority (e.g. a local newspaper site). He carved out an affiliate or supplement section on their domain and monetized hard.
- The pages flew to number one. Highest monthly affiliate income was about $550K.
- Sponsored rank-and-rent: for "best protein powder"-type keywords, he reached out to the brands and charged a flat fee plus a percentage to be listed at number one. The highest placement was $50K a month plus 50% commission.
- That stream is now "pretty much dead", at about $16-17K a month.
- He calls it "the most insane high" of his life.

chunks.heading: LLM SEO and Reddit manipulation
chunks.text:
- He doesn't sell services he isn't highly certain about. He is testing LLM SEO ("GEO" in A16Z's term) and says results are not yet conclusive.
- Direction he points people toward: Reddit and Quora, which he says are easy to manipulate. The method:
  1. Google a commercial query such as "best FBA courses 2025".
  2. Find the Reddit thread that ranks.
  3. List your own offer in it from a proxy account.
  4. Upvote it massively and add fake supporting comments.
  5. Appearing in those threads gets you into LLM answers.
- Cost claims: about five cents per upvote, farmed accounts for a few dollars each, and subreddit mods can reportedly be bribed for around $1,000.
- It won't work in high-competition niches like supplements, VPN or mattresses.
- He sees a service gap: proactive reputation building on Reddit, as opposed to reactive removals.

chunks.heading: Rank-and-rent and local lead gen
chunks.text:
- Core tactic: get the Google Business Profile location verified, "I don't care how you do it", and the calls start flowing, especially in tier two and tier three cities.
- Outside the US (Australia, Canada, UK, Germany) is even easier. He ranked a roofing keyword in Berlin in about two days as a case study for a friend, who then picked up a roughly $150K deal.
- Bridging trick: if a rank-and-rent site isn't ranking yet but you signed a client for $2K, put that $2K into paid ads while waiting for SEO. Cut spend as rankings rise.
- He sold towinglist.com, then the largest towing directory in the US, when a prospect he was selling to turned out to be sketchy and made subtle threats.
- A friend with a number of Google Business Profiles earns about $300-500 a day just sending calls through call networks. Going direct would earn more, but networks need no effort.
- He is interested in doing local SEO plus info coaching run at break-even to feed his software.

chunks.heading: Blogs, black hat, and Facebook traffic
chunks.text:
- Blogs still work, but most people do it wrong. Blasting hundreds of AI posts a day gets you hit by Google's filters, and weak domains are "blacklisted immediately". Nobody recovers anymore.
- His approach for legitimate blogs: optimize with a tool like NeuronWriter (cheap on AppSumo) and publish only one or two posts a day.
- Black-hat approach: buy a strong expired domain at GoDaddy auctions (e.g. an old crypto project that had a billion-dollar market cap) and push heavy affiliate articles across supplements, pills and similar. Try to earn the money back in the first few days before Google catches on.
- Organic Facebook for display-ad blogs (e.g. a vegan recipe site):
  - Buy page likes at fractions of a cent each, using clickbait like-bait pages ("like if you love golden retrievers").
  - Post clickbaity content and never link in the first post; put the link in the thread.
  - Send traffic to the blog and run it in high-RPM geos (US, Canada).
  - He cites 1-10K a day on Mediavine-type display income if posts go viral.

chunks.heading: Content, partnerships, and where he is heading
chunks.text:
- Daily YouTube is worth it. Viewers feel close and trust him, and a high share convert to the private community. He says most of his partnership money came from partnerships with other SEO people, which YouTube opens up, and that the opportunities alone make it worthwhile even if every other revenue stream stopped.
- Advice for beginners: post daily, then double down on the videos that perform. He knows of someone making about $100K a month in the info space with roughly 8K YouTube subs and no paid traffic.
- He is not a networker (he describes himself as "hard on the spectrum" and hating networking events) and leans on YouTube to bring deals to him.
- He has hosted invite-only meetups by application (his EA runs them, killers only). One cost about $10K in drinks with no direct ROI, though he enjoyed it.
- Next focus: consumer software using AI with his partner XFang. He bought about 100 US-based TikTok accounts for about $5 each and plans to farm them. He prefers to figure out organic and game the algorithm.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Jacky Chou walks through his dropshipping exit and its biggest mistake, how he sources cheaper from 1688, and why Amazon affiliates should sell their own FBA products. He also covers buying algo-hit sites and expired domains, and hiring operators by buying their sites or giving equity.

chunks.heading: Background and portfolio (as of Nov 2022)
chunks.text:
- Jacky has an electrical engineering degree. He found SEO by googling how to make money online the night before a failed final exam, and landed on Black Hat World.
- Career path: digital marketing jobs, then director of marketing at a Berlin startup, then his own agency. His reasoning: "why are you doing SEO for clients when you can do it for yourself" if you are confident in it. That led him to buy and sell websites.
- Portfolio: 40+ content sites, several e-commerce businesses, and various lead gen sites.
- Revenue: six figures in e-commerce, six figures in content sites, five figures in lead gen.
- Team: a director of ops, many writers and editors, and an operator for lead gen and the agency side.
- Content site monetization: display ads, Amazon affiliate, VPN affiliates, web hosting affiliates. Roughly 10+ sites were started from scratch and many more were bought.
- He is always buying affiliate sites, especially Amazon affiliate sites, and says he closes deals within two days.

chunks.heading: Dropshipping: how he scaled it and the biggest mistake
chunks.text:
- First attempt: he dropshipped manually before Oberlo, fulfilling orders with his own credit card. He spent about $1k on ads and made about $15k in revenue in two days. It died from ad fatigue because he had no idea how to run ads or make creatives.
- Second attempt: two years later his business partner proposed trying again. Each put in $5k of their own money, treating it as money to burn. They were down to about $1k of budget when one creative became a winner.
- Result: scaled to roughly $200-300k a month in revenue within a couple of months. The business later had a private equity exit, and he says they got burned on it and learned a lot.
- Biggest mistake: they kept dropshipping when they should have switched to private labeling immediately. He says it cost "hundreds of thousands of dollars" because competitors entered with faster shipping while he was content taking home about $100k a month.
- What he would do now:
  - Test ads with dropshipping.
  - When a product wins, source it, ship it in bulk to the market where the winners are, and hold it in a warehouse.
  - Customers then get products within a week, and you can build a returning customer base.

chunks.heading: Sourcing: 1688, 3PLs and finding products
chunks.text:
- 1688.com is the Chinese-language version of Alibaba, for Chinese buyers. He says prices are 20-30% cheaper and most of the Western world doesn't know about it.
- Three ways to access it:
  - Use Alibaba itself.
  - Use a sourcing company (his own has two people).
  - Hire a Chinese speaker, even a local exchange student, to find the same product on 1688 and negotiate.
- Ship the goods to a 3PL and fulfil from there.
- 3PL tip: the top Google results for 3PLs are expensive and "absolutely rip you off." Look on page two of Google, and those smaller 3PLs give better courier rates in exchange for your business.
- Product ideas: use dropshipping spy tools for inspiration, find a cheaper version on AliExpress, pick products with nice creatives, shoot your own video, and launch as many ad variations as possible.
- Store: use Shopify, not WordPress, for dropshipping. He says they tested it and Shopify is easier and more scalable even though WordPress is better for SEO. He recommends the paid Prestige theme for conversions.
- He says "dropshipping is dead" claims usually come from people whose stores look terrible, so store quality matters.

chunks.heading: Ad channels after the iOS changes
chunks.text:
- Facebook is very tough after the iOS changes.
- What works for his DTC company now: Google Shopping, and TikTok ads.
- TikTok creative needs a raw, ugc, non-polished feel. Aesthetic, Instagram-style content doesn't land. His younger brother, who is TikTok-famous, helps with it.
- Organic TikTok: he says viral reach involves manual curators, so content that looks too commercial or brand-led gets pushed down. Listicle-style content has a better chance.

chunks.heading: Amazon affiliates: selling your own products
chunks.text:
- Shopify vs Amazon test: sending affiliate traffic to a Shopify store converted at about 1.5%, versus about 30% on Amazon for the exact same product (supplements). He says it wasn't even close, because "people love buying on Amazon."
- His idea: successful Amazon affiliate marketers control the traffic but stop there. They should launch their own private label products on Amazon FBA and recommend those.
- Caveat: check local laws on referring your own products (FTC in the US), and add a disclaimer.
- FBA cost and cash flow:
  - Door-to-door from placing an order to the Amazon warehouse is about three months.
  - That means ordering about six months of inventory up front, paid up front.
  - So he says it suits established affiliate marketers who have flipped a few sites and have cash, who love the niche.
  - His team has a couple of FBA businesses and is still figuring out the formula.

chunks.heading: Link building and starting new sites
chunks.text:
- Delegates keyword research (Ahrefs).
- New site setup: connect socials with IFTTT so each published post also goes out there, and buy cheap Fiverr citations (about 50 for $5). He says most are nofollow but he is convinced they do something.
- Anchor text: for the first six months on a new site, build all homepage links with naked or branded anchors. He says exact-match anchors no longer move rankings, and many sites he sees have aggressive anchors and too many links to inner pages.
- On inner pages he uses branded anchors rather than naked URLs, which look odd in a blog post.
- He calls link building "an art": you keep testing and watch how Google reacts.
- Outreach:
  - He builds mostly niche edits, about 6k links last month across clients and his own sites.
  - Emails are two-liners that offer payment up front: "we want to link here, please let me know the price."
  - Everything, including follow-ups, is automated, and the back and forth is mostly price negotiation.
  - Minimum traffic on target sites is about 1k organic (or 500).
  - He pays about half of what he sells the link for, roughly $20-30, and uses scale as leverage ("if you accept this right now we will give you 30 other clients").

chunks.heading: Buying sites, expired domains and fixing penalized sites
chunks.text:
- Expired and auction domains:
  - His only metric is the number of Ahrefs ranking keywords. A DR2 with lots of keywords is a buy, because "Google likes them."
  - He says backlink profile doesn't even matter. A nasty profile keeps auction bids low (a couple hundred dollars versus up to $10k from domain resellers).
  - Let the revived domain sit on its old content with SSL for one to two months before building. This shows where the traffic trend steadies and gives a benchmark. He credits another SEO for the idea.
- Site buying:
  - He buys mostly in home niches and avoids tech and gadgets because they aren't evergreen. He prefers evergreen topics like curtain rails.
  - Due diligence is a gut feeling: a quick look in Ahrefs. Under about $20k he barely checks backlinks, since a larger portfolio spreads the risk.
- Algo-hit sites:
  - He loves them. Sellers who are demoralized will take cash up front with no due diligence at a low multiple.
  - He says about 20% of these don't work, and he takes those losses.
  - Example: a site bought for about $3k that peaked at $15k a month and was down badly. His team got it back to about $3k a month.
- Revival playbook, done every time:
  - Fix speed.
  - Redesign (he says the design is horrifying 99 times out of 100).
  - About 20 homepage naked or branded anchor links, niche edits, about 500 citations to the homepage, and a foundational link package.
  - Wait a month, then check whether it is reversing before looking at other fixes.
- Design and speed:
  - Fixing a site's look can take about 10 minutes: new logo from Canva, a better font, or a Fiverr designer to move from Figma to WordPress.
  - Speed tools: WP Rocket with Cloudflare, or NitroPack.
  - Page builders: Gutenberg is the fastest. Elementor sites score in the 80s, especially on the Hello Elementor base theme. Thrive sites land in the 70s. Keep each builder on its native theme.
  - Most sites he sees score in the 20s. They are working to get indexy.io from the 60s to 70.
  - Warning: a redesign made one site beautiful but extremely slow, and traffic tanked.

chunks.heading: Lead gen: the towing site
chunks.text:
- He bought a national "Yelp for towing" site making about $400 a month. It already ranked for "towing company near me" terms and the previous owner didn't know how to scale it.
- It now makes low five figures a month (about $10k). He says the site was worth about $250k at the time of one conversation.
- Acquisition of tow company customers:
  - Rank for B2B keywords such as towing leads and how to market towing companies.
  - Run Facebook ads targeting people with "towing" in their job description, offering a free month of calls.
  - Follow-up is automated: Zapier, then a five-email sequence, then a signup link for the free trial, then a subscription.
- Billing: moving billing from WordPress to SPP.co (a client dashboard) lifted conversion by about 50%. He recommends it for national lead gen.
- Hiring a call operator:
  - Tow owners dislike hearing an accent, so he hired locally in Canada or the US.
  - First a US person on commission only. Then a friend in Vancouver, convinced with base pay, large commission and equity.
  - The pitch: if the site goes from $250k to $700k, she gets a percentage of the sale.
- Staff incentives: his director of ops came by acquisition. Jacky bought 75% of his site and then hired him. He says buying a site from someone with a system in place is a good way to find staff, and he rates affiliate marketers above in-house and agency people.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Jacky explains why he prefers revenue-share partnerships on big authority sites over client retainers and niche sites. He covers rank-and-rent monetization, running paid ads to drive branded search, delegating with an EA, and keeping a team lean. He also argues links matter more than content.

chunks.heading: SEO partnerships: the model Jacky calls his biggest earner
chunks.text:
- Jacky says partnerships are his main business right now. He approaches a company whose core product is not display ads or affiliate revenue (a local newspaper, a publisher, a brand) and carves out a subdirectory on its site.
- He installs a separate WordPress in that subdirectory and builds an affiliate site inside the partner's domain, borrowing its authority.
- He monetizes the subdirectory three ways: affiliate commissions, display ads, and "retail rank and rent" (companies pay to be the top slot on a "best X" page).
- His example: he targets the same keywords across multiple partners. For "best protein powder" he has several pages on the front page of Google, so he can charge a protein powder company heavily for a slot. "They'll be foaming at the mouth."
- Deals are inbound. He keeps posting about it, e.g. "if you have a DR 70+ we can get you up to 300K a month," backed by a case study site.
- His reasoning for sharing openly: "the pie is so big." The more he talks about it, the more deals come in.

chunks.heading: Partnership economics and contract terms
chunks.text:
- One partnership does $300K a month, with $150K a month going to Jacky. He notes this is equivalent to roughly 30 retainer clients at his rates, which he would never want to manage.
- Splits vary. One deal was a 50/50 or 60/40 revenue share (the partner negotiated them down) plus a flat $10K a month retainer. The catch was that the partner owned the IP of the content, so they could cut him off after a year.
- The partner is hands-off when the numbers are good. For his biggest partner, he just sends an invoice-request at month end.
- Incentives are aligned because both sides earn more as revenue grows, unlike retainers.
- His contract is "very aggressive," including a cut if a partner exits. He tells people: "don't let these big companies bully you." He briefly sold the contract template (about 20-something copies in a week) and pulled it so it wouldn't saturate the market.
- His hope is partnerships last through the end of next year, and he plans to keep onboarding partners. The risk he names is Google deciding it dislikes authoritative sites, which he sees as unlikely because it would mean hitting Forbes and similar publishers.

chunks.heading: Amazon affiliate rates and e-commerce
chunks.text:
- Jacky ships about $2 million a month of Amazon products. His commission ranges from 3% to 8%, with 8% in home.
- He got the rate card by buying a portfolio of sites in a bundle. The sites went to zero but the rate card made the purchase worthwhile.
- Amazon raises rates by category, and you must prove yourself in each one. He says tech is least likely to go up because margins are thin, while categories like makeup can go high with volume.
- His advice on getting there: ship roughly $3-5 million a month, the level of The Verge and Forbes. His own request for higher rates was met with a Q4 freeze.
- He is "very bullish on Ecom." His DTC homeware brand Far and Away had a Black Friday "well into six figures," and it ships only to Europe, with Nordic-style products.
- His earlier path: he made his first million online dropshipping. After a Facebook feedback-request update led to ad account bans, revenue fell from about $250K a month to about $100K a month at roughly 10% profit, and they sold to private equity for about $150K. Half of it was an earnout that never paid. His lesson: he should have private labeled earlier.
- A cutlery set at $130 was their winning dropshipping product because it looked designer.

chunks.heading: Branded search and local SEO tactics
chunks.text:
- **Paid ads feed organic:** On an ecommerce site with an affiliate blog, paid ads drive branded searches. For example, $50K a month on Facebook, Instagram and Pinterest ads for Far and Away makes people Google the brand and read reviews. Jacky says that sends positive signals to the site and let him get away with weak content on the blog.
- **PBNs as local citations:** He uses PBNs as an unlinked mention (a citation), then links from the PBN to other citations like Yelp as a tier 2, boosting NAP (name, address, phone) consistency. He says it works and is cheap.
- **Unlinked mentions:** He argues that if Google can detect citations, it can detect unlinked mentions, so nofollow or unlinked mentions are not useless.
- **Hypothesis (untested):** If a brand appears at number one on every "best SEO company" listicle, it should find it easier to rank for "SEO company." He suggests brand name saturation across titles and profiles (he cites Julian Goldie) helps build knowledge panels.
- **Beginner advice:** Start with local rank-and-rent (a site like roofingaustin.org), drive leads, then find a partner.
- **His local start:** He ran local SEO for six real estate clients, reaching about $10K a month at peak. Citations alone were enough to get number one.

chunks.heading: What he likes, doesn't like, and where he's cautious
chunks.text:
- **Client retainers:** He dislikes them. He cancelled a $12K a month client recently, and says the math doesn't work compared with partnerships. He also finds the work unsatisfying (ranking a Vancouver lawyer for 100 searches a month).
- **Niche sites:** He labels them his weakest area. One example: a site bought for $10K, scaled to $20K a month, then fell to about $3K a month. His lesson: exit before the update. His site had guest posts (about 1 guest post to 20 own posts) and went too broad. His content is now all AI-written and human-edited, and he let writers go.
- **Informational content:** He thinks informational niche sites will be hit hardest by SGE ("what dogs can eat" is the easiest thing to replace).
- **Display ads:** He predicts a 70-80% drop in RPMs when third-party cookies are removed, and says ad-based sites face roughly "negative 90%" with SGE and cookie removal combined.
- **Past enterprise SEO:** At peak the agency did about $150K a month in retainers, serving Fortune 500 and public companies including Motley Fool. A big client, Overflow, found him via an interview about his dropshipping success.
- **Directories:** He sold a towing directory after learning many East Coast towing companies were mob-owned.

chunks.heading: SEO opinions: links vs content
chunks.text:
- Jacky says "content is king" is wrong. His partnership content is "mediocre at best" and still ranks, because the domains are authoritative.
- He says "links don't matter" is also wrong: "links are everything." He challenges anyone to name a significant-volume keyword where links don't matter, and offered $500 if he can't outrank it in a day. He excludes obscure long-tail examples.
- If you don't have a partnership, he says you need to build links.
- He likes fighting fire with fire: he competes against Forbes-type sites with similar authority, not a niche site "water pistol."

chunks.heading: Personal branding, newsletter and monetization
chunks.text:
- Jacky has posted on Twitter for about 2 years and recently began daily YouTube videos. He calls personal branding "a huge dub" because it attracts partnership deals, including household names.
- He thinks most SEO people on Twitter are "heavily under monetizing": everyone should put an offer at the end of a tweet.
- His newsletter, Marketing Letter, earns about $6K a month on about $1K a month in costs. He compares it to a Roth IRA: boring, passive and a fallback. Rhino Rank is one of its largest sponsors.
- His paid community brought in $6.2K that month, helped by annual sales on Black Friday.
- His other lines of business include display ads, directories, retail rank and rent, a link building agency, and short-term rentals in Lisbon.

chunks.heading: Running the team and operating style
chunks.text:
- Jacky has 17 people. He wants to stay lean after reading *Profit First*, and cites bloat as why some niche site builders went under.
- His rule: "I don't do anything more than once," so he delegates everything, with a person or two per task.
- His director of ops and his EA are both based in Kenya and are his top earners. Everyone else is VA or entry level. He starts people low, then promotes and raises often, and pays bonuses (sometimes a month's salary) for strong performance.
- His EA sends a morning update on which emails to answer and manages his calendar and Twitter DMs. He calls this "the greatest growth hack ever."
- For email, he suggests the free Missive app so an assistant can read and file without Gmail access.
- He reallocates the team by performance. If a site is struggling, he pauses it and moves everyone to a partnership that's working.
- His process is loose: bulk keyword research a couple of times a month, run in Sheets.
- Next plans: use partnership rankings to close the loop with owned products (e.g. sell protein powder if he ranks for it), and aim to retire within five years.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Jacky explains how he buys starter sites, scales them with content and varied link building, and measures everything by payback period. The core theme is risk management: diversify link tactics, sites and asset classes, and take chips off the table.

chunks.heading: How Jacky structures his businesses and diversifies risk
chunks.text:
- Jacky is an electrical engineer by education. He started making money online around 2015-2016 after failing courses and googling "how to make money online" the day before a final exam.
- His early attempts ranged from CPL offers to selling LinkedIn recommendations on Fiverr.
- His current mix, as of 2022:
  - A D2C homeware brand (Far and Away).
  - An SEO agency doing "mid five figures" a month.
  - A portfolio of about 34-35 content sites.
  - Traditional investments such as equities and crypto.
- The agency is "an extremely high margin" business. He puts its profit into content sites, which are revenue-generating assets, instead of spending it on lifestyle.
- The agency also lets him "practice what we preach" by ranking his own portfolio.
- He credits his risk mindset to years of trading crypto.
- Diversification is his main theme, and it applies to businesses, link tactics and investments.

chunks.heading: Dropshipping exit and the D2C brand Far and Away
chunks.text:
- His first big online money was dropshipping men's fashion accessories (beads) on WordPress, fulfilled manually from AliExpress. It reached about $15,000 in revenue in a month, with hundreds of orders a day.
- Later he ran a home decor dropshipping store doing about $250k a month at roughly 90% gross margin. It was sold to a PE firm in Detroit.
- He wasn't proud of selling "pretty much garbage from China", so he started a D2C brand "to do it right".
- Far and Away sells heritage products from countries not known for making them, such as Portuguese dinnerware, ceramics and cutlery. French scented candles are next, from the oldest candle manufacturer in the world.
- Sourcing is private label. He finds mom-and-pop manufacturers, negotiates a rate and good payment terms, and builds the brand on their storytelling.
- He picked the niche from data from the dropshipping store, which showed winning categories to zero in on.
- It averages about six figures a month in euros at roughly 65% gross margin.
- It is the biggest time sink of his businesses. He calls it the worst for "time to revenue".

chunks.heading: Delegation and operations
chunks.text:
- He learned delegation from Andrew Wilkinson of Tiny.
- When he buys a business, he keeps the seller on as operator with a minority stake. He tells them: "this is your piece of the pie", and offers his team's resources. He asks how they would grow it with infinite resources. This turns the work from "zero to one" into "one to a hundred".
- He has used this with four operators. The other ~30 sites run in-house.
- Content team: 8-12 writers paid a flat rate per word as contractors. Four editors upload and design posts and check readability against SOPs. A director of ops oversees the content sites and the agency.
- Content is prioritized by site health:
  - If a site is hit by a core update, the team pauses new articles and fixes existing ones.
  - If a site is doing well, they double down. One site went from about 20 articles a month to double that.
- His own workload is now 4-8 hours a day. In 2020 he worked 16-18 hour days during COVID.
- His routine: put out fires from overnight, work out, coffee, then knock out "the five things you dreaded" from the day before. He argues that being 1% better each day compounds.

chunks.heading: Buying starter sites and portfolio economics
chunks.text:
- Only about $60k a month in max revenue comes from the 34 sites. He says they aren't all generating "crazy revenue".
- His model is to buy many starter sites in different stages, add content and links, then wait. A large portfolio lets him test aggressive tactics on $5k sites before applying them to $100k sites.
- Volume matters because some sites simply won't rank even when best practices are followed.
- What he looks for in a $5-10k starter site:
  - Many indexed keywords in Ahrefs.
  - A trajectory that is "up and to the right".
  - Earnings don't matter at this price; the site can make $0.
- He buys any site ranking for products he sells, such as his Amazon FBA homeware brand. He pushes his own products there, like VPN Mentor did with its own brands.
- Due diligence is fast: only Ahrefs, plus verifying in Search Console. He can make an offer within about five minutes and be in escrow within half an hour. Speed is why sellers choose him.
- Deal sources: Facebook groups, and now mostly private deals. People message him before listing anywhere, especially after podcast appearances.
- He rarely builds from scratch now. He had one six-month-old mental health site.
- Buying saves months of time. "$5k a month to save months of time" is worth it to him because it is a small share of his net worth.

chunks.heading: Payback periods, risk and when to sell
chunks.text:
- His main metric is payback period. He buys sites at 2-3 years of payback. A custom Amazon rate card shortens that to just under two years.
- If a site survives the payback period, he is "in the green".
- Example: a large site that did $20k a month fell to about $3k after an update. He had paid about $60k for an ugly non-brandable 301 domain, so he had already made his money back.
- Starter sites are his moonshots. He buys many $5-20k sites hoping to reach $100k+ and a six-to-seven-figure exit. If a site makes $1k a month and then dies, he doesn't worry.
- He dialed back risk in late 2022 because of the economic climate.
- Selling rule: sell at peak euphoria, "when you think you don't need to sell", or when a site is too big a share of your net worth. Always take some chips off the table.
- A partial sale works. He would buy 70% and let the seller keep 30% for upside.
- He worries that some operators have most of their net worth in content sites. Updates can be "life-ruining" if a family depends on one site.
- Advice by situation:
  - With $5k in the bank and a $1k/month site (worth at least $30k), sell it and rebuild.
  - With $100k in the bank, buy starter sites.
  - Don't quit your job to start a site from scratch. Have at least 12 months of runway and a site already earning.
  - He flags survivorship bias in success stories.

chunks.heading: Content cadence and indexing
chunks.text:
- Publish regularly but not necessarily often. 4-5 posts a month is enough to show Google the site is alive. The main failure is letting a site "sit and die".
- Post volume on a new site:
  - Strong trajectory: about 30 posts a month.
  - Standard trajectory: 5-10 posts a month.
  - Heavy link building early, then adjust to how the site reacts.
- Process after purchase: keyword research, then scheduled posts.
- For indexing, the Rank Math plugin that uses the Search Console API worked well. Paid indexing tools also "work like crazy".
- He admits he can't explain why some sites went up and some down in the May 2022 core update. A site with poor speed and the same links as hit sites went up.
- He says with "very, very high certainty" that the update was not a link update.
- The sites hit hardest were ones where he had earlier reversed a penalty with a 301.

chunks.heading: Link building: vary tactics per site
chunks.text:
- Rule: use a different link-building mix on each site. A single SOP across all sites means a link update hits everything. He says you can't do all niche edits across all domains.
- His mixes by site:
  - Churn-and-burn sites: PBNs, which he says still work great.
  - Others: niche edits and guest posts.
  - Riskier sites: tier 2 links as well.
- He considers PBNs more dangerous than tier 2. He has never seen tier 2 get penalized.
- Tier 2 method: guest posts target the same keyword as the money site. For example, a guest post optimized for "top SEO agency 2022" links to the money site. He then points links at the guest post, like parasite SEO while still linking to his own page.
- He thinks of links in three classes: very good, middle, and very bad. He stays mostly in the middle and goes to the bottom side only when feeling risky.
- He believes in "quantity over hyper quality" because Google now mostly ignores links instead of penalizing them.
- For someone with one or two sites that feed the family, he'd skip PBNs and tier 2. He'd use guest posts on hyper-relevant sites, as Mushfiq of Website Flip does.
- Writers and the team keep a note of which tactic each site gets. He says it sounds complex but isn't.

chunks.heading: Site speed, E-E-A-T and video
chunks.text:
- Site speed matters for conversion. Based on his ecommerce experience, no one waits on pages that take more than 2 seconds, especially on mobile 4G. Slow pages mean fewer affiliate clicks.
- Expertise depends on the niche:
  - In home, he has writers write from the point of view that they've used the product, and this helped rankings.
  - In sensitive niches like VPN, cybersecurity expertise matters more.
- Video helps E-E-A-T, but he hasn't implemented it well. For his VPN sites he currently embeds other people's videos.
- He would like to make a how-to video for each article, especially those ranking for "best VPN".
- He thinks a single-site operator has an edge in video because they know the content well. At scale, with many writers, it is harder.
- His brother has about 300k TikTok followers. When he embeds his own recipe video, the post ranks quickly with almost no links and a poor backlink profile. Influencer friends see the same when they talk from a "used it" point of view and embed a video.
- He believes Google's language and video understanding is now strong.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Jacky Chou walks through his path from electrical engineering to SEO, a Drop Shipping win that crashed, and launching Far and Away via Kickstarter. He covers Facebook ads, conversion fixes, why e-commerce stores should add affiliate and display revenue, and how niche sites, agencies and e-commerce balance each other.

chunks.heading: Jacky's background and how he learns
chunks.text:
- Studied electrical engineering, hated it. Remembers a 15/50 midterm in a third-year course as the moment he knew he could not make money as an engineer.
- Googled "how to make money online", landed on digital marketing, took an internship in Berlin at a marketing agency.
- Early jobs: mobile marketing company (app store ranking, display ads), growth marketing at a hardware company (SEO), then director of growth at a photography startup (an Instagram/Getty-style stock photo product) doing SEO and lead generation. Later head of marketing at another startup, then consulting and his own businesses.
- Learned SEO purely by Googling and trial and error, with no formal training.
- He is "pretty against courses". His view: courses mainly give accountability, and if you are a self-starter you can learn anything from YouTube, Khan Academy, Harvard's online classes and similar. If you buy a course to get yourself to do the work, that is a mindset problem, not an education problem.
- He learns from podcasts (My First Million, All-In) by picking up terms they mention, Googling them and going down rabbit holes.

chunks.heading: Jacky's business portfolio and which model he prefers
chunks.text:
- **Indexsy** is the holding company for his content sites ("Niche sites"), his marketing newsletter and a prioritized SEO service. Together these are his largest revenue source. He also co-owns Far and Away (DTC dinnerware) and has smaller brands, including an online interior design company.
