- Preference: niche sites. No clients to deal with, he likes to tinker, margins are very high. He hates client calls, which rules out agencies for him.
- Downside of niche sites: 6 to 12 months to ramp up each site.
- Agency work is the cash-flow layer: "pretty decently high margin" and "extremely low risk". Niche sites and e-commerce can go to zero quickly, which has happened to him, so he is glad he did not go all in and kept the agency.
- E-commerce is "very tough to do right". He got burned earlier on a couple of FBA businesses, mostly from lack of knowledge and platform issues.
- Shopify is the only e-commerce platform he considers viable. He says anyone suggesting otherwise is wrong.

chunks.heading: Drop shipping to private label: the Far and Away path
chunks.text:
- He and co-founder Albert ran a drop shipping store on Shopify selling dinnerware from China. It proved product-market fit for luxury dinnerware. It hit 7 figures, scaled to about $300K/month (about $2M a year), then fell to about $100K/month.
- Why it fell: Facebook bans from long shipping times (post-purchase surveys led to negative feedback and low ad ratings) and the iOS update, which broke cross-device tracking and conversion data.
- Exit to private equity at a "crappy" multiple, under 2x, because the business was declining. The earn-out paid only about 70 to 80% because the buyer went bankrupt.
- He recommends e-commerce in 2023 for starting out. Use drop shipping (including onshore suppliers) to test products fast. When a product wins, source it, get it into a US warehouse, use 3PLs to fulfil, then private label and build a real brand.
- With the proceeds, they built Far and Away properly: visited 14 factories in Portugal over two weeks and partnered with a family-owned factory. COVID logistics and shipping costs nearly made them question the business, but it is now solidly profitable and has opened new revenue channels.
- Sourcing from Portugal rather than China makes COGS "absolutely sky high", a trade-off they accepted to build something they are proud to recommend.

chunks.heading: Launching with Kickstarter and validating products
chunks.text:
- Far and Away's first customers came from a Kickstarter campaign that raised about $100K all in, used to pay for the first inventory batch and confirm everything worked.
- Why Kickstarter: you do not need much cash and do not have to hit the factory's minimum order quantities. You visit the factory, shoot strong video and imagery, and launch.
- Traffic: Facebook ads plus Kickstarter agencies. Agencies have mature pixels of Kickstarter backers and email lists, so they retarget well, for a "fat fee". They also built their own list with their own ads.
- Kickstarter works "almost like SEO". Ranking on the front page is "a guaranteed six figure" campaign.
- Test product-market fit before launching a new product. A Kickstarter for French artisanal scented candles "flopped so hard". They had spent $20K producing assets, but it saved them the cost of a full launch.

chunks.heading: Facebook ads and conversion diagnostics
chunks.text:
- He says his partner runs the ads, but gives these keys: test many creatives, get targeting right, and mature the pixel.
- Maturing the pixel means burning money early to feed Facebook purchase data. After purchases come in, create look-alike audiences.
- His drop shipping launch: he and Albert each put in $5K. They burned $8K total, were about to pull the plug, and then one ad took off and paid for everything. "You just need one."
- Always run conversion-optimized campaigns optimized for purchase, never for events further up the funnel, even with zero purchase data, so Facebook can match look-alikes from other campaigns.
- Diagnostics when ads get traffic but no sales:
  - Cost per click under about 50 cents suggests a good ad.
  - Otherwise, look at the funnel (cost per view product, add to cart, initiated checkout), compare to industry norms and find the drop-off. It is typically add to cart.
  - Most often the problem is the website: no CRO (sticky add to cart, one-click purchase), slow load times (5 seconds and "it's over"). A set percentage of visitors will always convert, depending on the site.

chunks.heading: E-commerce margins and extra revenue streams
chunks.text:
- Margin rule: 70 to 80%+ gross margins (a $100 product should cost $15 to $25 to acquire). Shipping and weight count toward gross margin. Lower margins are possible only if the ads are exceptional.
- Dinnerware was a headache because of dimensional weight and breakage, now eased with insurance.
- He argues every e-commerce store should add display ads and affiliate revenue. Most stores run 5 to 10% net margins, and these streams lift that substantially.
- Far and Away's blog is not for selling products. It earns affiliate revenue (about $4.5K/month, the biggest non-e-commerce income there) and was about to turn on display ads, estimated at about $2K/month. His illustration: a $50K/month store at 10% net makes $5K/month free cash flow, and these streams add several thousand more.
- Benefits: raises the valuation, takes growth pressure off the core business, and lets them reinvest faster. He says e-commerce sites are currently favorable in Google because they do not look like niche sites gaming display and affiliate revenue.
- Epic Gardening is his example of a company doing display well.
- He says e-commerce should be run as a cash-flowing business, not VC-funded. He cites Allbirds, Casper and Made.com (whose domain sold for about $2M at a fire sale).

chunks.heading: Niche sites, AI and acquisitions
chunks.text:
- AI risk: display-ad content sites answering simple queries ("can dogs eat lettuce") will be hurt because AI answers in one line.
- Still viable: comparison and "best X" sites (for example best dog food), because people still shop by comparing and clicking links.
- Acquisition example: a mid-six-figure portfolio of niche sites that came with a custom-rate Amazon affiliate account paying 8% on home goods, versus the typical 2 to 3%. The previous owner was a large Amazon affiliate site owner who got hit by Google. He bought it mainly for the rate card.
- Moving any Amazon affiliate site onto that account adds immediate value, three to four times by his estimate. Payback on some sites drops to about a year, after which it is "pure profit". He is stacking recurring revenue this way and accepts the risk the rate could go away.
- He is now looking for distressed businesses, particularly VC-funded e-commerce brands that are underwater.

chunks.heading: Link building service
chunks.text:
- His agency's productized service sells backlinks. He says it is "not trade secret", just a lot of work requiring many VAs.
- Process: scrape sites and their emails, email offering to buy backlinks, negotiate wholesale rates by promising volume as an agency. Gross margins run about 40 to 80%, and he keeps the spread.
- Side benefit: he never has to worry about links for his own niche sites and builds the best ones for his own businesses.

chunks.heading: Income transparency and handling criticism
chunks.text:
- He shares income and net worth because the SEO industry is opaque and full of grifters. He wants to let people judge who the experts are. He notes others stop income reports when revenue drops, while he kept going. Reports are at marketingletter.com.
- Income mix: Indexsy (affiliate sites plus agency and productized service) is roughly 80% of income. The service side is typically 50%+ of that. Last month: Amazon affiliates about $45K, Mediavine display ads $30-something K, a short-term rental building in Portugal about $10K/month, and small affiliates (Binance, VPN) $3 to 5K/month.
- Net worth: mostly real estate equity, plus cash-like holdings and stocks, notably Tesla (rolled from GameStop call profits).
- Criticism: engage with valid, constructive points. Otherwise mute rather than block on Twitter. Blocked haters cannot comment, which loses engagement. Muted ones still engage and boost the algorithm while you do not see them, "a win-win".

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Jacky Chou walks through 50+ small online business deals, including wins (towing directory, sponsored brand placements) and losses (Amazon rate card removed, commodity web hosting). He argues software has no product moat anymore, so distribution, public building, diversification and taking chips off the table matter most.

chunks.heading: How Jacky buys, sizes and funds small online business deals
chunks.text:
- Jacky runs Indexy, a holding company that acquires and builds online businesses. He has built a portfolio of 50+ online businesses over about 10 years.
- His path: studied electrical engineering, hated it, Googled how to make money online, then found Black Hat World, drop shipping and affiliate marketing. Those profits became the capital he now invests.
- Deal sizes are small: from about $500 to $5K up to a largest deal of $800K.
- Deals are fully self-funded: no loans, no partners.
- Structure: asset sales, not share deals. He pays cash upfront with an earnout, or buys 51% controlling interest in the asset and has the owner stay on. If the asset takes off, he buys the owner out. If not, "crisis averted."
- When the existing owner stays on, deals "do really really well" because the owner stays invested. He then plugs in his own distribution engine.
- Sourcing is reactive, not active: marketplaces and DMs. People who know he is in the adult space send him adult-space sites. He only does a deal if it is a "no-brainer" priced under market value. In his industry the spread between price and value is large, and any spread is an opportunity.

chunks.heading: Due diligence and red flags on online business deals
chunks.text:
- Diligence takes him a day or two.
- Check where the traffic comes from. If it is organic, check Ahrefs and Google Search Console. Some sellers fake traffic numbers, and he has caught this a few times ("You said it's Google. It's definitely not Google").
- If traffic is not organic, he audits all the campaigns.
- He won't touch businesses whose traffic comes from LLMs such as ChatGPT. No tool like Ahrefs shows what you rank for there, so he can't audit it.
- Small software businesses often run on "duct tape in the back end," which is a problem once an engineer looks at the code.
- Avoid commodity businesses. His web hosting purchase was a dud at about $400/month. He had expected a home run because of hosting valuations, but the market is too commoditized.
- Pattern that works: he only builds or buys in a space where he is deep in the trenches. Before launching local SEO software he posted about local SEO daily for about 9 months, with a daily YouTube video. He knew the pain points and assumed most people share the ones he has. Outsiders can't easily replicate it because they don't know the industry's nuances.

chunks.heading: Platform risk, and what happened to his deals
chunks.text:
- He argues that content-site and rollup deals are "priced in" for high yield (e.g. 30% a year). Money can be returned in 1-3 years, but "the platform risk is insane."
- Of the sites bought three years ago, he estimates about 5% max are still alive. Most went to zero.
- Towing directory (success): bought for $10K from a founder in Lithuania who hand-dialed New York callers and lost them on accent. It ranked #1 for "towing near me" but made only about $500/month. The founder stayed on for about 10%. He built it into the largest towing directory in the US and sold it for $195K about 6 months later. He exited early because the East Coast towing contacts seemed linked to organized crime and began making subtle threats during negotiations.
- Affiliate site bundle (mixed): about $300K+ for 10 affiliate sites making about $10K/month total. The real value was a custom Amazon affiliate rate card paying about 4x the normal commission. The sites were spammy and all trended to zero within 12 months. He recovered the money only because of the rate card.
- The rate card's scale: about $40M a year in shipped revenue to Amazon. Roughly four months before this interview (Dec 2025), Amazon removed the rates with no notice, no email and no support.
- He had pitched large affiliate businesses: attach to his rate card, get 4x revenue, he takes 20%.
- He reports monthly revenue publicly. It ranged from about $70K at the low to $560K in a single month (about 50% net) at the peak, and sits around $200K now.

chunks.heading: Quick-win tactics for acquired affiliate and SEO sites
chunks.text:
- Fix web design first, especially ugly affiliate buttons. He says this alone can give about a 50% uplift.
- Change publish dates to the current month. Google may treat the article as fresh and boost it.
- Attach a higher affiliate rate card, where available.
- Sell sponsored placements. If you rank for something like "best protein powder," go to the brands and demand a flat fee (e.g. $10K/month) plus a high commission. Most affiliates don't do this because they're poor at sales and accept Amazon's roughly 10%.
- Results: at the $550K/month peak, about half came from these partnerships. At one point he ranked for most supplement-industry keywords. The most from one brand on one page was $50K/month plus about 60% commission, because brands wanted external traffic to lift Amazon sales velocity.
- He follows FTC rules and labels the #1 slot as sponsored.
- Media partnership model: he partners with a dying local newspaper and borrows its SEO authority with guides on its domain (e.g. "best Vancouver realtor"). He then pitches local businesses on being listed #1 (e.g. $500/month). That model makes about $30K/month.

chunks.heading: Why he now builds software instead of buying it
chunks.text:
- His thesis has shifted: "There is no product moat at all... in especially software." He thinks most B2B SaaS could be replicated in a couple of weeks at most, so "all you need is distribution."
- He mostly builds rather than buys software now. He'd only buy a small local SEO or SEO tool that is mostly built and doing low numbers.
- Market state: buyers are scarce. Rollups have no money and strategics are scared, so valuations are low and you "can value however you want." Exits to Semrush, Ahrefs or a large agency would be "pennies on the dollar."
- Ecom buyers pick up businesses at inventory value (he cites $30M/year businesses), fire the team and run them with their own people.
- Local SEO agencies are the one acquisition category he'd consider. Many are badly run and resell subcontracted services, and you effectively buy the retainers. Downsides: they sell at 2x on the low end (up to 3-5x if large), and once the founder leaves it gets iffy.
- Local SEO outlook: local ranking relies on directory mentions (e.g. Yelp), reviews and directions clicks, which differs from organic SEO. He doesn't expect Google to add AI summaries to local maps soon.

chunks.heading: Distribution engine and launching into an audience
chunks.text:
- His engine is YouTube, X and a newsletter. The audience is small but very loyal, and "would buy everything I sell."
- When a product aligns with his audience it hits hard. His local SEO software did $30K out of the gate. A small $100 service did about $6K in a couple of hours and should settle at $10-20K/month. He sees the ceiling for these small services at about $50K/month.
- Alignment is essential. The hosting product flopped because it did not fit the audience and was a commodity.
- He builds in public and says copying isn't the risk: "execution is like everything now."
- Test widely and decide fast. Cast a wide net, go all in if something has product-market fit, and cut or sell fast if not (pennies is fine).
- Daily routine: record a video every day, check ad campaigns, give product input to his tech co-founder, help with customer service if needed, then work on distribution and ad creatives. He films his Meta ad creatives himself because AI avatars aren't working on Meta.
- Advice for someone starting from zero: short-form content daily, YouTube short and long form, redistributed elsewhere. With all the time in the world, 3 short-form pieces and 1 long-form a day. Do it for 100 days and he believes you'd make at least a dollar online. Posting daily lets you see which videos get more views and do more of those.

chunks.heading: Team, portfolio and risk management
chunks.text:
- Team: about 13 full-time, mostly overseas. It includes AI-enabled VAs, video editors, a web developer, a front-end engineer and his tech co-founder. On acquisitions, he usually partners with a founder or operator who runs operations while he handles marketing.
- He let go of about 60% of his team because of AI. Content writing, editing, posting, formatting and graphic design are now done with AI (e.g. "one click is like thousand articles"), along with repetitive tasks.
- About 20 revenue-generating assets exceed roughly $500/month. Smaller ones are "dead residuals" he doesn't count. They include software, media partnerships, an SEO agency (about $50K/month) and a paid community.
- Community: Advice, an SEO / make-money-online community of about 500 members at $169/month (annual plan available), making about $30K/month by his figures. The culture is blunt and "grungy."
- Diversification: he holds a lot of cash (about 20-30%, perhaps 40% counting treasuries). His reasoning is that all his businesses are "risk on," so the rest of his holdings should be risk off.
- His advice to buyers: "Take your chips off the table periodically." Don't keep going all in. If you can exit even a portion, do it. "You wouldn't do that with Tesla stock. Why would you do that with a business?"

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Jacky Chou walks through his SEO income streams for 2024. He favors affiliate revenue and rev-share partnerships with struggling funded sites, sells top placements to brands, and expects informational and display-ad traffic to die. Includes tactics for landing a first client and why he's moving toward owning products.

chunks.heading: Affiliate SEO outlook for 2024: what still works
chunks.text:
- Jacky is "very, very bullish" on affiliate. He expects affiliate revenue to stay around.
- He calls display ads "clapped": third-party cookie removal plus Google SGE is "the perfect storm". Anyone bullish on display ads "needs to check themselves."
- He calls informational content dead within about two years. His view: a query like "can dogs eat lettuce" gets answered by SGE. He puts it at 90% certainty that a site fully reliant on Google informational traffic loses its revenue within five years.
- Content that needs nuance and has health or money impact survives better, e.g. "best testosterone boosters for men over 50", where people want to read reviews.
- He does not recommend expired or auction domains in 2024: Google catches them quickly. He has never seen one live more than two years in recent years. They are only worth it for short-term gains.
- Parasite SEO is here to stay for a while but is a cat-and-mouse game. A page on Outlook India might work for three months, get clapped, and then the play moves to Google Groups or LinkedIn Pulse. Parasite is for short-term gains.
- For long-term gains, he says to build from scratch properly and move toward partnerships.
- Link building needs more variety in 2024: citations, niche edits, guest posts, "a bit of everything". Treat the site like a real business rather than a niche-edit-only play.
- Niches:
  - Home is evergreen and needs no content updates.
  - Supplements require catching trends. If Huberman mentions something, publish immediately. One term went from about 100 searches a month to about 100k after a celebrity mention.

chunks.heading: The partnership (rev-share) model
chunks.text:
- Origin: a health-tech startup founder with a DR6 site (at the time) and a couple million sessions a month messaged Jacky. They were running out of runway and could not monetize the traffic. Jacky took a risk on a rev-share deal, which he had never done before.
- Deal structure:
  - Low share on display ads.
  - 50/50 on affiliate commissions.
  - No cut of the partner's core product revenue (e.g. their online TRT service). He only takes commissions from affiliate content on their blog.
- Result: that first partnership scaled from 0 to $300K a month in under three months.
- Why it works: he piggybacks on the partner's existing authority (built through VC funding, PR and a big team). The partner is struggling to monetize and needs cash.
- Why partners don't do it themselves: they lack the expertise in ranking, keyword research and industry outreach to thousands of brands a week, and they have full-time jobs.
- Jacky's view of the competition: niche sites have been clapped because the SERPs are owned by big companies and private-equity groups. His response is to "fight fire with fire" and partner with one of those big sites rather than compete with a DR5 niche site.
- He rolls up partnerships, but saturation hits fast. With 20 partners in one niche you have already dominated page one, so the next step is new niches or your own brand.

chunks.heading: Retail rank and rent on partnership sites
chunks.text:
- Plain Amazon affiliate articles on a ranking site might earn about $50k a month.
- The step further: once ranking for a term like "best protein powder", pitch the top brands directly. The offer is "pay us 20K a month, we'll put you on number one, and 50% commissions on top."
- It is a no-brainer for a brand with around 90% gross margin, since they still profit and are seen as number one.
- He calls these "retail rank and rents". They make up the majority of partnership revenue.
- This requires heavy sales: three full-time salespeople sending outreach emails.

chunks.heading: Finding your first partnerships
chunks.text:
- Start small. A DR90 software company doing $10M a year will not talk to a nobody.
- Think creatively about who you know. His example: a well-known downtown Vancouver restaurant he frequents, whose owner he knows, that is DR50. That could become a kitchenware affiliate site or a recipe site.
- Smaller-DR sites also work and do well, depending on the niche.
- E-commerce partnerships are another route. His pilot was Far and Away, his e-commerce company with a business partner (Albert):
  - He did a two-year proof of concept, scaling slowly before showing the partner revenue.
  - Informational and affiliate content irrelevant to the store now adds a flat $10-15K a month.
  - E-commerce runs at 10-20% net margins at most, so extra free cash flow is valuable. Far and Away did multi six figures in November with 20-30% net margins.
  - Paid ads to the brand also send positive brand-search and social signals to Google.
- He is bullish on e-commerce partnerships, especially with brands spending seven figures a month on marketing.

chunks.heading: Agency and landing the first client
chunks.text:
- Jacky is not taking traditional retainers. His minimum retainer has been raised to about $10K a month because he does not want to deal with them. Most of his growth now comes from partnerships.
- First-client tactic for a beginner: rank-guaranteed offers.
  - Rank for a low-competition local term, like "best Vancouver realtor" (about 100 searches a month). He says if you cannot do it, "maybe you should question yourself".
  - Example: he used a parasite asset on Outlook India to rank number one for "best Vancouver realtor", then did outreach: "I ranked you at first place." If they don't pay, move to the next realtor.
- Local clients pay at most about $2K a month. This is fine when starting out, but five of them at $10K total means five people breathing down your neck, which is tiring.
- Directories are a good source of local clients. Once you rank for a term, others ask to be ranked too.

chunks.heading: Directory-style rank and rent
chunks.text:
- Jacky defends James Dooley's rank-and-rent: it works at scale in high-CPA niches. For example, a job worth $20-30K at $10K a month per asset per city across multiple UK cities makes the math work. He says people should research before hating.
- His own approach differs: add directories to partnership sites. For a job-board partner he would build an SEO agency directory (e.g. jobboard.com/agency), copying the Clutch.co model.
- Clutch does about $30M a year selling Yelp-style ads to SEO companies. Jacky has spent $20K a month with them and says the deals were incredible.
- The idea: "Clutch for dentists, Clutch for daycares, Clutch for real estate agents".
- Closing is the hard part. Most won't pay, so he often takes ad revenue instead.
  - Easier in high-risk niches: in Canadian cannabis, he messaged two people and got "all right we're in for 2K a month".
  - Harder with Vancouver real estate agents, who close multi-million dollar deals but won't pay $500 a month.

chunks.heading: Closing the loop and diversification
chunks.text:
- 2024 goal: "close the loop" by launching his own products rather than only rolling up partnerships.
- Reasoning: he owns four or five slots on competitive supplement keywords. Keyword tools show a term at about 50 searches a month, while the Amazon volume he pushes is about 3K a day, so he has insight into what is selling that tools miss.
- Options: pass the insight to supplement partners and take equity, or launch the product himself. His Amazon logic: if he pushes $1K a day to a product via Associates, he could launch on Amazon, get about 10 reviews, take a 50% haircut and still make $500 a day.
- He does not chase virality-dependent traffic such as Pinterest or Google Discover. It is inconsistent and hard to project. He has sites with thousands of Discover visits a day and doesn't know why, so he finds Discover courses make no sense.
- Paid ads on Far and Away are his diversification beyond Google.

chunks.heading: Community and personal brand
chunks.text:
- He is putting more focus on his paid SEO community (Indexsy-style). It dropped to about $1,500 a month when he ignored it. Since he started focusing on it, it has grown to over 100 members who are active and refer each other.
- His audience skews toward people purely focused on making money, not in-house SEOs talking about schema.
- He is bullish on continuing to post on Twitter (most active there) and YouTube. His view: you can make a lot with few viewers if you dial in the content. Friends can't sit through his videos, but those who do have SEO expertise and a minimum income level, so the audience is valuable.
- He directs people to marketingletter.com for his net worth and newsletter.
- Last month's business revenue was an all-time high of $500K, with profit in the high 30s percent.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Jacky Chou explains how he uses public parasite SEO as a tester to attract publisher partnerships, then runs 50/50 deals with content ownership and residuals. He covers humanizing AI content, limiting publishing velocity, and monetizing rankings with 40%+ commissions via Amazon.

chunks.heading: Parasite SEO in late 2024: what still works and what doesn't
chunks.text:
- Jacky was an early public tester of parasite SEO. Last year, buying posts on big sites (e.g. Outlook India) ranked for almost anything, from "best protein powder" to "best CRM software". He ran the tests in public so he wouldn't risk his partnership sites.
- After Google's manual site reputation abuse action, he says well-known public parasite sites are much harder to rank on for competitive terms. He calls it "not really an update" because Google had to manually go in and hit people.
- Private or lesser-known parasite sites he tested still "work like a charm". As long as Google doesn't know about a site yet, it is still easy to abuse.
- He says Reddit is currently the easiest public parasite site to abuse and works best of the public ones.
- Free parasites have not worked for him except Reddit.
- Reddit risk: he 301-redirected about 10 domains to a Reddit subdirectory in public. It ranked well, then Reddit removed the whole subreddit.
- Parasites are a tester and a funnel for him. He posts tests in public to attract partnership leads.
- His total parasite earnings are under about $10k. He did not sell the "best Vancouver realtor" page he ranked.
- Over 99% of his revenue comes from partnerships.

chunks.heading: Partnership model: how Jacky sources publishers
chunks.text:
- Most deals are inbound. Publishers range from large bloggers at DR60 to private equity firms holding six or seven DR80+ sites. Once one signs, he gets access to their whole portfolio.
- He is now scaling outreach with a filter of DR60+ and contacts "anyone and everyone", which he calls a shotgun approach.
- He only works in English, since there is more money there. He sees Brazilian Portuguese and German as promising markets and notes Google hasn't hit parasites in other languages as hard. He believes Japanese and Korean publishers prefer local partners.
- He screens publishers by traffic history. If a site fell from about 1 million sessions a month to about 50k, he declines unless they accept adult content. His reason: he can only humanize a limited number of articles at once, so he won't produce hundreds of articles for a site that won't rank.
- He sets niche boundaries up front. His niches are mostly supplements and pharma (including peptides). He avoids casino and payday loans in partnerships, and asks whether publishers are open to OnlyFans content. In parasite tests he'll try anything.
- OnlyFans keywords are low competition, and he says real volumes can be 50-100% higher than tools show, sometimes up to 10x.

chunks.heading: Partnership deal terms and contracts
chunks.text:
- Always use contracts. He says publishers who offer handshake deals will "screw you in a heartbeat" once it takes off.
- The split is always 50/50 with the publisher. The publisher gets a maximum of 50%, and there is no negotiation. If a publisher wants less for himself, he points them elsewhere, since an inexperienced operator "is gonna run your site to the ground".
- Where a third party makes an intro, he gets a 10% kickback and the publisher still gets 50%.
- Terms: Jacky's side owns the content it creates and gets two years of residuals. If the publisher terminates, they must either remove all the content or buy him out for two years of revenue. He calls this aggressive.
- Example: one top partnership hit $500k revenue a month within two months. The publisher was paying an agency $250k a month for content, grew resentful of the cost, and has been trying to get out since. Their own attempts to replicate it in another subdirectory didn't rank.

chunks.heading: Content production and avoiding detection
chunks.text:
- For test pages he doesn't optimize. For pages he wants to rank, he humanizes and then re-optimizes.
- Humanizing: content must pass AI detector tests, then is optimized with Surfer or equivalent.
- Evidence: partnership sites he humanized and kept quiet about stayed fine, while sites where he went aggressive without humanizing all got hit. He doesn't publicly report the numbers of the surviving sites.
- On-page effort: heavy formatting, unique edited images, and E-E-A-T signals. Pages look like Forbes-style articles with "reviewed by" and "edited by" lines. He pays real people to sign off, using their names.
- Velocity matters. Sites where he blasted thousands of articles a month got hit quickly, while 50-100 a month stayed under the radar. He tested across more than 15 partnership sites.
- His guess (he says he doesn't know for sure): what matters is the ratio to the site's normal publishing rate. A site like TechCrunch could absorb 50 extra a day, while a newspaper posting one a day could not absorb thousands.
- Content cost is negligible. He uses Koala, with free credits as a large affiliate. The host mentioned a competing tool at 7-8 cents per 1,000 words, which Jacky did not claim as his own cost.

chunks.heading: Linking, maintenance and operations
chunks.text:
- Internal linking is always done: "no-brainer, it's free".
- Backlinks only as needed. He found no relationship between link building and success. Some sites he built links to never flew, while several with zero links took off after about six months.
- He builds links retrospectively, only for pages already on positions 5-10 that he wants in the top 3. He doesn't start until a page is around page two.
- Partnerships can take months. Some sites began climbing after six months, so he warns that cutting stagnant sites early may be a mistake.
- Planning: a massive content calendar. He pushes harder on sites that perform and cuts back on stagnant ones.
- Stack: Google Sheets, VAs, Trello, Slack, and a master partnerships sheet. He tracks thousands of pages across about 15 publishers.
- Freshness: he runs a plugin that changes the publish date and the first paragraph of each article. He updates pages when new, higher-paying offers come in.
- Keyword strategy: about 50-60% different keywords across domains to avoid footprints. The core keywords are shared across sites. He targets low-KD (0-10 on Ahrefs) but high-volume supplement keywords.

chunks.heading: Monetization: brand deals and affiliate commissions
chunks.text:
- He calls his model "retail rank and rent": brands pay him to be number one for a keyword, and he keeps a list of historical payers to re-approach.
- He asks for at least 40% commission on articles he ranks for.
- He prefers Amazon over custom affiliate programs like FanFuel or Sale Health at the same commission rate, since Amazon converts better and pays more overall. He notes those two companies sponsor him.
- He also promotes direct offers from manufacturers or retailers.
- Best payout: about $40k a month for being ranked number one plus 40% commission. He attributes it to VC-funded brands that don't care about cost.
- OnlyFans-adjacent traffic: he says some networks pay per click, so traffic doesn't need to convert.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Jacky Chou explains how Local Rank sells software by first building a paid education community, gating free checklists on X, and using YouTube to launch. He also covers local SEO ranking levers (reviews, citations, CTR) and how to sell local SEO to high-CPC niches.

chunks.heading: Local SEO basics: the three ranking levers for the map pack
chunks.text:
Jacky defines local SEO as ranking in the Google "map pack", the block between the ads and the organic results. Most people click there because the business is near them. Typical queries are "realtor near me", "dentist near me" and "gyms Vancouver". He treats it as any query where the searcher intends to drive or walk somewhere.

His 80/20 for ranking #1 in a city:
- **Google reviews.** Get a lot of them.
- **Citations.** Brand mentions listing name, address and phone number (NAP). Consistency of NAP across the internet is a local ranking factor.
- **Click-through rate.** The number of people visiting and driving to the Google Business Profile.

He says that as of August 1, 2025 local SEO is "stupid easy" and "super abusable". Some listings rank in seven days, which he says is impossible in normal organic search. Google can only draw on a limited set of signals because it is essentially just Google Maps. Hypothetically, if he started a plumbing business, he would hand out fives on the busiest street and expect to rank within 30 days.

chunks.heading: Gray-hat tactics for reviews, citations and CTR
chunks.text:
Jacky is open that these are gray hat. He says they work, and he does not know how long they will keep working.

**Reviews**
- If he were 18 and broke, he would stand on a street corner or a university campus and pay people $5 for a five-star review, writing the review for them.
- Different phones and local IPs make the reviews hard for Google to trace. He includes target keywords in the review text.

**Citations**
- One-click citation services exist now. With zero budget, he would hand-register about 50 directory listings himself, or buy them on Fiverr.
- To check that citations are live, search the exact-match business name in quotes on Google. It is a quick check, but imperfect for exact-match domains.
- Citations tell Google the business is real. They can also help a new Google Business Profile stick if it has a missing-place listing.

**Indexing the citations**
- He uses SpeedyIndex, a Telegram-bot indexer. He says it traps Google crawlers in a loop of sites and forces them to follow an outbound link to the submitted URL.

**CTR**
- Take an Uber from a few blocks away to the business, with the location set to the Google Business Profile. Tip the driver $5 for a five-star review.
- Jumper Media: his team tested it on one location. In 30 days the business went from outside the map pack to inside it. They piggyback on mobile app ad data to make it look like people travel to the location. They have a non-compete per niche in an area, so a second HVAC company would not be signed.
- His idea: partner with free step-counting or walking apps (Sweatcoin-style) and gamify walks to locations whose owners pay for CTR. Hundreds of people walking to one location a day should lift its ranking. He is looking for a developer to build it.

chunks.heading: Selling local SEO: niches, offers, pricing and outreach
chunks.text:
Jacky says fulfillment is the easy part and sales is the hard part, so the community teaches mostly sales.

**Which niches**
- Target high cost-per-click service businesses: personal injury lawyers, roofing, pest control.
- Method: look at the service categories on Thumbtack, find the highest CPCs in your geography, and pitch those companies on ranking higher on Google Maps.

**Offer**
- The offer has to be strong because the market is competitive. A ranking guarantee works.
- He notes Jumper's trick of guaranteeing a tiny radius (about 5 km), where the business probably already ranks. Many SEO companies guarantee long-tail terms.

**Pricing**
- Price off the customer's average order value (AOV). A roofing company in Vancouver can pay up to about $400-500 a month. A restaurant might be about $300 a month, with an actual cost of about $50.
- Start high and drop the price until they say yes, but leave margin for the fulfiller.

**Outreach**
- Do what overseas competitors cannot: cold calls (he says a local accent helps) and cold walk-ins. One community member bought $100 of donuts and closed the client the next day.
- Cold email: niche down (for example "easyroofing.com", not a generic SEO brand name) and send high volume. Put a naked, unclickable domain in the signature. He says it gets about a 10% visit rate, so 100 emails a day brings about 10 direct visits.
- Send the first email with no links and the second a day later with a link, to protect deliverability. He uses cheap SMTP servers. He cares about opens and traffic to the site, not reply rate.

chunks.heading: Local Rank's community funnel and TAM creation
chunks.text:
Jacky's product, Local Rank, sells to people who run local SEO agencies. He says the local SEO tool market is tiny because few people offer local SEO, so the company has to educate people and "build the actual TAM".

**Funnel**
1. Organic content on X: free swipe files, such as a 65-point local SEO checklist, are teased in a long post. The CTA is to comment "local rank" and get the file by DM. The post is in a "boring local SEO" style.
2. The email is required to receive the template. After sign-up: a VSL right away, heavy retargeting, and a roughly 40-email flow.
3. Direct-response ads retarget into the paid community, Local Rank Academy (the pitch: first client in 90 days). Everything taught uses Local Rank.
4. The software is upsold from the community.

**Numbers and lessons**
- The community did about $5K MRR in its first month. He runs it at break even to offset the paid ads budget, and treats the software as "the gravy".
- An enterprise client paid about $20K for the year, which he says came through the community and would not have happened without the education.
- Pushing people straight into the software did worse after heavy testing, because it is too hard to use without education.
- One month on X: roughly half a million impressions, which he equates to about $20K in Meta CPMs.
- His moat is that his team does local SEO for clients themselves, so they find small problems that copycats cannot.

chunks.heading: Channel results: YouTube, Meta, Google, Reddit
chunks.text:
- **YouTube:** he says about 90% of the roughly $15K MRR at launch came from YouTube, from a coupon he gave out on YouTube and X. He had talked about local SEO on the channel for about half a year to a year before launching. His advice: "go all in on YouTube" and dominate an industry, then launch. Demand is built first and then captured.
- **Meta ads:** about $120 CAC, payback in two to three months, churn maybe 10-15%. Profitable but worse than he expected.
- **Organic X:** the most profitable channel for him, via the funnel above.
- **Google and YouTube ads:** did not work. CAC was about $400 and he says they burned roughly $20K learning that.
- **Reddit ads:** about the same as Meta, targeting SEO subreddits.

chunks.heading: Reddit parasite SEO and moving search volume
chunks.text:
**Reddit parasite SEO**
- Parasite SEO means piggybacking on another site's domain authority.
- SOP: search the target keyword (for example "best creatine gummies"), open the top Reddit result, and leave a soft-sell comment on that thread with no link ("I tried XYZ creatine and liked it"). Buy about 50 upvotes and 10 comments. He says it can rank in about a week for roughly $10 of upvotes, versus years with a new site.
- He says it also feeds AI answers, since ChatGPT and Perplexity pull heavily from Reddit.
- He says upvotes and downvotes can steer a thread's direction, and that buying large subreddits from their mods (he guesses about $5K) is an opportunity.

**Lifting branded search for "local rank tracker"**
- He says Local Rank is #4 for "local rank tracker" on Google about a month after launch, above Semrush. Competitors have existed for years.
- Tactics: put "search local rank tracker on Google" in cold email signatures and in job listings.
- He used GSA to send about 70K contact-form fills in 7 days. The message names the brand and the search term, with no URLs, so his domains are not blacklisted. The goal is search impressions, not conversions.
- Result: Search Console shows about 6.5K searches a month versus roughly 1,900 in Semrush.
- He turned the idea into a product, Browser Blast, which mimics virality to push rankings. He says driving traffic and positive signals to one URL can lift rankings two to three pages at a time.

chunks.heading: AI SEO: what he sees and what he distrusts
chunks.text:
- He says no agency has figured out how to rank in LLMs consistently, and he would monetize it if he had. He warns buyers to be careful with agencies that claim to.
- He says the pattern so far is brand mentions: LLMs pull from popular subreddits and page-one-to-three listicles, and Google AI Overviews pull from press releases.
- Press releases and listicles that name you first (for example "best Vancouver SEO company") tend to get you into AI Overviews. A #1 spot in the biggest subreddit on a topic tends to get you into ChatGPT. He has not cracked Perplexity.
- His case study for a Vancouver physio clinic got press releases mentioned for "best physio Vancouver 2025", but not consistently.
- Idea he is testing: build your own subreddit, buy about 100K members, and simulate activity to see whether LLMs treat it as a major source.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Jacky walks through his timeline from a €450/mo Berlin internship in 2014 to about $500k/mo in revenue. It covers the Indexsy SEO agency, a dropshipping boom and bust, niche site flips, and the partnerships model that drove 2023 revenue. He also answers practical questions on partnerships and rank-and-rent.

chunks.heading: Timeline from $0 to about $500k/month (2014 to 2024)
chunks.text:
Jacky says Indexsy and his other ventures hit roughly $500k in a month in late 2024. His path:

- **2014:** Failing courses, so he took a year off for a paid internship in Berlin at €450/month with €300 rent. He ate canned bouillon plus two eggs daily for about 3 months to save money.
- **2015:** Back in Canada finishing his degree, working part-time at GNC (supplement store) for roughly 1,500 CAD/month.
- **2016:** First job out of college as a growth manager at a hardware startup (Contact IO) for €3,000/month. He started Indexsy, an SEO agency, the same year. First client paid $1K/month; total income reached roughly $4,500/month.
- **2017:** Head of growth role at a Berlin startup for €6,000/month. Indexsy had 2-3 clients at about $2K/month each. Total roughly $8,500/month pre-tax.
- **2018:** Dropshipping peak, averaging about $55k/month for his split, with the agency also doing well.
- **2019-2020:** Dropshipping collapsed. Profit margin fell from 60-80% to about 20-30%. Indexsy "kept the lights on", averaging about $44.5k/month.
- **2021-2022:** The "Covid run". 16-hour days, crypto and GameStop trading, flipping sites and watches. The agency did about $200k/month and ecommerce about $150k/month.
- **2023:** Niche sites were hit by Google updates. He exited many beforehand, including a couple of six-figure exits. February revenue bottomed at $74k with profit of roughly $10-20k/month. The year averaged $222k/month; November and December were the two best months, at roughly $5xxk and $483k.
- **2024:** About $500k in the most recent month.

chunks.heading: Dropshipping: what worked and why it died
chunks.text:
- **Start:** His partner Albert proposed it. They put in $5K each and burned about $99,500 before one product clicked.
- **Winner:** Cutlery sourced from China, peaking around $250k/month in revenue.
- **Why it collapsed (2019-2020):**
  - Facebook cracked down on dropshipping. After each purchase pixel fired, buyers got a quiz asking if they liked the product. Since the product hadn't arrived, they answered negatively, and enough negatives got the Facebook page and ad account banned.
  - The iOS update removed much purchase data.
  - Covid plus supplier problems: suppliers couldn't deliver for about a year after he paid $40-50k up front, tying up cash for a year and a half.
- **Lesson:** Revenue figures hid the damage. Going from $55k to $45k a month looked small, but margins went from 60-80% down to 20-30%.
- **Rescue:** Indexsy's agency income kept him afloat.

chunks.heading: Recovery: refocus on the agency and partnerships
chunks.text:
- After the February 2023 low ($74k revenue, $10-20k profit), he concentrated on the agency side.
- He then "stumbled upon partnerships", which he says drove huge revenue into the business and took 2023 to a $222k monthly average.
- Selling niche sites before algorithm updates preserved value. He exited a lot of them before Google hit.
- Diversified income (agency, ecommerce, site flips, affiliate) let one business carry him while another failed.

chunks.heading: Partnership SEO model: how Jacky works with site owners
chunks.text:
- **Access needed:** WordPress admin login on a subdirectory of the partner's domain (e.g. partnersite.com/advisor). He just needs a blank WordPress install there.
- **Content fit:** He prefers content relevant to the partner site's theme. They have stretched (home-ware sites pushing supplements) and it worked, but how far to stretch depends on the partner relationship.
- **Amazon affiliate:** Set up the account yourself, run it through your own tracking tag, and add the partner's site to your site list ("don't get clapped").
- **Optimization and authority:** SEO includes optimization; content still needs it. The partner's authority (e.g. a 10-year-old DR 63 domain) helps ranking but doesn't replace it.
- **OnlyFans:** They rank for OnlyFans keywords and push the traffic to an agency. He believes it's one of the best monetization methods in the space and is open to partnering with owners of OnlyFans content.
- **Links:** He vouches for a PBN seller whose links show up in Ahrefs.

chunks.heading: Affiliate and daily revenue tracking
chunks.text:
- Sample day: $10,800 total. Amazon $5,600, Mediavine $3,475, FanFuel and Cell Health about $600 combined, OnlyFans $1,088.
- **Amazon earnings estimate:** He multiplies ordered revenue (e.g. 104.4) by 54 as a running average to estimate earnings.
- **Levanta:** A platform where you push Amazon products and earn up to 80% commissions, working only with Amazon sellers. It earned $770 the previous day.

chunks.heading: Rank and rent and parasite SEO tips
chunks.text:
- **Google Business Profiles:** Can be bought, but he advises against it since it's illegal and people have been sued, though they do rank.
- **Citations:** Buy them for about $5 rather than building manually. He values his time more.
- **Lead forms:** A simple Contact Form 7 form emailed to you is enough.
- **Parasite posts:** Make as many as you want (e.g. "best massage therapy", "best kinesiology") redirecting to the same few rank and rent sites. The limit is budget, since parasite placements aren't free.
- **Traffic for a quiz or knowledge site:** He suggests trying Reddit comments.
- **YouTube automation channels:** He doesn't like them and recommends something more authentic, as he thinks YouTube is moving that way.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Jacky compares his revenue sources from a year ago (about $506k/mo) to the current month (about $200k/mo) after a Google hit. He explains the Partnerships/domain-rental push that built the peak, then gives his rules for repeating success: keep testing, don't trust SEO philosophers, and sprint all-in when something works.

chunks.heading: Revenue peak and drop: $506k/month to roughly $200k/month in a year
chunks.text:
- In Nov 2023 Jacky hit $506k in monthly revenue, with year-to-date revenue at $2 million at that point. He sustained roughly $500k/month for about four months before "getting clapped" by a Google update.
- By Nov 2024 revenue had fallen about 60%, to around $200k/month. He says enough time has passed that he can discuss it without resentment toward Google.
- He compares each revenue source from a year earlier against the most recent month (see the breakdown below).
- Daily snapshot on the day before the video: $2,260 total revenue (up $60 from the day before). Amazon $982, Mediavine $116, and the adult revenue source $1,166.

chunks.heading: Revenue source breakdown: then vs. now
chunks.text:
Figures are monthly, a year ago vs. last month, as Jacky reports them:
- **Advice (his SEO/marketing product):** $16.5k → $34.4k. The one source that grew a lot, helped by annual billings from Black Friday/Cyber Monday deals.
- **Rank and rent (retail-heavy):** $125k a year ago. He does not give the current figure clearly.
- **Mediavine:** $119k gross a year ago, of which his cut was only about $29k, because he took 20% of a $103k pool coming from partner domains.
- **Amazon Associates:** $113k → about $38k. He attributes the peak to heavy partnerships.
- **Indexsy:** $94.6k a year ago, much of it from newsletter sponsorships. He says most Advice and Indexsy sales come from his newsletter.
- **Lisbon short-term rental:** $15k → $9k, and he expects this month to dip.
- **Fan Fuel:** now only about $1k/month.
- **Smaller lines mentioned:** a VPN source, a bonds-related source, and a crypto-related "moon bag" holding. He calls one a 10-bagger and notes the bull market is back.

chunks.heading: What drove the $500k peak: partnerships and going all-in
chunks.text:
- Jacky says he identified "the power of partnerships," meaning leveraging other people's domains, and pushed it harder than people would believe.
- The team was "firing on all cylinders":
  - Bulk keyword research, because of the large team.
  - Heavy formatting work and daily article optimization checks.
  - Constant outreach.
  - Articles being rented out as soon as they were fixed.
- Takeaway: the peak came from one scalable lever (renting and partnering on other people's domains) plus massive team execution, which also made it fragile to a single Google change.

chunks.heading: Sprint on what works
chunks.text:
- Jacky's core rule: when a test hits, "you have to Sprint." Normal pace is walking and "smelling the flowers," but a working channel gets everything.
- Example: if he finds something working on a Saturday morning, he cancels weekend plans and puts the whole team on it.
- Example: Reddit comments. After he told his audience it worked, he says around five people made over $10k/month doing it.
- He frames this as setting yourself up to monetize luck: some luck is involved, but you position to capture it fast.

chunks.heading: Testing over opinions
chunks.text:
- "You have to be always testing." He says not to take anyone's word on what works or doesn't, because most are "SEO philosophers."
- Run tests properly, and once something hits, push hard (see the sprint rule above).
- He reports his results publicly, including declines, and says the numbers he posts are not lies. He tracks everything in a "Building in Public" reference sheet.

chunks.heading: Tactics and offers mentioned
chunks.text:
- **Black Friday plan for Advice:** a deal in November, then a price hike right afterwards. He describes dropping the price and then raising it back up, on top of prices that already go up every month.
- **Sponsorships:** he took one newsletter sponsorship for Black Friday this year and says the marketing newsletter is a huge converter. He notes he probably should take more.
- **Citations in foreign markets:** in answer to a question about non-US citations (e.g. Germany), he says the citations tactic works abroad. Buy the market-specific citation package, such as the German one. He says it works better in foreign markets, and that backlinks work well there too.
- **Channel membership:** $5/month, with proceeds going to charity.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Jacky Chou openly reports his lows: about $1.4M of niche site value went to zero in 2024 after Google updates hit his ecom brand Farway and several sites sharing one Search Console account. His main lesson is to stop talking publicly about a site once it hits meaningful revenue. He also explains why the public posting still paid off through partnership deals.

chunks.heading: Jacky's $1M+ SEO loss in 2024: what was lost
chunks.text:
- In a Day 331 build-in-public episode, Jacky says he lost over $1 million of site value in 2024 to Google updates. His reasoning: "if you can report the highs you got to report the lows as well."
- He estimates he spent about $400k on niche sites. All of them are at zero or effectively zero now. He says that in hindsight he should have sold most of his holdings the year before.
- Farway, his ecom brand, was the first big hit:
  - He built it from $0 to $20k/month in 3 months.
  - He valued niche sites at roughly 3x monthly revenue (annualized as 3x of $20k x 12 is not stated; he says about "$700k" of value).
  - It was hit in April and went to zero.
  - Its Mediavine revenue was around $6.7k-$7.8k (he says "67 8K" in the transcript, so the figure is unclear), with a lot of informational content.
- Several other niche sites he owned alone were hit with it, at roughly $500 to $15-20k/month each. That was about another $700k of value gone.
- Total value lost on these sites: about $1.4 million.

chunks.heading: Mistake: sites in one Google Search Console account
chunks.text:
- Jacky put Farway and several other niche sites in the same Google Search Console account. When Farway was hit, the others went down with it.
- His reasoning at the time: his partnerships were making about $500k/month, so $20k/month of niche sites didn't matter to him. His priority was "as long as you don't clap my 500k site."
- Lesson he draws: don't put assets of different value or risk in the same Search Console account.

chunks.heading: Mistake: talking publicly about a site's revenue
chunks.text:
- Jacky posted Farway revenue and Mediavine screenshots openly while it was growing. He says that in hindsight this was stupid.
- What he would do differently: stop talking about a site once it passes certain revenue thresholds. If people ask, he can discuss it, but he would not post proactively. His summary: "I think I just should have just shut up when money was good."
- He ties the sites' fall to the attention from posting, and says about $1.4M of value "went down the drain for no reason" beyond online clout.

chunks.heading: The trade-off: public posting still paid off
chunks.text:
- Jacky says posting openly about Farway got him his first partnership deals.
- Those partnerships grew to a couple million in profit in 2024.
- A snowball effect followed: he kept talking about partnerships, became "the partnership guy," and new brands came to him with deals.
- His conclusion is that he did most things right, and that posting probably earned him more than he lost. He still wishes he had stopped talking about Farway after January.
- One side benefit he sees: because he posted so openly, nobody doubts the numbers.

chunks.heading: Recovery and a new public build
chunks.text:
- Jacky says he has several new sites. Recovery of the affected ones is in progress, but he won't say which sites or what he is doing.
- Applying his lesson, he built a new site in public inside his Indexsy community (advise community). It went from $0 to $200/day, and then to $1,800/day in two months.
- He was reporting it from zero, but at $1,800/day he says "if I lose this it'll hurt," and he worries about leaks to Google.

chunks.heading: Revenue snapshot and routine
chunks.text:
- Revenue for one day he reports: $4,270 total, up $1,000 from the previous day.
  - Amazon: $1,366
  - Mediavine: $68
  - An adult revenue source: $2,830
- He maintains a build-in-public reference sheet with notes for each episode.
- He accepts random coffee meetups, including with people who have never built a site or who have a 9-5, because he likes hearing people's stories.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Jacky walks through the margins on his partnership model: partners attach sites to his Amazon rate card and Mediavine account, and he takes a cut. He also covers bundling a free indexer into his Revive plan, cold email response benchmarks, and following up relentlessly.

chunks.heading: Affiliate partnership model: Amazon rate card with a 20% cut
chunks.text:
- Jacky runs an Amazon affiliate account that partner sites attach to. Partners get onto his Amazon rate card and he takes a 20% cut.
- Amazon pays out net 60, so partners receive 80% of their earnings about 60 days after the sale.
- He says the cut is worth it for partners because "we ran the numbers and the uplift is more like 40% in most cases."
- Example: one partner's site produces 19.1k a month, and Jacky's 20% is 3.8k a month "from just existing."
- He added a couple of new sites to the Amazon account in this update.
- Day snapshot: about 11.2k total daily revenue, made up of Amazon 6,920, Mediavine about 3,000, FanFuel and Cell Health about 200, and OnlyFans about 1,059. Amazon ordered revenue that day was 128.2k, multiplied by 54 to get to the Amazon number.

chunks.heading: Partnership revenue splits and real margins
chunks.text:
- Jacky splits partnerships by deal type, from 20% (tag-on deals) to 50% (larger or more hands-on deals).
- Largest partnership: 50% of 94k, so his cut is 47k (the transcript reads "947k", which looks like a transcription error; 50% of 94k is 47k).
- Second partnership: 20% of 19k, which is 3.8k. Another tag-on is also 3.8k.
- Another 50% partnership, a newly onboarded DR 88 site, brings in 1.9k.
- One simmering partnership is a tag-on that gives him 600 a month "for nothing."
- Far and Away, the site he is building in public, hit about 10.6k in February, up about 40% from the month before. He credits the Revive plugin, which started February 14th. He says the site makes about 15K a month.
- Many small sites he owns 100% are weak earners.
- Core claim: if he had stuck with his own affiliate sites he would be making about 600 a month from them. He was making about 30k a month on his own sites before partnerships, and partnerships now add about 67k a month extra (excluding Far and Away). He says this is "straight to the bottom line."
- His blended margin on the partnership book comes out around 42.96%.

chunks.heading: Mediavine margins
chunks.text:
- His largest Mediavine partnership site has an RPM of $17 on 4.4 million sessions a month.
- His cut is 15K, which is 20% of 77k.
- Total net revenue per month is 21k out of 88k total, a margin of only about 24.5%. He calls it "very weak" compared with the affiliate partnerships.
- Far and Away has the highest RPM because it runs on WordPress, and he says Mediavine works well with WordPress. Sites on random other CMSs have noticeably lower RPMs.
- Far and Away was coming in at 4.7k from Mediavine.

chunks.heading: Revive pricing and the bundled indexer
chunks.text:
- Revive is his content refresh product. The refresh workflow is to rewrite the first paragraph of each article, change the publish date, and resubmit to Google for indexing. He calls this a strong freshness signal for Google and says they have had "incredible success."
- He built an indexer as part of the Revive plan. It went out as a tag-on to the "baller" plan at no extra charge.
- Competing indexer tools such as Tag Parrot and URL Monitor do the same thing for up to about $100 a month. Jacky "ripped the best features of the top three indexers" and included them in the baller plan.
- It wasn't hard to develop, and it pairs well with Revive because resubmitting refreshed pages is the main use case.
- He plans to raise Revive prices possibly the following month, depending on how things go.

chunks.heading: Cold email benchmarks and follow-up
chunks.text:
- Cold email tooling mentioned: Instantly, after 20 days of warm-up.
- Good response rate: 2 to 5% is decent. Under 1% means "your copy sucks."
- Once a subject line like "quick question Jacky" works, you don't need to keep checking open rates.
- For prospects who haven't replied, keep following up. "Don't be ashamed to follow up," and you can keep going "until they block you."
- He says US prospects are generally more open to being sold to, while Europeans (he gives Germans as the example) react worse to repeated follow-ups. He frames this as cultural.

chunks.heading: CTR manipulation tools: his test results
chunks.text:
- He tested CTR manipulation tools (SERP Clicks, Agency Assassin, CTR tools like CTR RFI) and is now cancelling the subscriptions.
- SERP Clicks: 5 clicks a day, about 400 credits (a couple hundred dollars, he doesn't remember exactly). His verdict: "I don't think so," meaning it did nothing noticeable.
- A free 7-day test (12th to 19th) at 10 searches a day for "physiotherapy East Vancouver": ranking went from 16 on the 12th to 6 by the 19th. After the campaign ended it trickled up, and he isn't sure it did anything.
- Agency Assassin on a client site (Movement Room) ran a month starting the 12th. Rankings for physio Vancouver went up a lot, so it might have done something, but he is unsure and says it "doesn't feel like it did much."
- Overall he can't attribute results to CTR manipulation and found some of the tools hard to use. He discovered one campaign had been paused the whole time.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Jacky Chou ranks online business models in a tier list, from scalable and reliable down to risky and scams. His view: agencies (especially SEO/LLM) are the most dependable, B2B SaaS and consistent YouTube are strong, while affiliate, ecom, blogging, day trading and forex rank low.

chunks.heading: How Jacky ranks online business models for 2026
chunks.text:
- Jacky ranks business models on a tier list built with tiermaker.com. The tiers run from "scalable", "pretty reliable" and "decent money" down to "kind of saturated", "risky" and "basically a scam".
- He says he has "started and tried almost every single business model online."
- His overall pattern: agencies and B2B software rank high. Content-, trading- and funnel-based models rank low. Anything that depends on a platform's payouts or a commoditized service ranks low.
- Most of his placements are quick gut calls, and he often changes them while placing the next item. Treat them as opinions, not researched rankings.

chunks.heading: Agencies: his top-ranked category
chunks.text:
- He says any agency is better than affiliate marketing in 2026. He puts agencies in "pretty reliable" or "decent money", not "scalable".
- A general online marketing agency is "pretty reliable" but too general. Specific agency types rank separately:
  - Google Ads agency: if it's local ads, he ranks it above a Facebook ads agency.
  - Facebook ads agency: if you get good at it, it sits above affiliate marketing.
  - Shopify agency: counts as an agency, so "decent money".
  - Web designer for local businesses (WordPress and similar): ranks above a social media management agency (SMMA), because you can resell the work.
  - Software development agency: you can white label it, but he says it "is going to zero". Probably saturated but still decent.
  - Social media management agency: a 2020-era model, but he says you can still make money if you can sell.
- Lead generation (rank and rent) is "decent money". It's an easy sell, and all you need is leads.
- Freelancing (web developer, SEO, etc.) is "decent money". He compares a freelancer to a mercenary: you do whatever the client needs.

chunks.heading: LLM/AI search agency: his favorite new bet
chunks.text:
- He says an "LLM agency" (selling visibility in AI search) deserves a high placement in 2026. He ranks it above ads and lead gen.
- His claim: "LLM is the new SEO", and he says it converts very well as a sales pitch.
- Tactic: when an SEO prospect comes in, he throws in LLM optimization because it is "basically pretty similar." He says that closes them: "we do that and it's game over. Like they're 100% in the door."
- He adds that he can sell it this way only because he knows SEO himself. An SEO agency is essentially sold as an LLM agency now.

chunks.heading: Software, platforms and content businesses
chunks.text:
- B2B SaaS (online tools): "pretty reliable". He says it's hard without a brand, so he places it a little below the very top.
- Platforms and marketplaces: the upside is "crazy" once both sides of the market exist, but they are kind of saturated. He ranks them above reselling sneakers.
- YouTube: he calls it the best platform, but only if you will grind. Posting daily puts it high. Posting about one video a month drops it to "risky but possible".
- Building a brand on social media: "pretty reliable" if you're willing to grind.
- Influencer or lifestyle creator: kind of saturated. He ranks it above affiliate marketing and above ecom, as long as you know how to monetize. He notes AI influencers are now a factor.
- Online courses: "risky but possible". He notes AI can generate full courses now, and he still ranks courses above affiliate marketing, influencer work and reselling sneakers.
- Online guru (course seller): "risky but possible", and pretty saturated. He jokes it's "funny coming from me."

chunks.heading: Saturated or declining models
chunks.text:
- Affiliate marketing in 2026: kind of saturated. Any agency beats it.
- Ecom: kind of saturated, and he says plainly "I hate ecom." Dropshipping is in the same tier, and he ranks it below ecom.
- FBA (Amazon): pretty saturated, but he places it above ecom.
- Tech support or managed WordPress services: hard to sell and "so commoditized nowadays". He ranks them below black hat.
- Black hat SEO: "risky but possible". He ranks it above live streaming.
- Compilation videos: "risky but possible". He says the RPM is "pretty trash". You can make money but not a lot.
- Live streaming: "pretty trash", and he ranks it below garage sales.
- Esports: risky, but above garage sales.
- Reselling sneakers, eBay flipping: "risky but possible". You can make decent money but it is a job.
- Blogging in 2026: "Hell no", basically a scam.
- Graphic designer: "Hell no". With AI available, he says you're better off in another model.

chunks.heading: Models he calls scams
chunks.text:
- Forex (foreign exchange): "definitely a scam".
- Day trading: "pretty much a scam", but he ranks it better than ClickFunnels.
- ClickFunnels: basically a scam.
- Crypto: risky.
- Online surveys: "100% a scam". He says you'd be better off getting a job at McDonald's.
- Adult content: he ranks it kind of saturated, below affiliate marketing, and says you're "selling your soul." This is his opinion, though one of his own revenue lines is labeled "the adult revenue source."

chunks.heading: His own numbers, from the intro
chunks.text:
- Revenue for the day before: $997 total, down $30 from the prior day. The line items were Amazon at $129, Mediavine at $70 and the adult revenue source at $798.
- He says last month's total revenue was "300 somethingk". He says he has already justified his margins in previous videos.
- Subscribers get a link to his revenue sheet and a monthly newsletter with a revenue update and a net worth update.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: A step-by-step playbook for using rank and rent sites as a foot in the door for local SEO agencies: pick a service plus city, build a structured site, run a citation and branded-link sequence, then monetize leads via partners and upsell them into full SEO. Covers pricing math, partner sourcing, and pitching channels.

chunks.heading: Rank and rent beyond local SEO
chunks.text:
- Jacky says rank and rent is not limited to local keywords. It does not have to be "accountant Vancouver"; it can be a broad national keyword such as "best protein supplement".
- He says he signed five-figure clients by ranking his own site for national keywords like that.
- Local keywords are still much easier to rank for, so local is the easier place to start.
- The model he describes: build a site that ranks and generates leads, own the asset, then get paid by a business for the leads it produces, instead of the business paying to own the site.

chunks.heading: Site structure and page-building tactics
chunks.text:
- A single page can rank in low-competition niches and cities. Jacky ranked "physio in East Vancouver" on a single-page site, which he showed on his YouTube channel.
- He does not recommend limiting yourself to one page. With AI, you can screenshot a reference site structure, paste it into Claude, and have it generate a whole site in one shot.
- Build service pages and suburb or location pages, such as "payroll services Round Rock", even when keyword plus city shows low volume.
- Reason: people searching "payroll services near me" from that location will surface those pages. So he says to check "near me" volume, not just keyword-plus-city volume, and to create the suburb pages anyway.
- He says he "used to be a non-believer" in this approach but changed his mind after seeing it work.

chunks.heading: Link building caution
chunks.text: - Jacky is particular about never pointing tier 2 links directly at the target URL, because the site will "collapse". Tier 2 links point at the citations instead.

chunks.heading: Finding and managing partners
chunks.text:
- He expects to cycle through a lot of partners. "Most local business owners are pretty trash at running a business." They are good at their trade, not at running a company, and many can barely hold it together.
- The tactic is to keep trying partners ("pepper your angles"). Once you find a dependable one, "hold on for dear life" and charge them accordingly so everyone wins.
- Meta ads are a method he taught for finding partners. Run a simple funnel with an ad asking "Do you want more leads?". Those who say yes fill out which service they provide. This gives a steady inflow, but the partners are often not dependable.

chunks.heading: Google Business Profile
chunks.text:
- Jacky calls a Google Business Profile "super super super valuable". He says it makes the economics work about 10 times better and makes leads far easier to get, especially in your own city.
- Click-through rate assumptions of 25-30% for position one apply to keywords that are not bid on in Google Ads. Realistically it is closer to half of that without a profile.
- With a Google Business Profile, he says you can go back to roughly a 30% click-through rate.
- His advice: if you can get one, get one.

chunks.heading: Pitching partners in person
chunks.text:
- Show proof in person, for example your rankings.
- Cold calling and walking in are "like a muscle". You will get rocked the first few times, so get your reps in and you will get far better.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Jacky walks through building a local SEO site for a vet clinic: a silo structure with pillar and sub-service pages, service-area pages for nearby towns, a repeatable location page template, early CRO wins to cut client churn, and Cloudflare hosting.

chunks.heading: Cloudflare as the default stack for local business sites
chunks.text:
- Jacky says Cloudflare is "non-negotiable" for local clients in 2026. He called Squarespace "freaking nasty".
- Local businesses don't need a blog. "Just Cloudflare and chill."
- The site is just served HTML, so it's fast, never goes down, has no bloat and is easy to optimize. The owner can still have code written for their own additions later.
- Migrating an old site to Cloudflare Pages is roughly a one-shot job for Claude, about 10 minutes.
- Example: a Newark, NJ vet clinic on Squarespace was already ranking #1 organically. It had a partial-match domain and the keyword plus location in the title. It was weak on Google Maps.

chunks.heading: Local SEO is mostly a set of "why not" on-page basics
chunks.text:
- Jacky argues local SEO is easy because most competitors do almost nothing. Doing the bare minimum should make a site "fly" in a low-competition niche.
- Schema (including on the Google Map embed) is "not part of the 80/20". It's a "just do it" easy win, not a big mover.
- Adding a landmark or neighborhood in the first paragraph is a cheap tip: "I just do it cuz it's so easy." With Claude or Codex you tell it to do it, so there's no reason to skip it. He doesn't claim data proves it helps.
- He endorses a page template used for sub-service and service-area pages. This is the framework Tristan walked through:
  - Front-load the target keyword in the title tag and H1.
  - Intro copy says who the business is, with a landmark or neighborhood.
  - A big contact form above the fold.
  - A process section for unique content.
  - Sideways internal links to the same service in nearby cities.
  - Links to other services in the same city, with the pillar page first.
  - A "why choose us" section with team and real reviews.
  - A Google Map embed.

chunks.heading: Site structure: pillar pages, sub-services and service-area pages
chunks.text:
- Jacky calls the structure "fantastic" and says it works for any industry, from low-competition vets to roofers and locksmiths.
- Core service pillars (for the vet: veterinarian services, animal hospital services, veterinary pharmacy) target the seed keywords.
- Sub-service pages hang off each pillar to capture long-tail searches, such as sick pet visits, wellness exams, puppy and kitten care, and flea, tick and heartworm meds.
- Each core page gets a service-area page for every nearby town. This expands the radius beyond what the Google Business Profile can capture.
- Every sub-service page links back up to its pillar page. This signals the hierarchy to Google.
- Expect 100-150+ new pages. Unique content on each matters so they don't look boilerplate.
- Branded content like process, team and reviews is the biggest asset because nobody can copy it.
- Watch for cannibalization. A new pillar page targeting the same keyword as the homepage could compete with it, so check the data first.

chunks.heading: CRO fixes on local service sites
chunks.text:
- Jacky audited the vet site on desktop and mobile and found it painful on both. Mobile was worse.
- A call to action must sit above the fold on mobile on every page. Book appointment should always be visible, so use a sticky book button.
- If a site like this ran paid ads, its conversion rate would be terrible.
- He prefers card-style internal links over in-content text links. He argues "ain't nobody clicking those" text links, and clicks and behavior signals from Chrome matter. "If your links aren't clicked, might as well not have a link."
- Poor click data matters less in a low-competition space with a partial-match domain.

chunks.heading: Citations, browser blast and the single-variable test
chunks.text:
- On organic, the vet's higher-value keywords were being outranked by Yelp and S6. Jacky thinks they can be beaten.
- His hunch is that "browser blast" (behavior signals) alone could outrank them, since those pages are already well optimized and likely just need more behavior signals.
- Local rankings will take more work. The plan was to build citations and run a browser blast, then re-check rankings a week later.
- If the owner is slow shipping on-site changes, that makes a clean single-variable case study. Citations alone go first, before any on-site changes.
- He dismissed a 40-citations-for-$20 purchase as "NGMI". With Local Rank he says one click gets 1,000 citations.

chunks.heading: Reviews and directory-site rankings
chunks.text:
- Ranking on directory sites like booking.com comes down to revenue and reviews. Jacky says it's "100% just revenue based and review based".
- The vet's local Maps competitor had about 700 reviews. A separate video was planned for the review game plan.

chunks.heading: Positioning a local SEO agency
chunks.text:
- Jacky says to carve out one industry and go laser-focused, such as being "the roofing marketing girl in your city". Don't be a general marketing consultant ("NGMI").
- He suggests starting where you already have contacts.
- A niche lets you build systems that get easier as you scale.
- Hyper-focusing also lets you buy an exact or partial match domain. "SEO agency of Houston probably prints cash."
- When starting out, take any lead you can get. A proper brand helps, but stay dialed into one practice.
- Fast results come from people who are "dialed" and "super hungry". You can tell early who will make it quickly.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Jacky Chou tested 10 link vendors (about $1,000 each) on 10 identical 12-month-old domains targeting 800 low-difficulty informational keywords. A PBN provider won, a no-links control beat several vendors, and he explains how he controlled variables and why results are caveated.

chunks.heading: Setup of the $10,000 backlink case study
chunks.text:
- Jacky (founder of Indexsy, nearly a decade in SEO) spent about $10,000 across 10 link vendors to see which had the biggest effect on rankings.
- He split the budget across vendor types: niche edits, PBN providers and guest post providers.
- Spend per vendor:
  - Control domain: $0
  - Fat Joe: about $1,000
  - Rank Authority: about $1,100
  - Hatred PBN: about $1,000 as budgeted (he ended up spending only about $200, see the results section)
  - Loganix: about $1,000
  - Rhino Rank: about $1,100
  - Growth Resolve: about $1,000
  - Grindstone SEO: about $1,000
  - Upttops: about $1,100
  - Indexsy (his own agency): about $1,100
