- He discloses the bias of including his own agency and tells viewers to exclude it from their own read if they want.

chunks.heading: How he controlled the variables
chunks.text:
- 10 different domains, all aged exactly 12 months. They were registered and sitting idle, never used for PBN content or anything else.
- The same 800 informational keywords were targeted across all 10 sites, e.g. "can dogs eat lettuce", "can dogs eat apples".
- Keywords had over 100 searches a month in Ahrefs and keyword difficulty under 20.
- All articles followed the same structure and were generated with an auto-blogging service, published directly to WordPress. He says it costs less than a dollar per article.
- Caveat he states himself: these are low-difficulty keywords, so results would likely differ for more competitive terms.

chunks.heading: Results ranking (worst to best)
chunks.text:
- **10th, Upttops (Vietnamese PBN seller):** popped up early, then tanked and never recovered. He had seen great results from them before, so he suspects a bad batch.
- **9th, Grindstone SEO (post-that-rank / niche-edit style service):** the owner warned that his links aren't the right pick for a brand-new site because they look unnatural. Part of the budget went to foundational links, but it didn't work. DR was around 8 to 13.
- **8th, Loganix (niche edits):** links looked good and they had the best ordering process and account management of all the vendors, with proactive updates. They let you pre-approve links. Jacky picked domains with the most traffic rather than the most relevant, which may be why it didn't move rankings. No penalty, just flat.
- **7th, Fat Joe (guest posts):** early growth then sideways. Solid links, weaker DR, no penalty. He used to resell their services to agency clients.
- **6th, "Powerhouse" (homepage PBN links, found on Black Hat World):** reached DR 45 on Ahrefs with about 500 referring domains and about 200 traffic after six months. He suggests it could suit content-farm builders.
- **5th, Growth Resolve (Michael Johnson):** 3 links for $1,000, on domains with 30k to 100k traffic. About 32 referring domains, mostly spam. Steady climb. The vendor knew he was in the study.
- **4th, control domain (zero links):** about 1,000 indexed keywords and nearly 500 traffic a month from content alone.
- **3rd, Indexsy:** instructions were just "20 referring domains, 100+ links". Affordable.
- **2nd, Rhino Rank (niche edits):** 22 links for about $1,150 (price has since risen to $1,425). Low DR, but rankings went up, stayed up and reached about 670 traffic a month.
- **1st, Hatred PBN:** about 1,200 traffic a month after six months. He wanted to buy 50 posts but the owner refused to protect his network and refunded about $800, so Jacky spent only about $200. It had the best results and best cost efficiency. The owner blocked the crawler, so link quality can't be inspected.

chunks.heading: Takeaways Jacky draws
chunks.text:
- Many vendors showed an early uptick followed by a drop that never recovered.
- The cheapest result (about $200 PBN) beat the pricier niche-edit and guest post services.
- A no-links control beating several paid vendors on low-difficulty keywords suggests that paid links are not always worth the money there.
- DR is a poor predictor: Rhino Rank had low DR but good rankings, while Powerhouse had DR 45 with modest traffic.
- Vendor relevance and link selection matter. He thinks he may have picked the wrong domains at Loganix.
- Vendors that limit how much they sell you (like Hatred) are protecting their network, which he reads as a sign of quality.

chunks.heading: Limits he acknowledges and his challenge
chunks.text:
- He admits the study can be criticized: tiny keyword difficulty, a single run per vendor, and vendors who knew they were being tested.
- He says Hatred's owner pointed out where the study went wrong.
- His challenge to critics: run a better case study. Doing so takes money and action. If someone's is better, he will share it.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Jacky argues partnership sites on high-DR domains rank with no backlinks, so most link building is wasted effort early on. He only builds links in specific cases: after ranking top 10 (niche edits), for parasite SEO pages, local guest posts, and tiered citations that never point a PBN at your own rank-and-rent site.

chunks.heading: Why Jacky doesn't build links to partnership sites
chunks.text:
- All of Jacky's revenue now comes from partnerships (he has one or two other sources, such as marketing letter sponsorships, which he mostly doesn't take outside Black Friday).
- He has never built backlinks for any partner site. On a high-DR site, he says all you do is have AI write the content, have a human humanize it, post it, and it ranks.
- His workflow for partner sites is: post, interlink, and occasionally some CTR (not really needed).
- He argues content quality barely matters right now. Before Forbes got manually hit, he says "you could probably get a 2-year-old to write a post about best credit cards and it'll rank."
- He loses some respect for in-house SEOs at DR90+ sites, because ranking there is easy.
- Hard cases are competitive terms like "best CRM software" on a new DR30 site. He'd be impressed by an in-house SEO who ranked that, and says they'd need parasite SEO or partnerships.
- Instead of links, he puts effort into more partnerships, content for partners, and digital PR for partners.

chunks.heading: Why Jacky rarely builds links to his own sites
chunks.text:
- He only builds links to sites he owns, and only about a year's worth of that.
- Most of his own sites are at zero traffic: de-indexed, not just down 50%. He says it's not backlinks. Causes he names: Google thinking he spammed the blog with AI content (some sites), and some caught together in the same Google Search Console account.
- The surviving sites grow slowly, around 3 to 4K organic visits a month, which he says isn't worth his time or link spend.
- He sees links as worthwhile in only four scenarios: rank and rent, parasite SEO, local links, and gambling-type plays (covered in the sections below).

chunks.heading: Jacky's link-building business and margins
chunks.text:
- Jacky sells backlinks as one of his services: niche edits, local SEO backlinks, and local retainers. He says the variety isn't huge.
- Backlinks bring in about $30-40K a month.
- Gross margin is roughly 50%. He calls that low for link building, since most sellers run about 80% margins by marking up 4x. He marks up only 2x, and says that's what makes it worth it.

chunks.heading: Rank and rent: the order of operations before buying links
chunks.text:
- Paid links (niche edits, guest posts) on a rank and rent site come only after the site hits roughly the top 10.
- Before any niche edits or guest posts, he follows his SOP (free on YouTube; a more succinct start-to-finish version is in the Indexsy community):
  1. Build citations.
  2. Tier the citations with a PBN. Do not point the PBN directly at the rank and rent site. He says 10+ people did this and then complained of ranking drops.
  3. Submit the citations to an indexer. He says most people skip this.
- He wants to drop CTR from the SOP because people overdo it. His example: someone ran 100 clicks a day on a keyword with about 100 local searches a month, got to the front page, and then got penalized.

chunks.heading: Parasite SEO, local links and gambling
chunks.text:
- Parasite SEO: sending links to a page on a parasite domain makes Google value that page. With multiple pages on the same parasite domain, Google will show yours on the front page. He calls it very easy to abuse right now.
- Example: any Southeast Asian country can rank for gambling terms with a few links from the US. He says one of his biggest "benders" is in gambling.
- Local links: a local guest post, a naked backlink, plus map embeds. He calls this extremely effective and probably the best way to grow right now.

chunks.heading: Fake address setup for local rank and rent
chunks.text:
- Jacky uses a fake address in the target city and adds schema markup.
- He picks an office building in the absolute center of the city.
- Reason: if he later wants to register a Google Business Profile, he can rent an office in that building, register legitimately, and open for business.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Jacky bought a high-traffic towing directory that was under-monetized, added a strong sales closer, and ran one Facebook lead ad campaign (about $25 CAD/day) to fill cold leads. Clients got the exclusive #1 slot per city with call forwarding, a guaranteed call volume, and a free trial. He sold it for $190K.

chunks.heading: How Jacky bought and flipped a towing directory for $190K
chunks.text:
- Jacky bought one of the top-ranking towing directories in the US when he was flipping a lot of niche sites.
- The seller (from Lithuania) was making only about $200-$300 despite heavy traffic. Jacky says he couldn't close clients himself, partly because his accent put off towing operators who hung up on him.
- Deal: the seller kept a small minority stake (Jacky says he doesn't remember whether it was 15% or 30%). Jacky bought the rest for $10K.
- He sold it for $190K (he shows an escrow screenshot). He did not own 100%, because of the seller's retained stake.
- His thesis: lots of traffic, poor monetization, so he could out-monetize the previous owner.

chunks.heading: The playbook: hire a closer, sell one slot per city
chunks.text:
- Step one was to "immediately hire a cracked sales guy" (a closer based in Utah) to work the existing inbound leads the seller couldn't close.
- Inbound leads and calls came from the site's traffic. Cold leads were generated on top of that with Facebook ads.
- Once a client closes, they get the number one slot on the directory for their city. Jacky's line: "number one in the country".
- Only one client per city, so exclusivity is the selling point.
- Calls are delivered with call forwarding: once a client signs, all calls are forwarded to them.
- The most he charged for one city was $2.5K per month, justified by the site's traffic.
- The business also inherited some Google Business Profiles (GMBs), which he calls the main sticking point of the asset. They were still live when he recorded this.
- He calls this a rank-and-rent / directory play that anyone can run, even for a single location.

chunks.heading: The Facebook lead ad campaign
chunks.text:
- One single campaign, objective called "Meta Leads" (Facebook lead ads with an instant form), at about $25 CAD per day. He describes setup as easy.
- Offer in the ad: "guaranteed 50 calls per month", positioned as "the largest towing directory in America".
- He says 50 calls per month is easy in towing. If a client didn't hit 50, they refunded the difference.
- Terms and conditions sat behind an asterisk on the ad.
- The form's description promised a free trial. Fields collected: email, full name, phone number and city, plus a privacy policy link.
- Sales flow: after a lead signs, they get a free trial, meaning leads are forwarded to them. If they close, great. If not, the lead moves on to the next person.
- He says the same Meta Leads approach could be applied to other local niches (he mentions plumbing as an example), with a closer on the other end, as a case study.

chunks.heading: Local Rank pricing change (his SEO software)
chunks.text:
- Jacky announced a plan change for Local Rank (local rank.so): the Pro plan moved from unlimited locations to 10 locations.
- Reason: unlimited citation locations were "too OP", users were abusing it on the back end, and throttling everyone's speed was needed. Limiting locations would make everything faster.
- Pricing: the Pro plan at $297 with unlimited locations, rank tracker and lead credits, plus 50% off Local Boost, was available only on the day of the announcement. Unlimited citation locations afterwards cost $447.
- This was a time-limited grandfathering offer to drive same-day sign-ups.

chunks.heading: Daily income snapshot (August 14, 2025, episode 613)
chunks.text:
- Total for the previous day: $1,086, up $200 from the day before.
- Amazon: $137. Mediavine: $455, which he'd now call passive income. An adult-niche resource brought in $486.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Jacky walks through each October revenue source (link building, Amazon affiliate, adult, private community, SEO agency, Levanta and more), what moved the numbers and how durable each is. His core stance: make-money-online niches decay, so earn aggressively in sprints, diversify, and park profits in lower-risk assets.

chunks.heading: October 2024 revenue overview: $231.6k across multiple sources
chunks.text:
- Jacky reported $231.6k in revenue for October 2024 and plans to make this a monthly update (also posted monthly on Twitter). Overall business was up 10% month over month.
- Sources and October figures he gave:
  - Indexsy: highest source, with $41k from link building.
  - Amazon affiliate: $38.5k.
  - Adult revenue source: $42.3k, of which about $18k came from a single site that was live only about two weeks.
  - Advise (private community): "popping off" this month, but no figure given.
  - Bonds: about $1,800.
  - Media Vine: $2,400.
  - Sell Health, FanFuel and VPN: roughly $2k combined.
  - Also listed: Binance affiliate, Levanta, the Lisbon short-term rental, Revive and a spin-off SEO agency (no figures given).
- Indexsy was up about $10k. Amazon was down, and gains elsewhere covered for it.
- He plans to cover each revenue source, his thoughts on it and its longevity.
- His monthly net worth update goes out through his marketing letter.

chunks.heading: Indexsy: link building and local guest posts
chunks.text:
- Indexsy is part link building, part client work, effectively a holding company. Of October's revenue, $41k came from link building.
- Link building covers niche edits and, mainly, "local guest posts". He believes Indexsy is still the only one on the internet selling them.
- A local guest post is a single link (orders of 1 to 10 links) on a page that includes a citation and an embedded map, which is how it helps local SEO.
- He recommends choosing the dofollow URL type, because local guest posts are "actually safe to use".
- It is currently a best seller, outselling niche edits.
- His spin-off SEO agency: Jacky's team still handles the SEO, while his business partner handles account management. Prospects DM Jacky on Twitter and he introduces them.

chunks.heading: Amazon affiliate and Levanta
chunks.text:
- Amazon affiliate made $38.5k in October. He calls that solid compared to most people but weak by his own history: his all-time high was around $100k months.
- He says it has been "clapped down heavily". Revenue comes from partnerships, and Google "seems to find all my partnerships at this point", yet he still manages to scrape by.
- Levanta matches affiliates with Amazon sellers, who then offer heightened commission rates, up to about 50% for him.
- He picks Levanta over FanFuel because it converts better. Pushing someone to a product with 4,000 Amazon reviews converts far better than sending them to sketchier sites. He still likes FanFuel and earns well from it.

chunks.heading: Community, parasite SEO and the Advise lift
chunks.text:
- Advise is his private community. Most of its levers come from Jacky himself.
- He credits this month's jump to two changes:
  1. He built a "$2k a day" parasite SEO site in public inside the community's secret channel.
  2. He ran a paid parasite opportunity for Advise members only. Around a hundred-plus people took part, and several said they made a couple hundred dollars each. He admits it is modest, but says "it pays for your membership".
- The $2k-a-day site was live only about two weeks and made about $18k before getting hit.

chunks.heading: Income volatility, longevity and diversification
chunks.text:
- He expects the adult revenue source to be very low next month because the $2k-a-day site got "clapped down", which shows how fragile this kind of revenue is.
- Media Vine went from about $100k a month to $2,400. Partners moved away and refused to pay a percentage. His fix was to create a partnership contract so partners cannot cut him out again.
- He argues making-money-online niches have poor longevity, so you should work in sprints: earn as much as possible in a short window, then invest aggressively in lower-risk assets. He has seen many niche site owners "completely rocked" recently.
- His Binance affiliate work produced his first million dollars. The many users he referred still pay out, which he calls "the Binance dividends".
- On the investing side, he prefers stocks over real estate and says portfolios need diversification. He considers himself overweight in real estate and has been moving heavily into equities over recent months.
- He agrees that hustling and saving aggressively when young, then putting money into index funds, is the easiest route to seven figures over a decade.
- His Lisbon short-term rental is an 8-unit building, bought for his Golden Visa, which has now gone through. Units are one bed plus a sofa bed, and he thinks he is undercharging per night.

chunks.heading: Revive: refreshing publish dates
chunks.text:
- Revive is a WordPress plugin that refreshes an article's publish date. He says this is a strong Google signal, confirmed in the Google algo leak.
- It goes a step further by using AI to rewrite the first paragraph of each article, which makes the refresh more natural because the content is genuinely edited.
- It also submits the page to an indexer, though he was unsure whether the indexer was still working and said he would check.

chunks.heading: Reputation removal tip
chunks.text: - When a client wants a negative Google Business Profile review removed, he suggests trying the Swapped gig and offering the client a refund if it cannot be done. Swapped refunds your money if it fails, so the risk is covered.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Jacky argues affiliate sites are unprofitable after Google's algo changes, which reward high domain authority over authentic content. He lays out a progression: short-term parasite SEO to get a first dollar, then rank and rent, client work, and finally partnerships. He also stresses daily consistency and building content around a hobby.

chunks.heading: Why Jacky says not to start an affiliate site in 2024
chunks.text:
- His answer to "would you start an affiliate site in 2024" is "hell no."
- Reason: it is not profitable, and effort is not rewarded. Authentic content does not get rewarded as of now, though that may change.
- Example: Retro Dodo went from 500k a month in traffic to 30k a month and was "decimated."
- Google promised to fix its algorithm but has not. He says it is prioritizing high domain authority sites.
- Because of that, he says to seek partnerships. He adds that when you approach sites for partnerships, they "don't like it."
- His closing line: "whatever you do don't start an affiliate site in 2024, you're going to get clapped."

chunks.heading: Jacky's recommended path instead of affiliate sites
chunks.text:
He lays out a sequence for people starting out:

1. Short-term parasite SEO (burn-and-churn) to make a first $50-$100 online.
2. Rank and rent sites.
3. Client work.
4. Partnerships for the long term.

Right now he says to focus on partnerships, client work and rank and rent. He mentions Cricas getting to about $10K a month, which he describes as client work.

chunks.heading: Short-term parasite SEO as a first-dollar tactic
chunks.text:
- He says short-term parasite SEO will get you to "probably a couple grand."
- He thinks many people give up too quickly, and may start recommending burn-and-churn parasite SEO to beginners.
- Why: once you make your first dollar online, "something switches in your brain." He says that was true for him.
- Steps he suggests:
  - Create around 10 Reddit accounts and farm them up.
  - Leave Reddit comments and make money from them.
  - Create subreddits and make money from those.
  - Aim for $50-$100 first, to "get on the board" and see that it is possible.
- He says the paid parasite SEO tactic in his Indexsy community is working "extremely well right now."

chunks.heading: Rank and rent, then local client work
chunks.text:
- Once you have a first grand from parasite SEO, build rank and rent sites.
- Example: his public physio rank and rent test in Vancouver, where he says he "only bought citations" and it ranked.
- After ranking, you rent the site out.
- His plan if doing physio in Vancouver:
  - Become "the physio marketing guy in Vancouver."
  - Take one client from each neighborhood.
  - Rank for all the suburbs to dominate the niche.
  - Become the local SEO agency for it.
- Income estimates (his confident estimates, not guarantees):
  - About $3-4K a month from rank and rent.
  - Easily over $10K, even up to $20K, from local client work in a single niche like physio.

chunks.heading: Long term: partnerships and content around a hobby
chunks.text:
- Long term, he would focus on partnerships. Example: bring the ranked local asset to local newspapers and sign them up for a partnership.
- He is "pretty bullish" on YouTube right now. He says his retirement plan is probably to find a hobby and create content around it.
- He also says affiliate-style content around a topic on YouTube could be a way to do it, rather than a new affiliate site.

chunks.heading: Consistency beats most people
chunks.text:
- Thought experiment: if posting a YouTube video every day for a year could replace your full-time salary, most people would say yes, but almost no one would stick with it.
- He says even he, at nearly a year of daily episodes (Day 342), skipped some days.
- He cites Harvard's intro programming course online: the first video has about 50 million views, and the second has roughly 5% of that. His read: "people just don't want to do work anymore."

chunks.heading: Daily numbers and small tactical answers
chunks.text:
- Daily revenue reported for the previous day: $2,149 total, up $70 from the day before.
  - Amazon: $126.
  - Mediavine: $78.
  - Adult revenue stores (which he does not discuss in detail): a figure he gives that is garbled in the transcript, so it is left out here.
- Foundation links: he describes them as profile links. They don't give much juice but are good for link diversity.
- He says to detect whether a Medium page is indexed using a detailed plugin (name not clear in the transcript).
- For newcomers asking where to start, he points to his back catalog: about 300 episodes of 10 minutes each, which can be watched at 2x speed.
- He observes that YouTube channel member Q&As have been more granular and higher quality than typical live streams, though members tend to ask more getting-started questions.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Jacky Chou's August 2025 revenue update ($261.6k across SEO, SaaS, real estate, affiliates). He explains why he diversifies after losing ~95% of $500k/month affiliate and display ad income, and how building in public and doubling down on traction drive growth.

chunks.heading: August 2025 revenue breakdown
chunks.text:
Jacky reports $261,661.15 in revenue from SEO and online businesses in August 2025, over $8,000 per day, while building in public. Overall business was down 3.2% vs July.

By stream:
- LocalRank.so + Trackings.ai: $71.5k
- Version.so (SEO agency): $57.7k
- Indexsy (mostly the BrowserBlast service): $51.1k
- STR Lisbon (short-term rental): $23.3k
- Advise.so (SEO community): $21.3k
- 0F (adult revenue source): $15.2k
- Binance Affiliate: $9.8k
- Amazon Affiliate: $4.2k
- Mediavine (display ads): $3.5k
- Fanfuel + Bonds combined: $1.9k
- Revive.so: $1.4k
- SimpleHost.so (hosting): $670

He also publishes monthly net worth updates at open.jackychou.com.

chunks.heading: Why Jacky diversifies revenue streams
chunks.text:
- A year before this update, he was making $500k per month from affiliate and display ads (Amazon and Mediavine). Those sources are now under five percent of that former level.
- He argues that if he had stayed all in on Amazon and Mediavine, he would be struggling.
- New ventures LocalRank.so and Trackings.ai added $71k in August alone.
- His framing: "Diversification is insurance against algorithm changes and platform risk."
- Rule: "Do not rely on a single revenue source because algorithms can change overnight."

chunks.heading: Double down when something works
chunks.text:
- LocalRank started about five months before the update and is already his largest revenue driver. Trackings launched three days before the post and was already moving fast.
- His rule: when he sees traction, he goes all in.
- He notes new projects can surpass old ones quickly. Five months earlier LocalRank did not exist.
- He teased another software project launching the next month, which he expected to be a "home run".

chunks.heading: Build in public as a distribution strategy
chunks.text:
- Sharing revenue numbers attracts attention. One tweet about his revenue went viral and gained him over 1,000 followers in 24 hours.
- He argues transparency fuels trust and product launches.
- He says reporting wins publicly builds authority and audience faster than ads.
- He uses the monthly revenue post itself to cross-promote his products: LocalRank academy (get your first local SEO client, guaranteed), BrowserBlast (Indexsy's main revenue source) and the net worth tracker.

chunks.heading: Balancing long-term and short-term plays
chunks.text:
Jacky splits his portfolio by role:
- STR Lisbon (short-term rental real estate): his "retirement plan", stable income.
- Software and SEO products: scalable growth.
- Smaller plays like hosting and affiliates: low-effort bonus revenue.

The mix across SEO products, SaaS, real estate and affiliates is what kept August only slightly down month over month.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Jacky Chou explains how he uses AI to publish thousands of People Also Ask posts a day, then has humans rewrite the ones that rank. He also covers topical authority, performance plateaus and branding, creator-led companies, and diversification.

chunks.heading: AI content for SEO: bulk-publish, then rewrite what ranks
chunks.text:
- Jacky uses AI for content creation and runs a couple of pure AI-automated sites that publish "people also ask" content.
- His reasoning: hiring writers gets very pricey at scale, and AI lets him test keywords at a scale that wasn't possible before.
- He uses a custom-built service that auto-posts to WordPress. He can publish thousands of blog posts a day and push them through indexing services.
- One of these sites was at about 1,500 views a day at the time. He calls the results "pretty surprising" and says he is "seeing some crazy success."
- He declined to name the service ("I'm gonna gate keep this").
- His observation on detection: AI sites that get publicly identified on Twitter get destroyed immediately. Sites that stay quiet and aren't doing huge numbers yet probably won't be found. So far Google isn't catching up, even though mainstream marketing outlets keep saying it will.

chunks.heading: AI content workflow: post in bulk, rank, then rewrite with humans
chunks.text:
- Current process: bulk-post AI content, see what ranks, then have a human writer rewrite it, then optimize it.
- AI content is not great for buyer-intent content right now, so he doesn't rely on it there.
- Its strength is building topical authority very quickly.
- Example: write a thousand posts on how to cut various things, then target "best chef's knives for cutting." That is much easier to rank than starting from scratch.
- He notes a full affiliate site made only of "best XYZ knives" pages wouldn't work anymore. The informational cluster is what carries it.

chunks.heading: Performance plateau: why paid direct-response stops working
chunks.text:
- Jacky describes the performance plateau as mainly relevant to large DTC and consumer brands, not niche site builders.
- Running paid direct-response ads for too long eventually stops converting. He cites Airbnb as saying it hit this plateau.
- The fix is branding campaigns. You saturate the people reachable on Facebook and Instagram, so you need to reach people who aren't on those platforms as often.
- Example he gives: Coca-Cola's expensive product placements in movies and on Netflix exist to extend brand reach once performance ads are saturated.

chunks.heading: Creator-led brands
chunks.text:
- He calls creator-led companies a popular topic right now. The biggest example he cites is MrBeast Burgers.
- The playbook: grow an audience first, then launch products easily because the audience is large.
- His view: building a brand around your own identity tends to make customers a lot more loyal.
- He expects a seismic shift in this space over the next couple of years.

chunks.heading: Why big tech is laying off, and what display ad RPMs signal
chunks.text:
- He cites Meta laying off 11,000 people, Twitter cutting about 50%, and Stripe layoffs, and says he periodically checks layoffs.fyi.
- His plain explanation of the cause: during Covid, online shopping and social media use spiked, and companies built projections off that usage. After Covid usage dropped, which they didn't anticipate. Amazon, Facebook and Stripe had to re-run projections, and the numbers looked bad, so they cut headcount to avoid running out of money in two years.
- A leading indicator he watches: display ad RPMs (he's seen it via Mediavine-style display ads) are much lower than a year earlier. His read is that advertisers are seeing less money come in, so they spend less on ads, so publisher payouts fall. He says the slowdown in consumer spending is "pretty alarming."
- Lesson he endorses: diversify. He says diversification is "nonexistent" in the niche site community, where many people rely on a single income source like display ads.
- He also notes Stripe's valuation was still around 40 or 50x annual revenue, which he calls absurd but plausible for a software business.

chunks.heading: Twitter, Meta and short-form video
chunks.text:
- On Twitter: he said he would invest as of then ("100%"). He calls Elon Musk probably the number one executor and operator among tech company leaders, with Mark Zuckerberg not far under.
- On Zuckerberg: he says people don't give him enough credit for keeping Meta relevant for years by copying competitors, for example Snapchat. He calls VR a Hail Mary and says "I wouldn't bet against Zuck right now, but I'm not betting for him." His stance: "I'd rather be late than wrong."
- Platform shifts he sees: kids aren't using Instagram, and Facebook skews older. He cites a poll saying 35% of Gen Z have TikTok, then Snapchat, then Instagram. He's more bullish on Snapchat.
- TikTok experiment: he ran a challenge posting two short-form videos a day and spent an hour a day on the app to learn what works. His advice is to use the app for about an hour so the algorithm learns what you want.

chunks.heading: FTX collapse and holding crypto
chunks.text:
- His summary of the collapse: a rumor spread that FTX was insolvent while crypto was falling. Binance's CEO (CZ) announced Binance would sell its FTX stake, worth about 2 to 3 billion, held in BUSD and FTX's own token, FTT. Selling on the open market (not over the counter) drove the price down. That created a domino effect, and FTX halted withdrawals. He says several friends lost millions.
- He notes FTX US and Binance US are separate entities from the international exchanges because of US regulation, and reports suggested FTX US users could withdraw.
- He cited Sam Bankman-Fried's net worth falling about 95%, from roughly 16 billion to 1 billion.
- Lesson he endorses: "not your keys, not your crypto," meaning trade on exchanges but move holdings off. He admitted he still held a significant amount on Binance and trusted it.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Jacky Chou and James De Lacey trade niche-site and brand tactics: refresh publish dates to jump rankings, interlink a "best X" roundup with individual product reviews, and use YouTube embeds as a ranking flywheel. They also cover the Made.com collapse as a warning on burn rate after the Covid boom, and expected pain for DTC and affiliate revenue.

chunks.heading: Refreshing publish dates to trigger recency boosts in SEO
chunks.text:
- Jacky changes the publish date on his blog posts to the most recent date about once a month or once every two months.
- He does it on sites he has owned for a while, and on sites he wants to push from rank 5-10 up to the top 5.
- When he buys a website, he immediately slaps on a nice theme, designs it well, and changes all blog posts to the most recent date. That "typically gives it a jump". He then optimizes the posts after the jump and builds from there.
- When he is lazy, he changes only the date and no content, and the rankings pop immediately.
- He says this works extremely well for tech niches because "tech's all about recency".
- He notes that if articles are good enough, there is always an excuse to go back, update small bits and change the date again.

chunks.heading: Recency and Google reviews in local SEO
chunks.text:
- Jacky points to an agency study that found a correlation between local SEO rankings and the recency of Google reviews. The finding: the more recent reviews a business has, the better it ranks.
- He cautions it may be correlation, not causation. A business ranking number one gets more traffic, so it gets more recent reviews.
- He sees a plausible mechanism: a business that consistently earns five-star reviews over months signals to Google that it is good, so Google keeps sending it traffic.
- He says Google reviews are easy to abuse and that the market rate for bought reviews is about $2 to $10. He says he has never done it. The risk is losing your Google My Business location.
- His advice: if there is any way to convert something into local SEO, do it.

chunks.heading: Original images for review content at scale (UGC-style visuals)
chunks.text:
- For reviews, he says the standard approach is to take your own photos of the product and post them so Google sees original content.
- At scale, or for products you cannot buy (he says you cannot buy every MacBook), he describes an "unethical hack":
  - Take stock images or Amazon product images.
  - Remove the background in Canva and add your own background, such as a photo of your table.
  - Flip the images so Google cannot find them in reverse image search.
- The result is new, original-looking images. He frames it openly as a shortcut, not a best practice.

chunks.heading: YouTube as a self-reinforcing loop for a site that already ranks
chunks.text:
- Jacky is "pretty bullish on YouTube right now". His team is editing long-form YouTube videos for an architecture site.
- One video was at 23K views after about a week and a half.
- His loop:
  - Organic YouTube views come in.
  - Embedding the video on a website that already ranks pushes more views to the video.
  - More views lift the video's rank on YouTube.
  - The video then pushes traffic back to the site.
- In the architecture niche he is also running a challenge of two TikToks a day for three months. It is going well for follower growth on Instagram and YouTube but is not yet driving much direct traffic to the site. TikTok itself has not been cracked yet.
- A Far & Away TikTok flopped, while the same content did OK on Instagram at about 15K views.

chunks.heading: DTC collapse, Made.com, and what it signals for niche sites
chunks.text:
- Jacky's account of Made.com, a DTC furniture brand: it was valued at about $1 billion about a year earlier and listed on the London Stock Exchange. It raised about $135M and did about $500M in annual revenue. It went bankrupt and sold its brand and domain for $3M.
- He also cites Touch of Modern, which did $120M in annual revenue and sold its assets for $7M.
- His diagnosis: online shopping surged during COVID, consumers did not return as projected, and the companies ran projections off the surge. Revenue dropped, burn rate was too high, and leadership did not cut drastically to a slow burn.
- DTC logic is to burn cash on ads to grab market share in hopes of profitability later. He expects a lot more pain for DTC and e-commerce aggregators, especially in Q1.
- Implication for niche sites: slowing consumer spending trickles down to who pays for display ads and affiliate commissions. He expects to feel it around Q2-Q3.
- His plan: offload some niche sites in January at whatever multiples he can get, and hold the big ones for a long time.

chunks.heading: Search engines, Bing traffic, and platform shifts
chunks.text:
- Apple search engine: he thinks it is a smart play, comparing it to Apple's iOS privacy update that hurt Facebook before Apple launched its own competing product. He flags possible antitrust risk. He agrees Google needs competitors even though his revenue depends on Google traffic.
- Bing: some of his sites get 15-20% of traffic from Bing. Funnily, the AI sites get a lot of it. He credits the Rank Math Instant Indexing API (instant index to Bing) and recommends installing it.
- Mastodon: he sees it as growing fast after Elon bought Twitter, but expects it to die within months. Open source and server-based instances make finding friends hard, and it is "not built to scale". He compares it to Clubhouse, which blew up and then faded.
- TikTok: he watches Chinese TikTok (Douyin) to see what TikTok will look like in the US in about two years. Examples are integrated one-click shops with a hovering buy-now button during live streams, where people buy off the streams as a daily routine. He also sees opportunity in live streams of people making products by hand, such as pouring candles, and selling them.
- He notes TikTok copied the BeReal format with a "now" feature.

chunks.heading: Building a personal-training and gym business model (side views)
chunks.text:
- On gyms, Jacky says the way to make money is to upsell members on personal training and on your own private-label protein powder, which is a generic powder sold at double the price.
- He says local SEO makes a gym a natural fit for the Google reviews tactic above.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: A buyer-first guide to selling an Amazon FBA business. It covers which business types sell (proprietary > private label > reseller), how to value it with SDE and EBITDA, the factors that raise the multiple, who buys at each price tier, and typical sale timelines.

chunks.heading: Can an Amazon FBA business be sold: business type decides saleability
chunks.text:
Jacky says saleability depends on three things: business type, age, and annual net profit (SDE/EBITDA). The rule for the whole process is to always consider the buyer's perspective. Without that, a listing "could sit on the listings for months."

Business types, from least to most sellable:
- **Reseller (buy box):** Buys wholesale and sells at retail on Amazon. Can be hard to impossible to sell even if profitable. The reasons are volatility (unlimited competition), unreliable supply (wholesale items may not stay available), and nothing proprietary (the buyer is only buying access to a Seller Central account).
- **Private label:** Own brand, full control of the product. More attractive because supply is consistent and the products have a sales history, so they are likelier to keep selling.
- **Proprietary products:** Only your company sells the product, so buyers pay a premium. He calls this the "gold medal" category.

Buyers rank unique brand and product highest. His example: supplements with a custom formula are worth more than generic supplements. Private label comes next, then reseller.

chunks.heading: Valuing an Amazon FBA business
chunks.text:
- Jacky says it is hard to know the true value until the business sells, but there is a rule of thumb: multiply annual net profit by two. In practice the SDE is usually multiplied by two.
- The offer is directly proportionate to net profit.
- SDE = Revenue – Expenses + Add-backs.
  - Expenses include cost of goods, employee fees, Amazon fees, software fees, fulfillment services, shipping services, and company taxes.
  - Add back any salary you pay yourself.
  - Personal expenses unrelated to the business do not count as expenses.
- SDE is the valuation basis for revenue below roughly $5 million to $10 million. EBITDA is used above $10 million.
- The buyer purchases inventory at cost, including the cost of getting it into FBA warehouses.

chunks.heading: Preparing your books so buyers don't walk away
chunks.text:
- Jacky says to know your numbers inside out and keep them organized immaculately before looking for a buyer.
- "Buyers are often looking for that one reason not to buy." Clean books remove at least one reason.
- Start keeping current, accurate records now if you don't have them. Savvy buyers study trends in the P&L: are sales trending up, down, or steady?
- Some buyers also check the Amazon Best Sellers Rank to see where the business is trending.
- Use accrual accounting to track profitability each month. A proper P&L shows exactly how much profit the business makes monthly.
- The business is only considered if it has turned a profit, and higher profit makes it more attractive.

chunks.heading: How to increase the sale price
chunks.text:
Jacky frames each lever through the buyer's lens.

**Age.** Buyers think in this progression: year one is discovery, years two and three are growth, and year four is optimizing net profit for sale.
- Under 1 year: not great, expect low-ball offers.
- 1 to 2 years: good.
- Over 3 years: great.

**Diversification.** The biggest risk of an FBA business is account suspension or losing Amazon rankings. Proving the business can weather a storm raises its value.
1. List multiple products in multiple niches.
2. Build profitable paid traffic inside Amazon (pay-per-click or sponsored ads).
3. Add traffic sources outside Amazon: a website, social media, email marketing.
4. Keep any single product or niche under 70% of the business's income.

**Defensibility.** How hard is it for a competitor to take your share? If the product is easy to source, anyone can launch a copycat listing. A patent raises value. Ways to increase defensibility:
- Proprietary products.
- Strong customer loyalty to the brand.
- Higher quality than copycat products.

**Competition.** Rankings can vanish overnight, and so can income, so buyers avoid businesses facing sophisticated FBA competitors. Keeping only one or two products in highly competitive markets removes that risk in the buyer's eyes.

chunks.heading: Sell or hold?
chunks.text:
Jacky offers these questions to ask yourself:
- Is managing the business a chore?
- Am I working on something more exciting?
- Do I simply want more cash in the bank?
- Could I put the capital from the sale into a new venture?

If you answer yes to one or more, it may be time to sell. If you answer no to all, holding a bit longer may be best. Make sure the business's value isn't declining as time passes.

chunks.heading: Who your buyer is, by price tier
chunks.text:
- **Under $500,000:** Mostly private investors seeking better returns than a bank.
  - They have low risk appetite because they deploy their own capital.
  - This tier holds the bulk of listings, so it is a buyer's market.
  - Many are new to Amazon and hunt for the best deal in range. They favor proprietary or own-brand businesses, which have a higher chance of finding a buyer.
- **$500,000 to $1 million:** A "black hole." Few private buyers will put down this much cash and it is a bit low for private equity, so the sale may take longer.
- **$1 million to $5 million:** "This is where the party is at." There are many cash buyers, and many want SBA financing, which goes up to $5 million.
- **$5 million and above:** Private equity buyers, strategic buyers, and family offices.

chunks.heading: Finding a buyer, timelines, transfer and payment
chunks.text:
**Finding a buyer**
- List on marketplaces such as businessforsale.com, flippa.com, or bizbuysell.com.
- Ask other FBA sellers if they know an interested buyer.
- Many recommend a trusted broker for a smoother process.
- Jacky doesn't offer brokering but recommends Thrasio. He has heard only good things from sellers and says it moves quickly, with deals closed in under 5 days.

**Average time to sell, by price**
- Under $100,000: 66 days
- $100,000 to $500,000: 118 days
- $500,000 to $1 million: 151 days
- $1 million to $2 million: 128 days
- $2 million to $5 million: 146 days
- Over $5 million: 170 days

**Transfer:** It depends on your country. You must notify Amazon of the change and get its approval of the new owner.

**Getting paid:** Jacky calls this arguably the most important part for the seller. Use an escrow service that holds the money until both parties are happy, then releases it to your bank account by wire transfer.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Jacky Chou's SEO essay ranks link-building vendors (Indexsy first, a self-admitted plug) and explains how to vet them. It covers effective link types (niche edits, outreach, broken-link, citations, PR) versus tactics to avoid (PBNs, article directories, volume-based packages).

chunks.heading: Why Jacky says link building matters and what a link-building service is
chunks.text:
- He calls link building "among the most important SEO tactics" and one of the heavily weighted Google ranking factors.
- His reasoning: Google ranks sites that show authority, trust and expertise. When other sites link to yours, Google reads it as an authority signal and rewards those pages with higher rankings.
- He calls it one of the hardest parts of an SEO expert's job, so he recommends outsourcing it to link-building experts who build a custom strategy.
- A link-building service is a digital marketing service from an SEO agency or consultant that speeds up the number of backlinks to your site.
- White-hat methods he lists: guest blogging, broken link building, and manual outreach campaigns that show people your content.
- His warning: genuine, quality providers are hard to find. Many get low-quality links through spammy tactics Google dislikes.
- He says he "spent $10k on backlinks" and published the results (the details are not in this piece).

chunks.heading: Jacky's niche edit approach and Indexsy pricing
chunks.text:
He openly calls recommending his own company, Indexsy, a "shameless plug" and says it is the best link-building service on the market. Indexsy focuses on niche edits.

**Why niche edits:**
- A niche edit places a link in existing content that has been live for months or years.
- That page has aged well and gained authority in Google's index, so he calls these links "the ultimate goal of all the links."

**Two-step process:**
1. Identify a relevant existing post for your site, based on the metrics you ordered.
2. Reach out and secure the link placement within that post.

**Starter packages (most popular):**
- Beginner, 5 links: $290
- Advanced, 10 links: $575
- Expert, 50 links: $2,750

**Authority packs (for high referring domains):**
- Starter, 10 links: $700
- Booster, 20 links: $1,350
- Domination, 50 links: $3,000

**Traffic packs (for more traffic and the highest impact):**
- Starter, 10 links: $1,200
- Booster, 20 links: $2,300
- Domination, 50 links: $5,500
- Intermediate, 10 links: $1,500
- Advanced, 20 links: $2,900
- Expert, 10 links: $7,000

**Build your own (single links):**
- Premium Single Link: $60
- Premium Deluxe Link: $75
- Platinum Single Link: $90

chunks.heading: Other link-building agencies Jacky lists and how they price
chunks.text:
- **Page One Power:** best for customized campaigns. It does discovery calls, builds a bespoke strategy and quotes per project. Content is built on research so authoritative site owners in the client's niche want to link to it. A project manager oversees the campaign.
- **Rhino Rank:** offers curated links and guest posts. Curated links go on content that has been indexed for months or years, the same two-step approach as niche edits. Entry price is as low as $95. He calls it among the best for affordability.
- **HigherVisibility:** an award-winning SEO agency for enterprise outreach, press outreach and high-end links. It stresses relevance as well as authority and sends monthly reports. Pricing is by consultation.
- **From The Future:** an enterprise agency for high-end links and press outreach. It typically works with clients on a $7,000 per month budget, and suggests less for link building alone. Its four steps: link analysis and audit, prospecting and value propositions, testing link types, monthly reporting. Link types tested include guest posts, resource links, unlinked mentions and sponsorships.
- **Whitespark:** a citation building service best for local businesses. It charges $4 per generic or national directory citation and about $5 for local or industry-specific directories. It also offers Google My Business management and a one-time-payment Yext replacement service.

chunks.heading: How Jacky says to evaluate and hire a link-building company
chunks.text:
**What a good company does:**
- **Discovery session:** it learns your business needs first and doesn't jump straight to a proposal. A tactic that worked for one site won't automatically work for yours.
- **Research and strategic recommendations:** delivered by email or on a call.
- **Contract with deliverables:** deadlines, resources, deliverables and budget spelled out in detail.
- **Client onboarding:** you share your website, blog and analytics, and they set how the project is managed.

**What to check before hiring:**
- **Competitor analysis:** do they study how many and what types of links successful competitors build?
- **Pricing:** shop around. Prices that look too good to be true versus other services are a red flag for low-quality links.
- **Bespoke strategy and roadmap:** tactics relevant to your industry, with a structured campaign plan.
- **Samples:** always ask for link samples and case studies to judge quality.
- **Team size:** his view is that large link-building companies decline in quality as they grow, because the mindset shifts from building quality backlinks to scaling the business.

chunks.heading: Link types Jacky says are effective
chunks.text:
- **Guest blogging:** pitch authoritative owners in your niche. The link should sit in the body of the content or the author byline.
- **Blogger outreach:** it can go well or fail badly because it resembles spam. The difference is personalization: target specific blogs and journalists and write personalized emails explaining why they should link. A variant is to create the best content on a topic, find sites linking to your competitors, and ask them to link to yours instead.
- **Resource page links:** find resource pages listing useful sites in your niche and ask to be added. Ideally find a page linking to a dead site and offer yours. Only works if your site is useful and offers new insight.
- **Citation links:** list your business with its NAP (name, address, phone) in business directories. This works best for local businesses and adds geo-relevancy. Citations cost about $5 each, while other links can cost from several hundred to a few thousand dollars each.
- **Broken link building:** find broken links on popular sites in your industry, create better content on the same topic, and suggest the owner swap it in. It works because dead links hurt user experience and webmasters want them gone.
- **Brand mentions:** find sites that mention your brand without linking and ask for a link. The author already knows your brand, so these tend to go well.
- **PR links:** create a unique angle on your business, write a press release and distribute it to PR syndication sites.

chunks.heading: Link-building tactics Jacky says to avoid
chunks.text:
His warning: link schemes may give short-term ranking gains but end in penalization, because Google is now better at spotting inorganic links. A respectable vendor shouldn't offer these.

- **Low-quality article directories** (ezinearticles.com, goarticles.com) with thin spun content. This stopped working with the 2011 Panda update.
- **Volume-based "link building packages"** that focus on link count over quality, built from one low-impact technique or a mix of link schemes.
- **Private blog networks (PBNs):** a black hat tactic of owner-controlled sites built to link out. He calls it an obvious attempt to manipulate rankings, and says most PBN providers only rent links that won't stand the test of time.
- **SEO press releases:** written for SEO rather than newsworthiness. The frequency voids the effort.
- **Spammy blog comments:** generic comments with links. Commenting is fine only when you genuinely engage with the blogger and readers.
- **Web 2.0 platforms:** setting up blogs to piggyback off domain authority. It is outdated, and providers spam many links, which doesn't work.
- **Low-quality directories:** directories users rarely visit. They bring no results and can take months to publish a submission.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: A practical guide to local SEO built around Google's three local signals (relevance, prominence, distance). It covers key ranking factors (NAP consistency, localized content, local backlinks, schema) and five tactics: Google Business Profile, citations, website optimization, content, and customer reviews.

chunks.heading: What local SEO is and how Jacky defines the strategy
chunks.text:
- Local SEO is SEO aimed at ranking in local search results pages so more customers find and visit a business.
- Jacky frames the strategy as the overall process a local business owner uses to optimize site content and online presence for higher local rankings.
- Traditional SEO builds visibility on a wide scale. Local SEO concentrates on attracting customers near the physical location and getting them through the door.
- He says it is critical for businesses that depend on foot traffic or serve a specific geographic area.
- He says it takes "a lot of time, planning, and perseverance", and the strategy must be monitored and improved as the search landscape changes.

chunks.heading: How Google ranks local results: relevance, prominence, distance
chunks.text:
- Jacky says Google mainly uses three signals for local rankings:
  - **Relevance:** does the business listing match the searcher's intent?
  - **Prominence:** is the business popular both online and offline?
  - **Distance:** how close the business is to the searcher at the moment of search.
- Distance can't be changed, so the strategy is to match the other two criteria well.
- If a searcher uses a location or "near me" and the listing matches the query well, the business can appear in Google's local 3-pack, which shows the top three matching local businesses.

chunks.heading: The five local ranking factors to target
chunks.text:
1. **Accurate NAP (Name, Address, Phone):** keep it identical across the website, all social profiles and local directories. Inconsistent NAP can confuse search engines into thinking the business isn't legitimate or that there are multiple businesses.
2. **Titles, headers and meta descriptions:** include the city and locally relevant keywords for the service or product, on the homepage, blog posts and other pages.
3. **Localized content:** write about neighboring attractions, upcoming town events, or how-to articles about the services offered to signal relevance and authority for local searches.
4. **Local backlinks:** get high-quality links from trustworthy sites in the industry. They strengthen trust and relevance signals and can lift rankings significantly over time.
5. **Local schema markup:** give crawlers factual business data such as address, phone number, hours, ratings and reviews. It also shows snippets of information directly in the SERPs and adds credibility.

chunks.heading: Google My Business optimization
chunks.text:
- Jacky puts the GMB page at the top of every business's local SEO to-do list as the simplest way to build brand awareness. A free listing improves visibility on Google Search and Google Maps.
- Stats he cites: GMB signals make up 33% of all local pack signals, and Google is the first place 63% of consumers go for reviews before visiting a business. Having no presence means losing customers to nearby competitors.
- Steps:
  1. Claim the listing. For multiple locations, use Google's Bulk Location Management Tool with a custom spreadsheet or Google's template.
  2. Fill in as much as possible: a short description, photos of products or services, and an eye-catching profile photo.
- He calls the profile photo one of the most important features for consumers in local results.
- Use a local search rank checker to compare review count and overall rating against local competitors and to find insights that improve reputation and rankings.

chunks.heading: Citations: finding and fixing them
chunks.text:
- Citations are any place on the internet where the business's basic information appears. He says they make up about 7% of local search signals.
- Two types:
  - **Structured:** listings you create by filling out forms or building a profile page.
  - **Unstructured:** mentions you don't create, such as news articles, blog posts and "Best of" guides.
- Every citation must match. Incorrect info across citations costs visibility and can lower SERP rank.
- Audit process:
  - Search the business name, address and phone number to see where it's listed.
  - Also try a misspelled brand name, a slightly different address, and look for duplicate listings to surface inconsistent citations.
  - Note and correct the wrong ones. If a guide or blog post has it wrong, contact the author with the right details.
  - Control as many listings as possible for consistency and to monitor customer feedback.
- Beyond GMB, claim Yelp Business Page, TripAdvisor Business Profile and a Facebook Page.
- Citation software and local listing management services can handle the manual work.

chunks.heading: Website optimization and content
chunks.text:
- Jacky argues ranking the company website on page one beats a third-party listing, because a click on your site (rather than Google's directory or Yelp) signals curiosity about your brand. Give visitors as much information as possible to make an informed decision.
- Website tactics:
  - Place valuable local keywords in content titles, site headings and image elements.
  - Add schema markup in the HTML to highlight relevant information.
  - For multi-location businesses, build a dedicated landing page per location and keep each URL basic so search engines and customers can find it.
  - Make the site mobile-friendly. He cites that 88% of local searches are on smartphones or tablets.
- Content:
  - He calls content "the backbone of any local SEO strategy" and says it can generate more leads than paid promotion and advertising.
  - It must be meaningful and useful, not just published in hope of leads. Keep tone and quality consistent across the site.
  - Pick broad topics that represent the business as a whole, not just ways to sell products. This shows industry understanding and positions the business as a thought leader on the local scene.
  - Search engines are the most common source of blog traffic, so include keywords related to the brand. Even a few high-quality pieces can set a business apart from competitors.

chunks.heading: Customer reviews
chunks.text:
- Jacky says reviews are one of the top three ranking variables for getting into the local pack, and most shoppers rely on them for purchase decisions. Review quality and quantity on local listings can pull customers in or push them to competitors.
- Respond to both positive and negative reviews. Good responses can turn a one-time customer into a loyal one or bring a critic back.
- Actively ask for reviews using a range of tactics:
  - Feedback kiosk at checkout
  - Post-visit emails
  - Website review landing pages
  - SMS notifications
  - Asking directly
- Offering several routes makes the request convenient, and a steady flow of reviews strengthens the business image.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: A generic SEO checklist for private equity firms. It leans on one stat (SEO leads close at 14.6% vs 1.7% for outbound) and then covers keyword research, on-page basics, backlinks, local and reputation, and technical hygiene. Mostly standard beginner SEO with little original insight.

chunks.heading: Why Jacky says SEO suits private equity firms
chunks.text:
- Jacky cites a stat that SEO-generated inbound leads have a 14.6% close rate, against 1.7% for outbound leads. The cited reason is that inbound leads come from people who initiated a call or navigated to a website, so they are actively shopping and intend to buy.
- His logic for private equity: potential investors search Google for relevant terms, so ranking for those searches puts the firm in front of them. A strong online presence makes a firm more likely to attract new investors and grow.
- SEO raises both the quantity and the quality of organic traffic, which comes from people searching specific keywords or phrases.
- He treats it as ongoing work: "SEO is an ongoing process," so monitor and adjust the strategy regularly to stay ahead of competitors.
- If a firm wants faster results, he suggests hiring an SEO company to save time.

chunks.heading: On-site SEO: keywords and content
chunks.text:
- Keyword research comes first. Investors find a firm through the terms they search, so those terms must appear on the site.
- Tools he names: Google Keyword Planner, SEMrush and Ahrefs.
- He recommends focusing on long-tail and LSI (semantically related) keywords. Long-tail phrases are more specific, less competitive and more likely to convert into leads. LSI keywords help search engines understand the context of a page.
- Content should be high-quality, informative, relevant and kept up to date.
- Include target keywords but avoid keyword stuffing.
- Use headings and subheadings to break content up, and lists and bullets to make it easy to scan.

chunks.heading: On-site SEO: tags, URLs, sitemap, schema and mobile
chunks.text:
- **Title tags:** include target keywords and keep them under 60 characters so they are not truncated.
- **Meta descriptions:** include target keywords, keep them under 155 characters, and make them compelling and clickable to lift click-through rate.
- **URLs:** clear and easy to understand, with target keywords, no special characters, and as short as possible.
- **XML sitemap:** list every page on the site, including pages not linked from elsewhere, so search engines can find, crawl and index them.
- **Navigation and schema markup:** clear navigation helps investors find information. Schema markup gives search engines extra detail about the firm and its services.
- **Mobile:** most people browse on mobile, so use a layout that adapts to screen sizes and make sure pages load quickly on phones.

chunks.heading: Off-site SEO: backlinks, social and reputation
chunks.text:
- **Backlinks:** inbound links from other sites signal credibility and authority. Quality beats quantity: a few links from reputable, high-authority sites are better than many low-quality ones.
- Ways he lists to build them: creating high-quality content, guest blogging and broken link building.
- **Social media:** keep profiles on LinkedIn, Twitter, Instagram and Facebook, post regularly and engage followers to build relationships with potential investors and drive traffic to the site.
- **Online reputation management:** investors often research a firm online before investing. Search the firm's name on Google and social media regularly, respond to negative comments or reviews, address issues promptly, and create positive content.
- **Reviews:** encourage clients to leave reviews as social proof that builds credibility and trust and can improve visibility and rankings.

chunks.heading: Local SEO, Google My Business and directories
chunks.text:
- Local SEO targets investors in a specific geography: use local keywords, create local business listings and build local reviews.
- Put the city and state in title tags, meta descriptions and content.
- **Google My Business:** a free tool for keeping name, address, phone number and hours accurate and consistent across the web. Add pictures and videos and respond to reviews.
- **Directories:** in addition to GMB, keep profiles on platforms like Yelp, Yellow Pages and BBB. They add visibility, help local SEO, build trust and bring in reviews.

chunks.heading: Measurement and technical SEO
chunks.text:
- **Google Analytics:** shows visitor numbers, where they come from and how they interact with the site, so you can spot patterns and opportunities.
- **Google Search Console:** shows how the site performs in search, flags issues hurting visibility, and reveals which keywords people use to find it so content can be optimized for them.
- **Technical checklist:**
  - Mobile-friendly, via responsive design or a separate mobile version.
  - Fast loading on desktop and mobile: optimize images, compress files and minify HTML, JavaScript and CSS.
  - HTTPS to encrypt data between server and client.
  - An improved XML sitemap to help crawling and indexing.
  - A robots.txt file to keep search engines from crawling pages not relevant to the business.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Jacky Chou explains what negative SEO is, the main attack types (link farms, fake link-removal requests, hacking, heavy crawling, duplicate content, fake reviews), and why Google's Penguin 4.0 makes link-spam attacks far less effective. He gives a monitoring and defense checklist: traffic and Search Console alerts, backlink audits, disavowing, securing admin logins, and site speed.

chunks.heading: What negative SEO is and why it happens
chunks.text:
- Jacky defines negative SEO as lowering a competitor's search rankings through dishonest or unethical means.
- It is not always deliberate. Link farms, private blog networks, and thousands of bot scraping sites generate links, and a clean site can get lumped in with them.
- Motives he lists: sabotaging a competitor, extortion, or simply causing chaos. Negative SEO services are sold openly online.
- Some attacks are accidental or come from inside. Family members, employees, or paid SEO companies may use black hat tactics to try to boost the site.
- He says searches for "negative SEO" have been rising over the previous 24 months and that the problem is not going away.
- Attacker methods include duplicating content, fake social profiles, hacking and link spamming, spammy misspelled anchor text, and getting existing links to the site removed.

chunks.heading: Does negative SEO work?
chunks.text:
- Google's official position (John Mueller, Gary Illyes) is "no", and Mueller has called it a meme.
- Jacky does not take that at face value. His view: negative SEO can still work, but it is far less of a problem than it was some years ago.
- Why it is harder to pull off now:
  - Since Penguin 4.0, Google devalues link spam instead of penalizing whole sites.
  - Penguin became more granular. It adjusts ranking based on spam signals rather than hitting overall ranking, and it targets the unsophisticated link spam most attacks rely on.
  - Spam-filled results would drive users away from Google and hurt its ad revenue, so ineffective negative SEO is core to Google's business.
- Link-based attacks are less common than they used to be, but attacks are not limited to links. A hacker can inject malicious code, outbound links to bad sites, or bogus negative reviews.
- Conclusion: finding and disavowing dodgy links is no longer enough. Monitor your whole online presence and use good security.

chunks.heading: Link-based attacks: link farms and fake removal requests
chunks.text:
- **Link farms:**
  - One or two spammy links rarely matter, so attackers use networks of related sites.
  - Most links share the same exact-match anchor text, either irrelevant to the target or a term that makes the owner look like they are manipulating their own link profile.
  - Case: WP Bacon, a WordPress podcast site, quickly accumulated thousands of links with the anchor "porn movie". In a week it dropped more than 50 places for most of its ranking terms. The webmaster disavowed the spammy sites and regained most of its positions.
- **Fake link removal requests:**
  - Unethical SEOs email sites that link to you and persuade them to remove some of your best links.
  - It is uncommon but can be devastating. Losing several top backlinks in a day can significantly drop rankings.
  - You can't stop the emails. Defend by watching for signs of an active removal attempt and acting fast, using Ahrefs Alerts.

chunks.heading: Technical and on-site attacks and their fixes
chunks.text:
- **False URL parameters:**
  - Parameters used for sorting and filtering (common in e-commerce) can be abused if the site is not configured properly, so many near-identical versions of a page get indexed.
  - Detection: the Coverage report in Google Search Console. A rise in indexed pages can signal an attack.
- **Heavy crawling:**
  - Aggressive crawling raises server load, slowing or crashing the site. Repeated incidents can cost search credibility.
  - Fix: ask your host or webmaster whether a slowdown is maintenance, organic traffic growth, or an attack. Options include firewall rules or routing traffic through a DDoS protection provider.
- **DDoS:**
  - Floods the server until resources run out. Attacks that only slow the site are sneakier than ones that crash it, because page speed and Core Web Vitals are ranking factors.
  - Fix: continuously monitor incoming traffic and requests. Subtle attacks can be spotted this way, but massive ones can take a site down in seconds.
- **Hacking:**
  - Can inject low-quality or duplicate content, change links, add new links, or alter robots.txt to disrupt indexing.
  - Fix: regular site audits with a tool to catch small changes that would otherwise go unnoticed.
- **Duplicate content:**
  - Content is scraped and republished elsewhere, and Google has to decide which copy to rank, which is not necessarily the original.
- **Pogo sticking:**
  - Bots search for terms you rank for, click your result, and leave immediately, signaling that your page does not satisfy the query.
  - Fix: regularly monitor your most important pages' stats in Google Analytics.

chunks.heading: Reputation attacks: fake reviews and fake profiles
chunks.text:
- **Fake reviews:**
  - He treats reviews as just as important as quality backlinks. A flood of negative ones hurts local search results and the business itself, and reviews are easy to manipulate.
  - Fix: check Google My Business often and read every new review. Fake reviews violate Google's policy.
- **Fake social profiles:**
  - Attackers create profiles in your name and misuse them to attack your credibility.
  - Fix: use social listening tools (HubSpot, Hootsuite, Social Mention) that alert you when your name is mentioned. Respond quickly and directly to criticism so it doesn't gain traction.

chunks.heading: Protection playbook
chunks.text:
1. **Detect early.** Watch organic traffic in Google Analytics. A drastic drop often signals a Google penalty. Search Console emails you about indexing problems or manual penalties, and the sooner you know, the sooner you can respond.
2. **Secure the admin login.** Hackers usually need admin access, so extra layers of protection reduce the chance of altered SEO properties, changed critical files, and modified redirects.
3. **Disavow.** Google's disavow tool (released October 2012 after public outcry over negative SEO) tells Google you don't want credit from low-quality links. It is especially useful against link farms and Google bowling.
4. **Review SEO settings regularly.** Periodically check on-page elements, robots.txt, headers, and image alt tags.
5. **Prevent hacking.** Set up Search Console alerts, run frequent site audits, and consider hiring cybersecurity companies or staff. A hacked site may carry spammy signals you can't see even though you still have full access.
6. **Fight fake backlinks.**
   - Run a backlink audit tool regularly and watch the score indicator for suspicious changes.
   - Track your authority score trend, since a drop can mean something is wrong in the backlink profile.
   - Update your disavow file regularly when new harmful links appear that you can't remove.
   - For hundreds of bad links, handle it like a manual action: go link by link, group them by criteria, and disavow.
7. **Speed up the site.** Use Google Analytics alerts to catch slowdowns. Fixes: enable caching, disable resource-heavy plugins, optimize image sizes, delete excess code, and block spammer activity.

chunks.heading: Relying on Google
chunks.text:
- Jacky says Google works behind the scenes against negative SEO but can't share details, since that would give spammers a head start.
- Google wants you to trust it to rank sites properly, but he asks: "Do you really want to rely on Google to remove all of the spammy links?"
- His stance: "It is always better to be safe than sorry." Whatever attack is underway, it can be fixed, and you don't have to sit back and watch it happen.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: A practical SEO essay on paid link building: brands buy links to save time and keep pace with competitors, safety depends on vendor quality, and price is driven by link quality, niche, and brand strength. Fairly generic, with some self-promotion of Indexsy's niche edits.

chunks.heading: What link buying is and the forms it takes
chunks.text:
Jacky defines backlinking as getting other websites to link back to your site. It can be black hat, white hat, or somewhere in between, depending on how it is done, who does it and why.

Forms of buying backlinks he lists:
- Guest posts. He recommends Rhino Rank, Outreach Pete and FatJoe.
- Sponsored posts.
- Niche edits (link placement in existing content). He recommends Indexsy, which he says ranks #1 on Google for "niche edits".
- Product reviews.
- Paying for a link to be published on another site.

chunks.heading: Why brands buy backlinks
chunks.text:
Jacky gives three reasons: save time, get faster and better results, and keep up with competitors.

**Saves time.** Doing link building yourself through outreach is a long chain, even in the best case:
- Create high-quality content optimized for search.
- Prospect for opportunities and vet whether you qualify.
- Build rapport with each prospect and request the link.
- Wait for responses and customize content per site.
- Test different outreach approaches.
- Create content for approved sites, hiring a freelance writer if you have no in-house writers.
- Monitor and repeat.

If SEO, content and outreach are not your core business, this pulls you away from your primary work. He recommends outsourcing it to a provider devoted to link building.

**Faster, better results.** Outreach companies already have relationships with reputable bloggers in almost every niche. They have tested link building strategies and know which work for which industry. You then focus on content ideas, creation and optimization, and combined effort gets results faster.

**Competition.** If competitors buy high-quality links to rank, you may need to do the same to level the playing field. If you avoid it, they will be "miles ahead", rank better and grow their customer base. If your industry demands buying links, keep up with the trend.

chunks.heading: Is buying backlinks safe?
chunks.text:
Jacky's position is nuanced:
- Buying links is safe when the provider follows a white hat approach and industry best practices. A skilled provider will protect your safety and privacy.
- He also states plainly that buying links is black hat SEO because it goes against Google's TOS. Because the line is thin and SEO is increasingly competitive, he still urges getting links only from reputable brands.
- Avoid low-quality, cheap, irrelevant and non-niche-specific links. Links from PBNs (private blog networks) hurt your profile, are easily detected by Google and can jeopardize your site.
- Trust only providers with proven track records and integrity who help you gain an edge without compromising your site.

chunks.heading: How to vet a link seller
chunks.text:
Jacky's checklist for a link selling site or vendor:

1. **Clear information on link types.** A good vendor explains the types of links in layman's language, explains how to stay within Google's TOS, and has a support team to answer doubts. If all you see is sales hype about being number one in search results, be careful. You may be duped and they may not follow best practices.
2. **Quality backlinks.** Check the vendor's own site: DR, DA and Google rankings. Check whether links on their sites look natural or forced. Read their policies and terms. A good brand talks about quality links rather than spam links and offers a guarantee.
3. **Long-term safety.** Black hat tactics may lift rankings in the short term, but reputable vendors do not use them. They emphasize practices that raise rankings steadily and keep your site safe over time.
4. **White label.** Prefer white label vendors, whose links and reports are unbranded and customizable. This matters for long-term well-being and for transferring or reselling.
5. **Affordability.** Compare prices and commit only to what you can afford. Do-follow and no-follow links do not cost the same, and paid links on high-authority sites cost more but can lift organic traffic and rankings. He adds that backlinks are not the only determinant of ranking.

chunks.heading: Where links come from and what you are actually buying
chunks.text:
Sellers of paid links include:
- Manual outreach
- PBNs disguising themselves as real sites
- Brokers
- Webmasters and contributors

What they sell:
- Guest blogging opportunities
- Features or interviews
- Contextual links on webpages
- Backlinks to existing content on the site
- Community posts
- PBNs

chunks.heading: What drives backlink pricing
chunks.text:
Jacky says there is no simple answer on cost. Six factors drive it:

1. **Link quality.** Older, high-domain-authority sites charge more and limit placements per month, often using higher prices to limit applicants. If you are a beginner without a big budget, they are not the place to pitch.
2. **Content.** Sites with excellent, optimized content have no trouble finding link partners, are picky, and their partners can be pricey. If your site is new, use SEO tools to measure it and hire excellent writers, which brings you closer to guest-post opportunities.
3. **Industry.** Niches where money flows fast cost more. Finance links are pricier than gardening links.
4. **Creative control.** Specifying rules, such as an exact anchor text, adds work to placement, so you pay more.
5. **Brand strength.** A renowned blog with many social shares and comments gets its outreach emails answered sooner and gets more offers. A new, unknown site waits longer and pays dearly for placements on high-quality domains.
6. **In-house costs.** If you skip freelance writers, staff time goes into content and outreach. Factor employee time into the true cost of links.

chunks.heading: Do backlinks still work, and how to make them work
chunks.text:
