Jacky says backlinks still work, citing Moz, whether paid or natural. Quality is what matters. A backlink is a vote of confidence signaling authority in your industry, and unnatural links can bring a Google penalty that hurts rankings significantly.

His rules for making links work:
- Get high-quality links from high-authority sites in your niche.
- Pair links with high-quality content optimized for search engines and your audience.
- Use links naturally, with informative anchor text.
- Check the authenticity and quality of vendors before buying.
- Understand the link types and which ones are likely to improve your profile and organic traffic.
- Watch trends in link building services and follow them.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Jacky Chou's beginner guide to guest posting as an SEO and growth tactic. It covers setting goals, finding and qualifying sites, pitching, writing, tracking results, and spammy practices that risk Google penalties.

chunks.heading: What guest posting is and what it does for SEO
chunks.text:
- Jacky defines guest posting (guest blogging) as writing and publishing articles for other sites, usually under your byline as a "guest author" or "contributor".
- Payment varies by publication. Some pay, and others give non-monetary rewards such as a link to your site or social accounts.
- He lists these SEO and growth benefits:
  - More organic traffic, because guest posts lift domain authority and rankings.
  - More brand visibility, from exposure to a larger audience on popular industry sites.
  - More backlinks, via the author bio or links inside the post body. He calls backlinks a crucial factor in search ranking.
  - Stronger topical authority, when posts on topics related to your site link back to relevant pages. Google evaluates a site's relevance to specific keywords to decide how high it ranks.
  - Higher-quality traffic, because people who click through from a guest post are more interested in what you offer and more likely to convert.
  - Relationships with other thought leaders, plus a promotional boost when the host shares the post with their network.

chunks.heading: Setting goals and finding guest post opportunities
chunks.text:
- Step 1: set the goal before you pitch. Goals include leads or sales, backlinks, visitors, and brand awareness.
- Not every guest post has to be about backlinks. One article can build awareness and sales and also strengthen your backlink profile.
- Step 2: find opportunities in four ways:
  - Contact influencers to see if they'd want your guest post.
  - Look for blog posts relevant to your industry.
  - Search online for sites that accept guest posts.
  - Check competitors' backlinks and try to secure guest posts on the same sites.
- He suggests Google search operators built on phrases like "accepting guest posts", "guest post", "guest post guidelines", "guest article" and "guest author".

chunks.heading: Qualifying guest posting sites
chunks.text:
Jacky says to vet a site before pitching it. His checks:
- High traffic.
- Good domain authority.
- Well-written, informative content.
- A site built for more than accepting guest posts. If every published post carries outbound links to random websites, it was most likely designed to sell links, and he recommends avoiding it.

He also warns against writing for unrelated websites. Their readers won't click through to you and the post won't help your rankings.

chunks.heading: Pitching and writing the guest post
chunks.text:
**What a pitch should include:**
- The type of article you want to write.
- A quick overview of the proposed article.
- Why you want to blog for that site.
- Why the article fits the site.
- How the site owner and readers benefit.
- How you plan to promote the piece if it's accepted.

A pitch that is well-crafted and customized to the site is more likely to be accepted.

**Writing rules:**
- One link to your domain in the author bio.
- A few contextual links to your site, thematically relevant to the pages they point to.
- The right anchor text, with no keyword stuffing.
- Fit the site, and use well-researched, high-quality content. He says the article reflects your brand and you want it to rank for its keywords.

chunks.heading: Promoting, measuring and iterating
chunks.text:
- Build backlinks to the guest post itself. This raises the post's PageRank and so the link equity it passes to your site through contextual links.
- Track results in Google Analytics:
  - Sales or leads generated from the guest post.
  - Visitors who reach your site from the article.
  - Changes in page authority and domain authority.
  - Changes in search rankings for the linked pages.
- Use the data to adjust future guest posts. Two warning signs he names: the post drives lots of visits to the host's site but little direct traffic to yours, or the lead quality differs from what you expected.
- Each new post should move you closer to your goals.

chunks.heading: Guest posting practices that risk Google penalties
chunks.text:
Jacky notes that guest blogging has been heavily manipulated and some practices have become spammy. He flags these as penalty risks:
- Posting repeatedly on the same few sites. Leaning too much on them can look spammy.
- Posting on low-authority sites, such as the flood of low-quality "news" sites that have poor editorial standards and sometimes accept weak posts for payment.
- Putting a half-dozen backlinks in the post body.
- Over-optimizing keywords in anchor text.
- Spinning content: slightly rewriting an already published piece to place it elsewhere for more backlinks.
- Writing weak content with little value, made only to get a link.
- Writing on a subject you don't know well enough to deliver value to the site's audience.

chunks.heading: Is guest posting black hat? Paid links and hosting guest posts
chunks.text:
- He says guest posting isn't black hat in itself, but newcomers can repeat black hat habits.
- Google doesn't support paid guest writing. He says you'll be penalized if Google finds that a guest blogger was compensated for your backlink.
- Links from gambling sites and other questionable sources can hurt SEO performance. He recommends learning Google's guidelines first.
- A backlink is a link from one site to another. A guest post is a post you write for someone else's site. Backlinks matter because they signal to Google that your site is valuable to others.
- He considers guest posting worth the effort because it reaches an established pool of readers who may visit your site for more.
- Accepting guest posts on your own site is, for him, a way to expand the site with little effort. Guest authors share and promote the content, which brings free promotion, social shares and referrals.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: A practical checklist of twelve channels and tactics an SEO agency can use to generate leads and win clients: directories, free audits, niching, forums and Q&A, social, speaking, pillar content, LinkedIn, partnerships, packaged pricing, testimonials, and email outreach. The theme is to show expertise, reduce risk for the buyer, and build trust before asking for money.

chunks.heading: Getting SEO clients: free audits as the opener
chunks.text:
- Jacky argues clients need to understand what they're buying before they pay, which is why a free audit works. It breaks the ice, introduces the services, and shows the depth of the agency's capabilities and experience.
- He notes the average SEO client knows they need help but not how badly or how urgently. The audit shows them, and gives the agency a natural moment to explain how it would fix things.
- Target businesses that neglect SEO, especially local businesses that rarely update their websites. Find them, run a free audit, and send it.
- When these clients see results, he says they come back each time they need SEO services and refer other companies.

chunks.heading: Positioning: niche down to stand out
chunks.text:
- Jacky says SEO is competitive and many agencies sell the same services, so an agency needs a strategy to show it delivers what a prospect is looking for.
- His main answer is to narrow the niche. Pick a specific industry based on your expertise or where you see profitable opportunity.
- If the agency is strong at technical SEO, make that specialty clear on the website.

chunks.heading: Finding clients where they ask for help
chunks.text:
- Jacky recommends going where prospects describe their SEO problems and helping there, which shows expertise and builds trust before any sale.
- Example: someone asks how to rank for a keyword. Take that keyword and offer to bring the site to the top. If they get results, the lead is far more likely to convert to a paying client.
- Places he lists:
  - SEO and business forums: BlackHatWorld, SEO Forum, the Moz community. Most people there aren't looking for paid services, so don't expect immediate money. Contribute in discussions and someone will eventually reach out.
  - Quora: you may not find paying clients at first, but good answers bring requests for help. Quality answers can also rank on Google and bring in more leads.
  - Facebook and LinkedIn groups, subreddits, YouTube channels: participate so the target audience recognizes you and contacts you when they need help.

chunks.heading: Building authority: content, social, LinkedIn and speaking
chunks.text:
- Content: post educational content regularly. He says this gives audiences new content, keywords, backlinks and social engagement. Basics he lists:
  - Keyword research, using the industry's key and trending terms in titles, subheadings and body.
  - H2, H3 and H4 headings so content is scannable and search engines understand it.
  - Links to other articles and sites, to improve usability and pass link juice.
  - Clear formatting so the value is easy to take in.
- Social media: prospects check whether an agency is active. Post useful SEO content, memes, opinions on the latest Google update, or videos explaining services.
- YouTube: he suggests a channel with informative videos, since videos can be optimized to rank and attract clients.
- LinkedIn: use it to educate, entertain and inspire. For outreach, he says to send "non-scammy" messages: mention something personal at the top, then give value in the first message.
- Conferences: speaking at marketing conferences isn't instant, but he calls it effective for the long term. After a talk, one or two people usually ask whether you offer SEO services. Meeting face to face builds trust fast.

chunks.heading: Partnerships and directories
chunks.text:
- Partner with design agencies and digital marketing agencies. Web designers often get asked about SEO by their clients, so a partner will refer those clients to you.
- List the agency on directory sites. Fill in as much information as possible and get customers to leave reviews on them. Some directories aren't worth the time, but most can be useful. Examples he names: Agency Spotter, Digital Agency Network and SEOBlog.com.

chunks.heading: Pricing and social proof
chunks.text:
- Jacky recommends offering monthly SEO packages. Most customers ask about pricing before starting, and transparent packages improve the odds of being chosen over competitors without them.
- Gather testimonials from current clients. He cites research that 72% of clients say positive reviews and testimonials help them trust a business, and 88% trust online reviews as much as personal recommendations.
- Video testimonials are best because they're more engaging than written ones. Written testimonials still give "social proof" if video isn't possible.

chunks.heading: Email outreach
chunks.text:
- Jacky calls email outreach one of the most reliable ways to generate leads, and says email remains one of the most practical ways to stay in touch with existing and potential clients.
- Cold email works well for some businesses, while others get better results from an opt-in approach. Opt-in means you're dealing with people who have shown active interest in your work.
- His closing advice: pay attention to every detail, deliver great work, and educate prospects about SEO with evidence. The more clients you want to onboard, the more work that takes.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Jacky Chou's guide to using AI for SEO: keyword research, link building, content generation, voice search and analytics prioritization. AI saves time and cuts manual errors, but output still needs human review and personalization. Google penalizes low-value content built to manipulate rankings, not AI origin itself.

chunks.heading: Where AI helps in the SEO workflow
chunks.text:
Jacky frames AI as a complement to traditional SEO, not a replacement: "AI SEO improves and complements traditional SEO practices." Its main value is automating manual, repetitive work so the process is faster, more accurate and cheaper, which he says matters most for small businesses with limited resources.

- **Fewer manual errors:** AI tools reduce costly mistakes such as picking the wrong keywords, under-using a target keyword, or writing on the wrong topics.
- **Strategy input:** AI surfaces insights about which topics a site is most likely to rank for.
- **Time saved:** it automates topic generation, keyword research and content promotion.

chunks.heading: Using AI for keyword research
chunks.text:
Jacky lists four ways AI speeds up keyword research:

- **Trends:** analyzes keyword data, spots the latest trends and suggests keywords likely to perform.
- **Suggestions:** proposes keywords you may not have considered.
- **Competition analysis:** finds less competitive keywords that are still relevant to the business.
- **Long-tail keywords:** identifies specific, relevant long-tail terms that drive targeted traffic.

chunks.heading: Using AI for link building
chunks.text:
He names three link-building uses for AI tools:

- Analyze your site and find relevant link-building opportunities.
- Monitor your backlinks and recommend ways to improve their quality.
- Analyze competitors' backlinks and suggest new opportunities.

chunks.heading: Content generation and voice search
chunks.text:
- Google's Search Quality Evaluator Guidelines say the highest-quality pages show the author's knowledge, authority and trustworthiness. Jacky ties content quality to that standard.
- Standards differ by content type: news should be in-depth, well-cited and accurate; artistic content original and unique; informational content comprehensive, accurate, clearly communicated and reflecting expert consensus.
- AI can automate parts of content work, such as improving internal linking or identifying authoritative articles on a topic.
- **Voice search (VSEO):** most voice searches are questions, so he recommends using AI tools to surface the questions searchers ask, then building content that answers them. He cites a stat that 57% of teenagers use voice search often, and a prediction that by 2030 voice searches will account for most consumer purchases.
- VSEO is "hypercompetitive" because voice assistants give one answer only, the one at the top of the SERPs.

chunks.heading: Prioritizing with analytics
chunks.text: AI-driven analytics can produce automatic insights on opportunities and anomalies, but people still decide which steps to take. Jacky's point: any SEO tool can recommend hundreds of low-value tasks, and it is more compelling to offer three recommendations that greatly boost the site's statistics.

chunks.heading: Limits of AI content
chunks.text:
He lists three weaknesses of AI-generated SEO content:

- **Reduced creativity:** it is hard to get a human touch, so content can be less engaging and less unique.
- **Lack of context and depth:** AI can imitate a tone but not the nuance, empathy or conversational depth that make writing relevant.
- **Lack of innovation:** output is based on existing data, so it struggles to produce new ideas and can lack common sense.

chunks.heading: Will AI content rank, and what Google allows
chunks.text:
- AI content can rank, but it needs human creativity and editing to be both engaging and search-friendly. AI tools are "not a substitute for human-written SEO content."
- Google doesn't ban AI content because of its origin. The problem is content that offers readers no value or is made to manipulate rankings.
- Per Google Search Central, spammy AI content includes: text that makes no sense to readers but contains SEO keywords; low-quality content with no reader value; AI content published without a human checker; and content with no concern for reader experience.
- His conclusion: publish meaningful, informative content and there is no reason for Google to penalize it.

chunks.heading: Review and personalize before publishing
chunks.text:
Jacky's manual checklist for AI-generated drafts:

- **Spelling and grammar:** AI suggestions can introduce errors or change a statement's meaning.
- **Writing style:** humans add nuance based on how the audience connects (ad copy, for example, doesn't need perfect grammar).
- **Tone:** make the content match the brand's emotion and voice.
- **Structure:** check headings, subheadings and flow; Google also checks for proper structure.
- **Context:** make sure every paragraph ties to the main idea and flows together.

Then personalize with real expertise, since "your perspective and real-world experience are what give your content value":

- Link to reliable sources that support your claims.
- In product reviews, add images and tell the story of how you used the product.
- In ads and social captions, bring in brand voice, human emotion and the right personas.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: A beginner's roadmap to becoming an SEO specialist. It covers how search engines work, the three ranking factors (relevance, authority, value), the four SEO categories, then learning by building a real site, specializing as a T-shaped SEO, and showing results in a portfolio.

chunks.heading: How Jacky frames what an SEO specialist does
chunks.text:
- SEO is fine-tuning a website to rank higher in search results and attract more targeted visitors.
- He cites that over 93% of internet activities begin with a search engine, and that 95% of search traffic comes from the first page.
- He says a good SEO doesn't just stuff keywords into content. They pick keywords that reach the intended audience while staying consistent with the searcher's intended query.
- He argues Google updates prioritize content that meets users' needs, so user experience matters.
- Core job responsibilities he lists:
  - **Keyword research:** classify user intent as informational, navigational, transactional or commercial, then use it to shape strategy or improve existing pages.
  - **Content strategy:** a long-term plan combining topics that satisfy intent with keyword research, including how content is distributed, promoted and measured, then repeated and improved based on results.
  - **Pay-per-click:** often managed alongside SEO. It does nothing for organic rankings, but the SEO tracks which terms convert and feeds that into the SEO plan.
  - **Website improvement:** reporting on campaign results, competitor sites and new SEO developments, with recommendations tied to company goals and resources.
  - **Performance review:** never create content or make changes without monitoring results.

chunks.heading: How search engines work (the foundation)
chunks.text:
- Search engines send "spiders" that locate pages and crawl their source code.
- Crawled pages are added to the index, a cached collection of pages. Google results come from this index, not real-time, which is why results return in milliseconds.
- Google's algorithm weighs hundreds of factors to return relevant results.
- Jacky says this understanding is a fundamental skill for any SEO.

chunks.heading: The three ranking factors to get right first
chunks.text:
Jacky warns that many people waste time perfecting minor factors. His advice: "Ensure you control significant elements before worrying about page speed and title tags."

- **Relevance:** the page must match what the searcher expects, not just the topic. Example: someone searching "how to make peanut butter" wants instructions, not products, which is why page one has blog content and no shopping results. Optimizing for search intent means answering the "why" behind the search.
- **Authority:** Google treats links as votes of confidence. The number of quality backlinks correlates with rankings. The best links come from sites with authority in their field and relevance to the linked content. His answer to low authority is mostly "building more links."
- **Value:** matching intent isn't enough. The content must deserve the top spot. Study the leading pages to learn from their successes and mistakes.

chunks.heading: The four SEO categories
chunks.text:
He compares SEO to a jigsaw puzzle where practitioners need to understand how the pieces interact.

1. **On-page SEO:** optimizing pages for rankings and organic traffic. Examples: keyword modifiers in title tags, engaging meta titles and descriptions, descriptive image alt tags, optimizing for search intent.
2. **Link building:** accumulating inbound links from other sites. They raise rankings and organic traffic and can also bring referral traffic.
3. **Technical SEO:** making the site good for users and easy for search engines to crawl and index. Examples: fix broken internal and external links, improve page performance, use canonical tags to avoid duplicate content, add hreflang tags for multilingual content, tune robots.txt for crawl efficiency, avoid thin indexable content.
4. **Keyword research:** finding the terms people search on Google. His rule of thumb is to target keywords with traffic potential (they drive traffic if you rank), business value (they can bring in clients) and low competitiveness. The best keyword strategy combines high search volume, click-through rate, business value and minimal ranking difficulty.

chunks.heading: Learn by doing: start your own website
chunks.text:
- His analogy: reading about golf helps, but you only win tournaments by picking up clubs and practicing. Theory matters, but "nothing beats getting your hands dirty."
- Steps:
  1. Pick a subject you're passionate about.
  2. Get hosting and a domain.
  3. Build a simple website.
  4. Create content.
  5. Apply your SEO knowledge: optimize content, build a few links, and make the site technically sound.
- The more you repeat this, the more SEO you learn.
- Writing content takes the longest of all the tasks. Outsourcing it is fine if you have the resources, but give writers specific guidelines so the output is optimized for search.

chunks.heading: Specialize and build proof
chunks.text:
- **Be T-shaped:** SEO is too broad to master everything. Link building and technical SEO have so little overlap that improving one doesn't improve the other. A T-shaped SEO is strong in one area with broad knowledge of the rest.
- You can still make a living offering SEO to all kinds of companies, but he says you'll have more success specializing. Choose a niche that can at least break even and still holds your interest.
- **Courses:** certification isn't required for most SEO roles, but fundamentals (how search engines work, HTML, key ranking factors) help, and they prepare you for advanced work in keywords, content marketing, link building and technical optimization. Free or low-cost options he lists: UC Davis SEO Specialization (Coursera), HubSpot's SEO Certification, and Google's Fundamentals of Digital Marketing Certification.
- **Portfolio:** compile your work, including course projects, into a portfolio that accurately reflects your abilities. Show the results of the SEO tactics you tried and include stats and numbers so hiring managers can see where you excelled.

chunks.heading: Why learn SEO yourself
chunks.text:
Benefits he lists:

- **Traffic and rankings:** you can use increased rankings and search traffic to make money blogging or build an online business.
- **Less agency reliance:** in-house SEO expertise lets you grow without outside help.
- **Cost savings:** bloggers and solo operators save significant money by doing SEO themselves.
- **Better hiring:** knowing SEO lets you judge what's in an agency's packages and whether their recommendations will genuinely help rankings.
- **Not optional:** sites not built with SEO in mind struggle to survive in a competitive internet. He calls SEO and search engines "the best investment you can always make" for your business and personal skills, since both are "here to stay for years."
